abortiporus-biennis:
A rosette-forming bracket fungus, pinkish-white with a wavy margin, that stains reddish brown when bruised or old. It usually grows at the base of hardwoods (especially oak) or from buried roots, causing a white rot. Sometimes it develops as misshapen, coral-like masses.
The flesh is tough with a sour smell; it is not eaten.
agaricus-abruptibulbus:
A ringed, whitish champignon whose stem base is abruptly swollen (bulbous). It bruises yellow slowly and has a sweet, aniseed-like smell. It usually grows in woodland on leaf and needle litter.
It is regarded as edible, but because the yellow-staining champignons include poisonous species such as Agaricus xanthodermus, never collect it without checking the smell of the stem base (phenol/ink).
agaricus-albolutescens:
A moderate-sized, stocky champignon that bruises slowly but persistently yellow (amber) and has a pleasant smell. It is a saprotroph of grassland and open woodland.
It is regarded as edible, but because yellow-staining champignons can be confused with poisonous species, always check for a phenol-like smell.
agaricus-arvensis:
The horse mushroom is a large champignon with a cap that can exceed 20 cm, a double-layered ring and a white to cream colour. It yellows when touched, smells of aniseed and almond, and its gills turn from grey-white to chocolate brown with age. It appears in meadows, pastures and woodland edges after summer and autumn rain.
A tasty edible, but it can be confused with the poisonous Agaricus xanthodermus (phenol-smelling stem base) and with deadly Amanita species whose gills stay white, so check gill colour and stem base.
agaricus-augustus:
The prince is a big champignon recognised by its large cap covered in golden-brown scales, its skirt-like ring and its almond smell. It appears in coniferous and mixed woods and along roadsides in summer and autumn.
It is considered very tasty, but it can accumulate heavy metals such as cadmium, so frequent or large meals are not advised. Check for the almond smell to avoid confusion with yellow-staining champignons.
agaricus-benesii:
A champignon of the genus Agaricus distinguished by a white cap and known in English as the mull mushroom. It is a saprotroph.
It is regarded as edible, but because the genus also contains poisonous species, do not eat it without checking for staining and a phenol smell.
agaricus-bernardii:
One of the few champignons that love salty ground: it grows on sea shores, salt-marsh edges and salted roadsides. It has a thick, short stem and a thick-fleshed, cracked cap, and the flesh turns pinkish red when cut.
It is edible and tasty, with a distinctive salty, sea-like smell.
agaricus-bisporus:
The button mushroom is the most widely cultivated mushroom in the world and the most commonly sold in Turkish supermarkets. Native to grasslands of Eurasia and North America, it has been grown in France since the 17th century. The same species is sold as white button, brown cremini and large portobello depending on age and colour.
It is grown on compost under controlled humidity and temperature. It can be eaten raw, and cooking brings out its flavour; it is low in calories.
It also occurs wild in grassland and manured ground, but wild specimens can be confused with poisonous champignons.
agaricus-bitorquis:
Also known as the pavement mushroom, it is strong enough to push up compacted soil and even asphalt. It is recognised by its short, stocky, whitish form and a double ring on the stem. It appears along roadsides, in parks and gardens in spring and autumn.
It is edible and tasty, but mushrooms growing beside roads can accumulate exhaust and heavy metals, so choose the collecting spot carefully.
agaricus-buckmacadooi:
A champignon from the Pacific coast of North America that is regarded as poisonous.
Poisonous Agaricus species typically cause stomach and bowel upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea) and resemble edible ones, so do not eat it.
agaricus-campestris:
The field mushroom is a well-known champignon with a white cap and gills that turn from pink to chocolate brown. The stem has a single thin ring, and the flesh does not yellow when cut. It appears from late spring to autumn, especially after rain, in meadows, pastures and manured grassland.
A good edible collected for centuries. It can be confused with deadly Amanita species whose gills stay white (such as A. virosa and A. verna) and with yellow-staining poisonous champignons. Pink-to-brown gills and no volva (sac) at the stem base are the key checks.
agaricus-comtulus:
A small, delicate champignon described by the Swedish mycologist Elias Fries in 1838 and known in English as the ornamented mushroom.
It is regarded as edible but small and of little value; identification should be confirmed because of the risk of confusion with similar champignons.
agaricus-crocodilinus:
A large champignon also called the macro mushroom. It is a saprotroph.
It is regarded as edible, but because the genus includes poisonous species, check for staining and smell.
agaricus-cupreobrunneus:
An edible champignon known as the wet mushroom or brown field mushroom. It resembles the field mushroom (A. campestris) and grows in meadows and pastures.
Check for pink-to-brown gills and for the absence of the volva found on deadly Amanita species.
agaricus-deardorffensis:
A poisonous champignon that is common in the Pacific Northwest of North America.
Poisonous champignons cause gastrointestinal poisoning and can be mistaken for edible ones, so they should not be collected for eating.
agaricus-dulcidulus:
A small champignon found in the deciduous woods of Europe and recorded elsewhere. It is recognised by its pinkish-brown scales and small size.
It is regarded as edible but is small and of little value; it must be told apart from similar poisonous champignons.
agaricus-fuscofibrillosus:
A champignon with a dusky cap whose flesh can redden when cut, also called the bleeding agaricus.
It is regarded as edible; because the genus includes poisonous species, careful identification is needed.
agaricus-hondensis:
A champignon named for its felty ring, found on the Pacific coast of North America and related to the yellow-staining poisonous Agaricus species.
It should not be eaten, as it can cause gastrointestinal poisoning.
agaricus-impudicus:
A champignon (the tufted wood mushroom) that can be found in tufts in wooded places, especially coniferous forests.
It is regarded as edible, but because the genus contains poisonous species, identification must be confirmed.
agaricus-langei:
A scaly-capped champignon of woodland (the scaly wood mushroom) whose flesh can turn reddish when cut.
It is regarded as edible; check smell and colour changes to separate it from poisonous yellow-staining champignons.
agaricus-lilaceps:
The giant cypress agaricus is a very large champignon that grows especially under cypress trees. Apart from its size it resembles other big champignons in cap and ring.
It is regarded as edible.
agaricus-macrosporus:
A large-spored champignon (the macro mushroom) belonging to the group of big champignons of grassland and open ground.
It is regarded as edible; check smell and colour changes to separate it from look-alikes.
agaricus-moelleri:
The inky mushroom is recognised by its dark grey-brown scaly cap and a stem that yellows when cut, with a phenol (carbolic) or ink smell. It is common in European woods, parks and lawns and is also listed among poisonous mushrooms in Türkiye.
It causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, and because it resembles edible champignons it is a frequent cause of poisoning.
agaricus-pattersoniae:
A champignon found in North America in association with cypress trees.
It is regarded as edible, but identification should be confirmed because the genus also contains poisonous species.
agaricus-perobscurus:
Known as the princess, this is a choice edible champignon that resembles the prince (A. augustus) in its large cap and smell. It grows in woodland in North America.
It is regarded as edible; confirm identification to avoid confusion with look-alikes.
agaricus-pilatianus:
A rare poisonous champignon of Europe. It is white to cream and changes colour when cut or bruised.
It should not be eaten, as it can cause gastrointestinal poisoning.
agaricus-placomyces:
A poisonous champignon of North America that closely resembles edible ones; its cap has darker grey-brown scales towards the centre.
It causes gastrointestinal poisoning, so do not eat it.
agaricus-pocillator:
A champignon of woodland in southeastern North America.
It is not regarded as edible and can be confused with poisonous look-alikes.
agaricus-subrufescens:
The almond mushroom is a champignon originally from Brazil, known for its strong almond smell and also called Agaricus blazei or A. brasiliensis. It is cultivated for its flavour and sold as a food supplement; its health claims are not yet well proven.
It is eaten cooked and sold both dried and fresh.
agaricus-sylvicola:
The wood mushroom is a slender, aniseed-scented champignon that yellows when cut or touched. It grows in coniferous and mixed woods.
It is regarded as edible; it differs from poisonous yellow-staining champignons by smell (aniseed versus phenol), so sniff carefully.
agaricus-urinascens:
A very large champignon with a cap up to 30 cm and a stem up to 12 cm thick (the macro mushroom). It fruits in clusters in grassland and open ground.
It is regarded as edible and easy to recognise by its size, but identification should still be confirmed.
agaricus-xanthodermus:
The yellow stainer is a poisonous champignon that looks very much like the field mushroom. Its key feature is that the stem base turns chrome yellow immediately when cut or scratched, and it gives off a phenol (medicine or ink) smell, especially when cooked. It is common in parks, gardens, lawns and woods in summer and autumn.
It causes nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and dizziness; it does not affect everyone but is a risky species and a frequent cause of poisonings when mistaken for edible champignons.
agrocybe-pediades:
A small, honey-brown-capped mushroom of lawns, pastures and manured ground (the common fieldcap), with a brown spore print.
Eating it is not recommended: small brown-spored mushrooms include deadly Galerina and Conocybe species, so confusion risk is high.
agrocybe-praecox:
The spring agrocybe is a ringed, cream-to-brown mushroom that fruits in spring on wood chips, mulch, gardens and lawns, with a flour-like smell.
It is regarded as edible but of low value, and can be confused with poisonous and deadly brown-spored mushrooms (Galerina, Hebeloma, Cortinarius).
agrocybe-rivulosa:
The wrinkled fieldcap is a recently spreading species first recorded in 2003. It usually grows on wood chips and mulch.
It is regarded as edible; identify it carefully because of brown-spored look-alikes.
albatrellopsis-confluens:
The fused polypore grows on the ground in clusters, cream to orange-tinted, with several fruit bodies joined at the base. It forms mycorrhizae with conifers.
It is regarded as edible but can be bitter; young specimens are preferred.
albatrellus-ovinus:
The sheep polypore grows on the ground in coniferous forests of Europe and North America, white to cream, singly or in groups. Despite the name 'polypore' it is not a wood-rotter: it forms mycorrhizae with tree roots.
It is regarded as edible; it yellows and loses flavour with age.
albatrellus-subrubescens:
A whitish-pale mushroom growing on the ground in coniferous forests that yellows or reddens on touch.
It is regarded as poisonous and should not be eaten.
aleuria-aurantia:
The orange peel fungus looks like a discarded piece of orange peel with its bright orange, cup-shaped body. It appears on bare soil, paths and gravel in autumn and is a saprotroph.
It is regarded as edible but is bland; eating it cooked is safer.
alloclavaria-purpurea:
The purple club coral grows in clusters on the mossy floor of coniferous woods as slender purple-amethyst clubs.
It is regarded as edible but of low value.
amanita-arocheae:
The Latin American death cap is a deadly poisonous Amanita found in Colombia, Central America and nearby regions.
Mushrooms like this one containing amatoxins are especially dangerous because symptoms start late; urgent medical help is needed.
amanita-basii:
A relative of Caesar's mushroom (A. caesarea) found in Mexico, with an orange-red cap, that is eaten locally.
Because of the risk of confusion with deadly members of the genus, only local experts should identify it.
amanita-battarrae:
The grey-zoned ringless amanita is a grey-brown Amanita with a zoned cap margin, found in autumn in Italy and eastern Europe; it has no ring and a sac-like volva at the base.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
amanita-bisporigera:
The eastern destroying angel is a pure-white, ringed, sheath-volva, deadly poisonous Amanita that fruits in eastern North American deciduous woods in summer and autumn; like the death cap it contains amatoxins. Its name comes from its basidia usually bearing two spores.
Symptoms start 6–24 hours late and can lead to liver failure. It is mistaken for white champignons and field mushrooms; if in doubt, go to the emergency room at once.
amanita-caesarea:
Caesar's mushroom (in Turkish 'imparator mantarı', locally also 'yumurta', 'gelincik', 'paşa' or 'padişah mantarı') is an Amanita recognised by its striking look: an orange-red cap with a striate edge, yellow gills, a yellow stem and ring, and a white, sac-like volva. It is named for being eaten at the tables of emperors in Ancient Rome. It occurs in southern Europe and North Africa, and in Türkiye too, in oak, linden and chestnut woods, at forest edges and at the edges of hazelnut orchards towards late summer. It likes warmth and is mycorrhizal.
It is a very good edible and a rarity in the genus Amanita. Young specimens at the 'egg' stage are eaten raw or cooked in Italy as 'ovolo'.
Important warning: confusing it with the poisonous fly agaric (A. muscaria; white stem and gills) and the deadly death cap (A. phalloides) can cause deaths. Caesar's mushroom has yellow gills and stem; the young 'egg' stage also looks like other Amanita eggs, so it should only be eaten with expert confirmation.
amanita-calyptroderma: The Pacific amanita, or 'coccora', is a large white-spored Amanita that forms mycorrhizae with oak and conifers in the Sierra Nevada and Pacific coastal regions. It has an orange-brown cap and a white, sac-like volva. It is collected as an edible locally, but because deadly species occur in this genus many foragers avoid it.
amanita-caojizong:
Chiu's false death cap is an Amanita of East Asia, especially China. In some districts it is eaten locally, but it resembles deadly death caps and is therefore very risky.
Never eat it without expert confirmation.
amanita-ceciliae:
The snakeskin grisette is a ringless Amanita: its grey-brown cap is covered in dark grey warty remnants and the stem base has a sac-like volva. It is mycorrhizal and fruits in coniferous and deciduous woods in summer and autumn.
It is regarded as edible only when thoroughly cooked (it is poisonous raw), but because of the risk of confusion with deadly relatives it is not recommended for beginners.
amanita-chrysoblema:
A poisonous Amanita known as a white variant of the American fly agaric; despite its name, effects close to those of the fly agaric (hallucinations, nervous system symptoms) are expected.
It should not be eaten.
amanita-citrina:
The false death cap is a common Amanita with a pale lemon-greenish-yellow cap and a distinct round, rimmed bulb at the stem base. It smells of raw potato, which separates it from the death cap (A. phalloides). It fruits in coniferous and deciduous woods in summer and autumn.
It is inedible and may contain mildly toxic compounds. Because it resembles deadly mushrooms, do not eat it.
amanita-codinae:
An Amanita found around the Mediterranean with a whitish to pale brown cap.
Because of the risk of confusion with deadly members of the genus, eating it is not recommended.
amanita-cokeri:
Coker's amanita (the solitary lepidella) is a large, white, scaly Amanita of eastern North America. It is regarded as poisonous.
It should not be eaten; white Amanita species can be deadly.
amanita-crenulata:
The poison champagne amanita is a very common Amanita of the northeastern United States. It is poisonous.
It should not be eaten.
amanita-crocea:
The saffron ringless amanita is common in Europe, with an orange-saffron cap, no ring on the stem and a sac-like volva at the base. Although regarded as edible when cooked, sources disagree, and some list it as poisonous.
Because of the risk of confusion with deadly Amanitas, eating it is not recommended.
amanita-echinocephala:
The solitary amanita is recognised by its large, whitish-ivory cap covered in spiny, warty scales. It grows on limy soils in warm woods. In Türkiye it appears in the list of poisonous mushrooms under its synonym Amanita solitaria.
It should not be eaten.
amanita-eliae:
An inedible Amanita of Europe, described by Lucien Quélet in 1872.
It should not be eaten, so as not to be confused with deadly Amanitas.
amanita-elliptosperma:
Atkinson's destroying angel is one of the deadly poisonous members of the genus Amanita and contains amatoxins. Its white colour is typical of this group.
Symptoms start 6–24 hours late and can progress to liver failure; go to the emergency room at once if in doubt.
amanita-excelsa:
The European false blushing amanita (grey spotted amanita) has a grey-brown cap covered in grey warts, a grooved ring and a bulbous stem base. It fruits in woods in summer and autumn.
It is regarded as poisonous and resembles the panther cap, so it should not be eaten.
amanita-exitialis:
The Guangzhou destroying angel is a deadly poisonous Amanita of eastern Asia containing amatoxins.
Because symptoms start late, it is extremely dangerous.
amanita-farinosa:
The floury amanita is a small to medium grey-brown Amanita of eastern North America with a striate cap margin and a floury powder coat.
It is regarded as poisonous and should not be eaten.
amanita-flavella:
A mycorrhizal Amanita with a convex lemon-yellow cap up to 9 cm across.
It is regarded as poisonous and should not be eaten.
amanita-franchetii:
Franchet's amanita is recognised by its yellow-brown cap, yellowish veil remnants and yellowish ring. It fruits in deciduous and mixed woods of Europe and North America in summer and autumn and is also in Turkish lists of poisonous mushrooms.
It is an inedible species.
amanita-fuliginea:
The East Asian brown death cap is a deadly poisonous Amanita containing amatoxins. Its smoky brown cap resembles other death caps.
Because symptoms start late, it is extremely dangerous.
amanita-fulva:
The tawny grisette is a ringless Amanita with an orange-brown cap, a striate margin and a white sac-like volva at the stem base. It occurs in woods of Europe and North America in summer and autumn, under birch and conifers.
Although its toxins are said to disappear when cooked, it is poisonous raw and sources such as Mantarlı Yaşam do not recommend eating it. Ringless Amanitas can also be confused with deadly species.
amanita-gemmata:
The gemmed (jonquil) amanita has a pale yellow cap covered in white warts. It occurs in sandy soils in coniferous and deciduous woods in Europe and North America. Like the panther cap and fly agaric it contains ibotenic acid and muscimol.
It is poisonous and affects the nervous system. It should not be eaten.
amanita-hygroscopica:
The pink-gilled destroying angel is a deadly poisonous Amanita containing amatoxins.
Symptoms start late and can lead to liver failure; go to the emergency room if in doubt.
amanita-jacksonii:
Jackson's slender amanita (the American Caesar) grows in eastern North America with a bright orange-red cap, a striate margin and a white sac volva. It is regarded as edible and is related to Caesar's mushroom (A. caesarea).
It can be confused with the fly agaric, which has an unstriate cap margin, a ring on the stem and a bulbous base.
amanita-magnivelaris:
The great felt skirt destroying angel is a highly toxic Amanita containing deadly amatoxins.
Symptoms start late; go to the emergency room at once if in doubt.
amanita-muscaria:
The fly agaric is the world's most famous poisonous mushroom, known from fairy tales, cartoons and illustrations for its red cap with white warts. Young mushrooms are egg-shaped; the cap reaches 5–22 cm, the gills are white, and the stem bears a ring and volva remnants. It forms mycorrhizae with birch, pine, spruce and fir and fruits from midsummer to late autumn, often in rings.
Its ibotenic acid and muscimol act on the nervous system: intoxication, confusion, delusions and hallucinations, agitation and clouded consciousness may occur; death is rare but poisoning is serious. The name comes from its use to stupefy flies.
When rain washes off its spots it can be confused with the edible Caesar's mushroom (A. caesarea), whose stem and gills are yellow.
amanita-neo-ovoidea:
An Amanita found in China and Japan that is regarded as poisonous.
It should not be eaten.
amanita-nivalis:
The snow ringless amanita (mountain grisette) is a small, ringless Amanita of high mountains and the alpine belt. It is whitish at first, then the cap takes on grey and pinkish tones.
It is regarded as poisonous and should not be eaten.
amanita-ocreata:
The western North American destroying angel grows under oak on the Pacific coast and is a white, deadly poisonous Amanita that may take on a yellowish tint. Like the death cap (A. phalloides) it contains amatoxins; its appearance in spring is notable.
Symptoms start 6–24 hours late and lead to liver and kidney damage. It can be mistaken for edible white mushrooms such as champignons.
amanita-ovoidea:
The bearded amanita, or European white egg, is a large, entirely white Amanita with cottony fragments on the stem and cap margin. It grows in oak and pine woods around the Mediterranean and is eaten in some districts.
The risk of confusion with deadly white Amanitas (A. virosa, A. verna) is very high; it is definitely not recommended for beginners.
amanita-pachycolea:
The western grisette is a large, ringless, dark-brown-capped Amanita of the Pacific coast, regarded as edible when cooked.
Because of the risk of confusion with deadly Amanitas, it is not recommended for beginners.
amanita-pantherina:
The panther cap has a dark milky-brown cap covered in white warts of different sizes. The stem is white, with a swollen base wrapped in a rimmed volva, and two ring remnants may be visible. It fruits in summer and autumn under pine, spruce and especially beech.
It is more dangerous than the fly agaric: ibotenic acid and muscimol are present in high amounts, and it can cause intoxication, convulsions, confusion and loss of consciousness. It can be confused with the blusher (A. rubescens) and with brown champignons.
amanita-persicina:
The peach-coloured fly agaric is an Amanita whose cap centre has a peachy tone. Like the fly agaric it contains compounds that act on the nervous system.
It is poisonous and should not be eaten.
amanita-phalloides:
The death cap is the deadly poisonous mushroom responsible for most mushroom deaths worldwide and reported to cause about 90–95% of fatal mushroom poisonings in Türkiye. The cap is 4–15 cm, olive-greenish yellow and radially fibrous; the gills are white and free; the stem has a ring and a white, sac-like volva at the base. It is mycorrhizal and fruits from late summer to autumn in oak, beech and chestnut forests.
Its amatoxins (α-amanitin) and phallotoxins are not destroyed by cooking, freezing or drying. Symptoms begin 6–24 hours after eating (severe vomiting and diarrhoea), followed by a deceptive improvement and then liver and kidney failure. About 20–25 grams can be lethal; there is no fully effective antidote, and treatment is given in hospital.
Most deaths result from confusion with the edible straw mushroom (Volvariella volvacea), Caesar's mushroom (A. caesarea) and some Russulas. If in doubt, go to the emergency room at once and keep a sample of the mushroom eaten.
amanita-porphyria:
The grey veiled amanita grows in coniferous woods with a grey-brown cap and a purple-grey ring. It is inedible and regarded as mildly poisonous, and is also in Turkish lists of poisonous mushrooms.
It should not be eaten.
amanita-proxima:
A deadly poisonous Amanita of France, Italy and Spain that can cause kidney failure.
It can be confused with other white Amanita species and must not be eaten.
amanita-pseudoporphyria:
Hongo's false death cap is a poisonous Amanita of East Asia that resembles the grey veiled amanita with its grey-brown cap.
It should not be eaten.
amanita-regalis:
The royal fly agaric (king of Sweden amanita) has a brown cap with white warts and grows in spruce forests of the north. Like the fly agaric it is poisonous and acts on the nervous system.
It should not be eaten.
amanita-rubescens:
The blusher is a ringed, fleshy Amanita whose flesh turns from pink to red when cut or bruised. The cap is pinkish brown and warty, and the ring is striate on top. It fruits in deciduous and coniferous woods in summer and autumn.
It is regarded as edible when thoroughly cooked but is poisonous raw (it contains a haemolytic compound). However, confusion with the very similar panther cap (A. pantherina) causes serious poisonings, so it is not recommended for beginners.
amanita-smithiana:
Smith's amanita grows in coniferous and deciduous woods and is a deadly poisonous Amanita that causes kidney failure. Symptoms start 2–12 hours after eating with nausea and vomiting and may progress to kidney failure within 2–6 days. Poisonings from mistaking it for the matsutake mushroom on the Pacific coast are known.
It must not be eaten.
amanita-sphaerobulbosa:
An Asian Amanita regarded as poisonous, with a round, onion-shaped stem base.
It should not be eaten; it can be confused with white Amanitas that may contain amatoxins.
amanita-strobiliformis:
The warted amanita is a rare, heat-loving and large Amanita of limy soils under deciduous trees (oak, linden). The cap is white and covered in large pyramid-shaped warts.
It is regarded as poisonous and should not be eaten.
amanita-subjunquillea:
The East Asian death cap is a deadly poisonous Amanita of East and Southeast Asia containing amatoxins.
Symptoms start late; go to the emergency room at once if in doubt.
amanita-submembranacea:
The olive amanita is a ringless Amanita native to Europe and North America.
It is regarded as poisonous and should not be eaten.
amanita-vaginata:
The grisette is a ringless Amanita with a grey cap, a striate cap margin and a sac-like white volva at the stem base. It fruits in woods in summer and autumn. In some countries it is eaten after thorough cooking; it is poisonous raw.
Because it lacks a ring, it risks being confused with deadly Amanitas (specimens that have lost their ring), so it is not recommended for beginners.
amanita-velosa:
The springtime amanita is a ringless Amanita with a salmon-orange cap that fruits in spring under oak in California and neighbouring regions. Although eaten locally, it requires great care because of the genus's dangers.
The risk of confusion with deadly Amanitas is high.
amanita-verna:
The spring death cap (fool's mushroom) is a pure-white, ringed and volva-bearing deadly poisonous Amanita seen in spring and early summer. Like the death cap it contains amatoxins.
Symptoms start 6–24 hours late and can progress to liver failure. It is a frequent cause of poisoning because it is mistaken for white champignons and the field mushroom.
amanita-virgineoides:
The false virgin's lepidella is an Asian Amanita with a white, scaly cap, regarded as poisonous.
White Amanitas can be deadly, so it should not be eaten.
amanita-virosa:
The European destroying angel is a pure-white, slender, ringed and sheathed-volva deadly poisonous Amanita. It fruits in late summer to autumn in coniferous and deciduous woods on acidic soils and is mycorrhizal, with a faintly sweetish smell.
Like the death cap (A. phalloides) it contains amatoxins: symptoms begin after 6–24 hours and lead to liver failure. It is a frequent cause of poisoning because it is mistaken for white champignons, field mushrooms and small puffballs.
Every white mushroom whose gills stay white is potentially deadly.
amanita-vittadinii:
Vittadini's lepidella is a large, white, scaly saprotroph of European grassland and gardens.
It is regarded as poisonous and, because it can be confused with white Amanitas, should not be eaten.
amanita-xanthocephala:
A colourful, ringless Amanita (the vermilion grisette) whose cap is in bright red-orange tones.
It is regarded as poisonous and should not be eaten.
amanita-xylinivolva:
The cottony volva amanita is an Amanita of the Colombian Andes.
It is regarded as poisonous and should not be eaten.
amanita-zambiana:
The Zambian slender Caesar is a ringed Amanita from Africa regarded as edible.
Because of the risk of confusion with deadly relatives, only local experts should identify it.
ampulloclitocybe-clavipes:
The club-foot is a grey-brown, funnel-shaped mushroom whose stem swells like a club at the base; the gills run down the stem. It fruits in woods in autumn in Europe and North America.
It is regarded as edible, but a disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, palpitations, nausea) when eaten with alcohol has been reported; do not eat it with alcohol.
armillaria-borealis:
The northern honey fungus is a honey fungus found in clusters on wood and at tree bases.
Some sources list it as poisonous; honey fungi are usually eaten well cooked, but there is no firm safety record for this species.
armillaria-ectypa:
The marsh honey fungus is a rare honey fungus growing in peatland and sphagnum bogs.
It is classed as inedible.
armillaria-gallica:
The French honey mushroom is a honey fungus with a yellowish-brown cap and a ring, fruiting in clusters at tree bases. It lives as a weak parasite on living trees and on dead wood and is common in the northern hemisphere.
It is eaten well cooked and can upset some people's stomachs. Because it can be confused with deadly wood-growing mushrooms such as Galerina marginata, check the spore print (white).
armillaria-luteobubalina:
The Australian honey fungus is an important root-rot pathogen of eucalypt forests.
Although regarded as edible in Australia, wood-growing look-alikes call for care.
armillaria-mellea:
The honey fungus (Armillaria mellea) has a honey-yellow to brown cap, a ring on the stem and fruits in clusters at tree bases and on stumps. It spreads through tree roots by black, bootlace-like rhizomorphs; it is a parasite causing root rot in living trees and also lives as a saprotroph on dead wood. It fruits abundantly in autumn after rain.
It is eaten well cooked; raw or undercooked it causes stomach and bowel upset, and some people cannot tolerate it even well cooked. Eat only a small amount the first time.
It can be confused with the deadly Galerina marginata (rusty-brown spore print) and the poisonous Hypholoma fasciculare; the honey fungus's spore print is white.
armillaria-ostoyae:
The dark honey fungus (A. solidipes) is a honey fungus that causes root rot in conifers. A single individual of about 9–10 km² has been found in Oregon, USA, one of the largest living things on Earth.
Young fruit bodies are regarded as edible when well cooked.
armillaria-tabescens:
The ringless honey mushroom is a honey fungus without a ring on the stem, usually fruiting in clusters at the base of oak trees.
It is regarded as edible when well cooked.
arrhenia-epichysium:
A very small mushroom with a small brown to dark grey cap growing on decaying wood.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
artomyces-pyxidatus:
The crown coral is a coral fungus whose branches fork into crown-shaped tips and which grows on dead poplar and aspen wood. It is cream-pink when young and turns brown with age.
Young specimens are regarded as edible and may taste slightly peppery.
ascocoryne-sarcoides:
Jelly drops form pink-purple, jelly-textured cushions on dead wood and are common saprotrophs.
It is inedible.
aseroe-rubra:
The anemone stinkhorn is recognised by its red, sea-anemone- or starfish-shaped arms and carrion-like smell. It is native to Australia and has spread to other continents. Flies are attracted to it and carry its spores.
It is inedible.
asterophora-lycoperdoides:
The star bearer is a small, rounded mushroom growing on decaying Russula and Lactarius mushrooms, covered in brown powdery spores.
It is inedible.
asterophora-parasitica:
A parasite that lives on other mushrooms (such as Russula).
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
astraeus-hygrometricus:
The hygroscopic (barometer) earthstar opens its arms in moist air and closes them when dry. It differs from true earthstars (Geastrum).
It is inedible; the young form is eaten in some places but is not recommended.
aurantiporus-fissilis:
The greasy bracket is a plant pathogen that causes rot in apple and other deciduous trees.
It is inedible.
aureoboletus-auriporus:
A bolete with golden pores found in woods in Europe and North America.
It is regarded as edible; since bitter and poisonous boletes exist, confirm the identification.
aureoboletus-flaviporus:
The viscid bolete has a sticky, slimy cap and yellow pores; until 2010 it was placed in the genus Boletus.
It is regarded as edible.
aureoboletus-innixus:
A bolete with a reddish-brown cap found in eastern North America.
It is regarded as edible.
aureoboletus-mirabilis:
The admirable bolete, or velvet top, is known for its velvety reddish-brown cap and grows on and around conifer stumps.
It is regarded as edible with a slightly sour taste.
aureoboletus-projectellus:
A bolete found in North America and, recently, in Europe, growing in coniferous woods.
It is regarded as edible.
aureoboletus-russellii:
The jagged-stemmed (Russell's) bolete is easy to recognise because its stem is covered in shaggy, net-like scales. It fruits in oak woods in summer and autumn.
It is regarded as edible.
auricularia-auricula-judae:
The wood ear is an ear-shaped, brown-purple, jelly-like mushroom. It grows on dead branches of elder and other deciduous trees and can be seen all year in mild, damp weather.
It is edible; in Chinese cooking it is dried, soaked and used for its crunchy texture in soups. It should be eaten cooked.
auricularia-cornea:
The hairy wood ear is a jelly fungus resembling an ear with a hairy outer surface, grown commercially in China.
It is eaten cooked and stored dried.
auricularia-mesenterica:
The tripe fungus forms semi-horizontal, zoned, hairy tiers on dead deciduous trees and is a jelly fungus.
It is regarded as edible but of low quality.
auriscalpium-vulgare:
The pinecone mushroom grows on buried pine cones, with a small, hairy, kidney-shaped cap and spines underneath.
It is inedible: very small with a tough texture.
baeospora-myosura:
The conifercone cap is a small mushroom fruiting in small groups on buried spruce and pine cones in autumn and winter.
It is regarded as edible but is not worth eating.
baorangia-bicolor:
The two-coloured (red and yellow) bolete has a red-pink cap, yellow pores and flesh that turns blue when cut. It grows in deciduous woods of eastern North America.
It is regarded as edible; the blue colour disappears when cooked.
battarrea-phalloides:
The desert drumstick is a rare mushroom with a tall, scaly, woody stem topped by a dusty cap, growing in dry, sandy soils.
It is inedible.
bisporella-citrina:
Yellow fairy cups are lemon-yellow, millimetre-sized cups that fruit by the hundred on dead wood.
They are inedible because they are so tiny.
bjerkandera-adusta:
The smoky polypore is a common bracket fungus with grey, smoky pores growing on dead wood of deciduous trees.
It is inedible with a tough texture.
bolbitius-titubans:
The yellow fieldcap is a bright yellow, very fragile and short-lived mushroom of manured lawns and pastures, found on every continent except Antarctica.
It is inedible.
boletinellus-merulioides:
The ash-tree bolete grows under ash trees and has wrinkled, gill-like pores; it is known to be linked with ash aphids.
It is regarded as edible but of low value.
boletopsis-grisea:
The grey falsebolete is a grey, fleshy, pored mushroom growing on the ground in pine woods.
It is regarded as edible but can be bitter.
boletus-aereus:
The queen bolete (dark cep, 'black head') is a prized bolete recognised by its dark bronze-brown cap and a net-like pattern on its stem. It fruits in summer and autumn under oak and chestnut in warm, limy regions and is much sought after around the Mediterranean. The flesh is firm, white and does not change colour when cut; its flavour is held to be even better than the cep (B. edulis).
It is edible and highly valued. It differs from look-alikes such as the bitter Tylopilus felleus by pore colour and net pattern.
boletus-auripes:
The butter-foot bolete has yellow pores and a yellow stem and occurs in eastern North America.
It is regarded as edible with a good flavour.
boletus-barrowsii:
The white king bolete is a cep relative known for its pale cap, growing under pine in North America (the southwest).
It is considered a choice edible.
boletus-edulis:
The cep (porcini) is one of the world's most sought-after wild mushrooms. The cap is 7–30 cm, chestnut brown and slightly sticky when wet; the stem is stout, barrel-shaped, with a white net pattern near the top; the pores are white at first, then yellow-olive. The flesh is white and does not turn blue when cut. It fruits after late-summer and autumn rain under pine, spruce, beech and oak; the Black Sea forests are especially rich.
With its nutty aroma it is eaten fresh, dried or frozen and is also exported from Türkiye. It is eaten by insect larvae as it ages, so young, sound specimens are preferred.
It differs from look-alikes such as the bitter Tylopilus felleus and the poisonous Rubroboletus satanas by pore colour and by whether the flesh changes colour when cut. The name 'ayı mantarı' is used in some sources for poisonous species too, so do not identify it by that name.
boletus-fibrillosus:
Known as the 'fib king', this cep relative was described from Mendocino, California.
It is regarded as edible.
boletus-hiratsukae:
An edible cep relative found in Japan, described by Eiji Nagasawa in 1994.
It forms mycorrhizae with tree roots.
boletus-mamorensis: An edible bolete native to Morocco, closely related to the queen bolete (B. aereus).
boletus-nobilis: The noble bolete is an edible cep relative of eastern North America.
boletus-nobilissimus:
An edible bolete long regarded as a variety of the European cep.
It forms mycorrhizae with deciduous trees and occurs in eastern North America.
boletus-pallidus: The pale bolete is an edible bolete described by Charles Frost in 1874.
boletus-pinetorum: An edible cep relative of pine forests, generally found in Fennoscandia.
boletus-pinophilus:
The pine bolete (pinewood king bolete) is a cep relative with a dark reddish-brown cap that grows especially in pine forests and is a very valuable edible like the cep. Pores that turn from white to yellow-olive and flesh that does not change when cut are key identification points.
It is eaten fresh or dried.
boletus-regineus: The queen bolete is a highly regarded edible cep relative found in southwestern North America.
boletus-reticulatus:
The summer cep (B. aestivalis) is a lighter, brown-beige-capped bolete whose entire stem is net-patterned. It is named for fruiting from early summer under oak, beech and chestnut.
A very valuable edible prepared like the cep. Check that the flesh does not change colour when cut and is not bitter.
boletus-rex-veris: The spring king bolete is a choice edible cep relative that fruits in spring in coniferous forests of western North America.
boletus-rubriceps: An edible bolete officially described in 2014, although it was known earlier.
boletus-rubroflammeus:
A red-capped poisonous bolete first described from Michigan in 1971 and found in eastern North America.
It should not be eaten, as it can cause gastrointestinal poisoning.
boletus-subvelutipes:
The red-mouth bolete has red pores that turn dark blue when touched and forms mycorrhizae with deciduous trees.
It is regarded as poisonous and should not be eaten.
boletus-tylopilopsis:
An edible bolete that resembles Tylopilus species in form.
Edible if not bitter; Tylopilus relatives are often bitter.
boletus-variipes: An edible bolete native to North America that forms mycorrhizae with hardwoods.
boletus-violaceofuscus:
A purple-brown-toned bolete native to China, described by W.F. Chiu in 1948.
It is regarded as edible.
bondarzewia-mesenterica:
Bondarzewia montana is a bracket fungus that forms giant rosettes at the base of conifers and oaks; its fused, layered bodies can exceed 20 kg.
Young, soft specimens can be eaten cooked.
bovista-nigrescens:
The brown puffball is a grassland mushroom that is round and white at first and turns dark brown-black with age.
It is edible while the inside is solid and pure white; yellowed or darkened ones are not eaten.
bovista-pila:
The tumbling puffball is a small puffball that dries, detaches from the ground and is blown about by the wind, scattering spores.
It is edible while the inside is white.
bovista-plumbea:
The paltry (tumbling) puffball is small, white when young and lead-grey in its outer skin with age, and it rolls in the wind when dry.
It is edible while the inside is white.
bovistella-utriformis:
The mosaic puffball (Handkea utriformis) is a large, convex puffball with a cracked surface pattern, fruiting in pastures and meadows in summer and autumn.
It is edible while the inside is white and firm.
buchwaldoboletus-lignicola:
The wood bolete grows on rotting coniferous wood in Europe and North America.
It is inedible.
bulgaria-inquinans:
The black bulgar (black jelly button) fruits in clusters on oak logs as rubbery, black, cup-shaped bodies that leave black stains on the hands.
It is inedible.
butyriboletus-appendiculatus:
The butter bolete has yellow pores, a red-brown-toned cap and a yellow, net-patterned stem, and it turns blue when cut. It grows under oak and beech on limy soils.
It is a very tasty edible.
butyriboletus-fechtneri: The pale bolete grows on limy soils in Europe and was formerly placed in Boletus; it is edible.
butyriboletus-floridanus: An edible bolete described by Rolf Singer in 1945 and found in Florida.
butyriboletus-frostii:
Frost's (apple) bolete has a red, glossy cap and red pores and turns blue when cut. It grows under oak in eastern North America.
It is regarded as edible when cooked.
butyriboletus-loyo: An edible bolete of South America (Chile) known locally as 'loyo'.
butyriboletus-regius:
The royal bolete (red-capped butter bolete) is a striking bolete with a pink-red cap and yellow pores. It fruits in summer and autumn in warm, limy deciduous woods of Europe.
It is considered a choice edible and turns blue when cut.
byssomerulius-corium:
The netted crust is a common thin, crust-like fungus on dead deciduous wood.
It is inedible.
byssonectria-fusispora:
A European fungus forming small, brightly coloured cups on the ground.
It is inedible.
caloboletus-calopus:
The bitter bolete has a red stem, a pale cap and flesh that turns blue; it is intensely bitter. It forms mycorrhizae with beech and conifers.
The bitterness is not removed by cooking; it is regarded as poisonous and not eaten, and it can ruin a dish of other mushrooms.
caloboletus-radicans:
The rooting bolete is a large, pale, bitter bolete that turns blue when cut. It grows under deciduous trees on limy soil in Europe.
Because it is bitter it is not eaten and is regarded as poisonous.
calocera-cornea:
The small staghorn is a bright yellow, small, rubbery, horn-shaped jelly fungus on dead wood.
It is inedible.
calocera-pallidospathulata:
The pale stagshorn is a pale, spatula-shaped jelly fungus on rotting wood.
It is inedible.
calocera-viscosa:
The yellow stagshorn is a bright yellow-orange, branching, rubbery fungus on rotting conifer stumps.
It is regarded as edible but is tasteless and tough.
calocybe-carnea:
A small grassland mushroom with a pink cap and white gills.
It is regarded as edible but is small and can be confused with similar poisonous mushrooms.
calocybe-gambosa:
St George's mushroom is named for fruiting around St George's Day (23 April). It is a cream-white, fleshy, mealy-smelling mushroom that grows in rings or arcs in grassland, under hedges and at woodland edges. Fruiting in spring is an important clue.
Its mealy, cucumber-like smell and flavour are loved, and it is one of the valued edibles of spring.
However it can be confused with the deadly Inocybe erubescens and the poisonous Entoloma sinuatum, both of which can appear in the same season. The pleasant mealy smell is the main way to tell it apart.
calocybe-indica:
The milky white mushroom is an all-white, sturdy mushroom native to India, cultivated in tropical climates and widely eaten in India.
Edible.
caloscypha-fulgens:
The orange cup is a small, orange-yellow cup fungus that appears in coniferous forests in spring after snowmelt and stains greenish blue when touched.
It is inedible.
calvatia-booniana:
The western giant puffball is a very large, cracked-surface puffball of western North America.
It is edible while the inside is entirely white.
calvatia-craniiformis:
The brain (skull-shaped) puffball is a large, beige-brown puffball with a depressed middle.
It is edible while the inside is white and solid.
calvatia-cyathiformis:
The purple-spored puffball is a large puffball whose inside turns purple-lilac with maturity.
It is edible while the inside is white; once the colour changes it is no longer eaten.
calvatia-gigantea:
The giant puffball is a huge puffball that can reach 30–50 cm or more across. It fruits in late summer and autumn in meadows, fields and woodland edges. Before maturity the inside is pure white and firm; with age it turns yellow, then olive-brown powdery spores. A single mushroom can produce billions of spores.
It is sliced and fried while the inside is pure white (the Turkish Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry also accepts the whole mushroom as food).
It can be confused with the young 'egg' stage of deadly Amanitas: cut the mushroom lengthwise; if you see the outline of a cap and stem inside, do not eat it, as it should be homogeneous white flesh only.
calvatia-pachyderma: The elephant-skin puffball is a medium-sized edible puffball with a thick, leathery outer skin.
calvatia-sculpta:
The sculpted (pyramid) puffball is covered in large pyramid-shaped spines and fruits in spring in the Sierra mountains and similar places.
It is edible while the inside is white.
candolleomyces-candolleanus:
The common brittlestem is a delicate mushroom with a pale brown cap and brittle stem, common on wood debris and lawns.
It is regarded as edible but is tiny and worthless, and can be confused with brown-spored poisonous mushrooms.
cantharellula-umbonata:
The grayling (humpback) has a slightly convex grey cap 2–5 cm across and gills that can redden when touched. It grows in mossy, damp places.
It is regarded as edible.
cantharellus-alborufescens:
A whitish-cream chanterelle found in Europe.
Edible and tasty.
cantharellus-amethysteus:
The amethyst chanterelle has a cap covered in violet-amethyst scales and occurs in deciduous woods in Europe.
Edible and tasty.
cantharellus-appalachiensis:
A chanterelle of eastern North America named after the Appalachian region.
It is a popular edible.
cantharellus-applanatus:
A chanterelle found in India, China, Japan and Korea.
It is regarded as edible.
cantharellus-cibarius:
The golden chanterelle (kantarel; in Turkish sarıkız, kazayağı, yumurta mantarı) is egg-yolk yellow, funnel-shaped, apricot-scented and one of the world's best-loved wild mushrooms. Instead of true gills it has vein-like ridges running from the stem onto the cap (false gills); the flesh is whitish-yellow and tears in strings when cut. It forms mycorrhizae with oak, beech, chestnut and conifers, so it cannot be cultivated and is only picked wild. It fruits abundantly from May to November, especially in rainy summers and autumns, in the humid forests of the central and western Black Sea.
It is eaten fresh or sautéed in butter, and its aroma and texture are prized when cooked. It toughens at high heat and should be cooked slowly.
It is confused with the poisonous Omphalotus olearius (jack-o'-lantern): that has true, sharp-edged gills, grows in tufts on stumps and is orange. The false chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca) also looks similar, but has orange, thin, forked gills.
cantharellus-cinereus:
The ashen (black) chanterelle is an ash-grey to black, funnel-shaped chanterelle related to the horn of plenty, found in woods.
Edible and tasty.
cantharellus-cinnabarinus:
The cinnabar (red) chanterelle is a small, bright red-pink chanterelle that fruits through summer in woods of eastern North America.
It is regarded as edible; being small, it is mostly mixed with other mushrooms.
cantharellus-concinnus:
A chanterelle of Australia that fruits in groups or clusters.
It is regarded as edible.
cantharellus-confluens:
A chanterelle of North America whose fruiting bodies often fuse together.
Edible.
cantharellus-enelensis:
A North American chanterelle discovered in 2017 as a member of the C. cibarius group.
Edible.
cantharellus-ferruginascens:
A yellow-orange chanterelle found in Europe.
Edible and tasty.
cantharellus-flavus:
The American golden (eastern yellow) chanterelle is a yellow chanterelle that fruits through summer under oak in eastern and midwestern North America.
Edible and tasty.
cantharellus-formosus:
The Pacific golden chanterelle is a commercially harvested chanterelle that fruits under spruce, fir and hemlock in the Pacific Northwest of North America, abundantly from autumn into winter.
Edible and much loved.
cantharellus-friesii:
The velvet (orange) chanterelle is a small chanterelle of Asia and Europe whose cap ranges from deep yellow to reddish orange.
Edible.
cantharellus-iuventateviridis:
A chanterelle of North America, assessed as 'data deficient' as of 2026.
Edible.
cantharellus-lateritius:
The smooth chanterelle is yellow and funnel-shaped like the golden chanterelle but with an almost smooth underside. It fruits under oak in eastern North America.
Edible and tasty, with an apricot smell.
cantharellus-lilacinus:
A species with lilac tones (also referred to as Cuphophyllus cheelii in older naming).
It is regarded as edible.
cantharellus-minor:
The small chanterelle of eastern North America is one of the smallest of the genus.
Edible, but of little value because of its size.
cantharellus-parvoflavus:
A small yellow chanterelle found in Mexico.
Edible.
cantharellus-persicinus:
The peach (pink) chanterelle is a pinkish chanterelle of the Appalachian region of eastern North America and is mycorrhizal like other chanterelles.
Edible.
cantharellus-phasmatis:
A North American chanterelle described as new to science in 2013.
Edible.
cantharellus-spectaculus:
A North American chanterelle described in the early 2010s.
Edible.
cantharellus-subalbidus:
The white chanterelle is a cream-white chanterelle of western North American conifer forests that bruises and darkens easily.
It is a popular edible.
cantharellus-subpruinosus: A European edible chanterelle formerly regarded as a variety of C. cibarius.
cantharellus-tabernensis:
A chanterelle described as new to science in 1996.
It is regarded as edible.
cantharellus-velutinus:
A chanterelle of North America with a velvety surface.
Edible.
catathelasma-imperiale:
The commander (imperial mushroom) is a large, thick-fleshed, brown-capped mushroom with a double ring on the stem, growing in coniferous forests. In the Carpathians it is known as 'korban'.
Edible.
cerioporus-leptocephalus:
The blackfoot polypore grows on dead deciduous wood with a black stem and a tough texture.
It is inedible.
cerioporus-squamosus:
The dryad's saddle (pheasant's back) is a large, scaly, cream-beige, fan-shaped bracket fungus on living or dead trunks of deciduous trees. It can grow very big and causes white rot in the tree; its smell resembles cucumber. It is seen in spring and early summer.
Only young, soft edge portions are edible, as it becomes woody with age. It should be identified carefully.
cerrena-unicolor:
The mossy maze polypore is a moss-green bracket fungus with maze-like pores growing on dead deciduous wood.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
chalciporus-piperatoides:
A small-pored, peppery-tasting bolete found in North American woodland.
It is regarded as edible and used sparingly as a seasoning.
chalciporus-piperatus:
The peppery bolete is a small bolete with a copper-brown cap, yellow-red pores and a hot, peppery taste. It fruits in summer and autumn under pine and birch.
It is not eaten because of its hotness, though dried it is sometimes used in small amounts as a pepper substitute.
chalciporus-rubinellus:
The purple-red bolete is a small bolete with purple-red pores found in coniferous woods.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
cheilymenia-fimicola:
The eyelash dung cup is a small orange cup fungus with eyelash-like margins that grows on dung.
It is inedible.
cheilymenia-granulata:
A very common European small orange cup fungus found on dung.
It is inedible.
cheilymenia-stercorea:
A cup fungus forming orange-red discs up to 3 cm across on dung.
It is inedible.
chlorociboria-aeruginascens:
The green elfcup stains rotting wood blue-green, and this stained wood was once used in wood inlay work (Tunbridge ware). Its fruit bodies are small emerald-green cups.
It is inedible.
chlorociboria-aeruginosa:
The green elfcup is a small cup fungus that stains rotting hardwood blue-green.
It is inedible.
chlorophyllum-molybdites:
The false parasol (green-spored parasol) is a poisonous mushroom that closely resembles the parasol mushroom but has greenish-grey gills and a green spore print. It grows on lawns, in parks and gardens in warm seasons; poisonings are common around the world, including in children.
It causes nausea, severe vomiting and diarrhoea; it is usually not fatal but causes a severe gastrointestinal poisoning. Checking the spore print (a green mark on paper) is the safest way to tell it apart.
chlorophyllum-rhacodes:
The shaggy parasol is shorter than the parasol mushroom (Macrolepiota procera), with a brown scaly cap and flesh that turns saffron-red when cut. It fruits in woodland and scrub edges in summer and autumn.
It is edible when well cooked, though it can upset some people's stomachs. It can be confused with the poisonous green-spored parasol; check the spore print (white).
chondrostereum-purpureum:
The silver leaf fungus causes silver leaf disease in cherry, plum, apple and other rose-family trees. It forms purple-tinged crusts on wood.
It is inedible.
chroogomphus-rutilus:
The brown slimecap (copper spike) grows under pine, with a copper-brown, slimy cap and yellowish-reddish flesh; it turns dark purple-black when cooked.
It is regarded as edible with a modest flavour; the slimy skin is peeled before cooking.
chroogomphus-tomentosus:
The woolly pine spike is a pine mushroom endemic to western North America, with an orange-brown, woolly cap.
It is regarded as edible.
chroogomphus-vinicolor:
The wine-cap chroogomphus grows in pine forests, with a wine-red-brown cap.
It is regarded as edible.
chrysomphalina-chrysophylla:
A small mushroom with bright golden-yellow gills found on decaying coniferous wood in the north temperate zone.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
ciboria-amentacea:
The catkin cup is a small, brown, stalked cup that grows in spring on fallen catkins of hazel, alder and similar trees.
It is inedible.
clathrus-columnatus:
The column stinkhorn emerges from an egg-shaped structure as 2–5 red-orange columns joined at the top and smells foul. It is a saprotroph.
It is inedible; the smell is bad.
clathrus-ruber:
The latticed stinkhorn is a red-orange, cage-like mushroom that emerges from an egg and smells of carrion. It occurs in gardens, on mulch and in woods around the Mediterranean and in other mild regions.
It is inedible; the smell attracts flies, which spread the spores.
clavaria-amoena:
The yellow coral fungus has slender, cylindrical, golden-yellow fruit bodies that grow in grassland and mossy places.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
clavaria-fragilis:
Fairy fingers (white worm coral) are white, thin, worm-shaped, brittle clubs that fruit in tufts in grassland and woods in autumn.
They are regarded as edible but bland.
clavaria-fumosa:
The smoky fairy club has grey, smoky-coloured, slender, tube-shaped clubs.
It is regarded as edible but worthless.
clavaria-zollingeri:
The violet coral is a bright violet-magenta, branched, coral-like fungus widely distributed in grassland and woods.
It is inedible despite its striking looks.
clavariadelphus-ligula:
The strap coral is an unbranched, strap- or club-shaped fungus growing in the litter of coniferous forests.
It is inedible: bitterish with a spongy texture.
clavariadelphus-pistillaris:
The common club coral is a large, club-shaped, yellowish-brown mushroom 5–25 cm tall. It fruits in beech forests in autumn and is rare.
It is regarded as edible but can be bitter; cook it well.
clavariadelphus-truncatus:
The truncate club coral is an orange-yellowish club with a flat, truncated top that grows in coniferous forests.
It is known for its sweetish taste and is regarded as edible.
claviceps-purpurea:
Ergot is a parasitic fungus that develops in the ears of rye, other cereals and wild grasses. Dark purple-black, horn-shaped hard bodies (sclerotia) replace the grains and contain ergot alkaloids.
It caused historic epidemics of ergotism (nervous disorders, convulsions, hallucinations and gangrene of the limbs), known in the Middle Ages as 'St Anthony's fire'. Today grain cleaning and inspection largely prevent it. Medicines (for migraine and postpartum bleeding) and LSD (Albert Hofmann, 1938) have been derived from these alkaloids.
It is highly poisonous and must never be eaten. If found in grain, the crop must not be consumed.
clavulina-amethystina:
The amethyst coral is a branched, purple-amethyst coral fungus.
It is regarded as edible.
clavulina-cinerea:
The gray (ashy) coral grows on forest floors with blunt, forked grey-ash branches.
It is regarded as edible with a modest flavour.
clavulina-coralloides:
The crested (white) coral fungus is a white-cream coral whose branch tips are crested, fruiting in woods in autumn.
It is regarded as edible but not especially tasty.
clavulina-rugosa:
The wrinkled coral is a white, unbranched or sparsely branched, wrinkled worm-shaped fungus found in woods.
It is regarded as edible but bland.
clavulinopsis-corniculata:
The meadow coral is a yellow, branched coral fungus growing in grassland.
It is inedible.
clavulinopsis-fusiformis:
Golden spindles are bright yellow, unbranched, spindle-shaped clubs fruiting in tufts in grassland and mossy places in autumn.
Sources disagree: some regard them as edible while ultimate-mushroom.com lists them as poisonous; do not eat.
clavulinopsis-helvola:
The yellow club is a yellow-orange, club-shaped fungus found in grassland.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
clavulinopsis-laeticolor:
The golden fairy club is a bright orange-yellow, slender, club-shaped fungus found in grassland and mossy places.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
clavulinopsis-umbrinella:
The beige coral is a coral mushroom that is white when young, then beige with brown tips.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
climacocystis-borealis:
A large, white, soft bracket fungus with a sour smell, growing on coniferous stumps.
It is inedible.
climacodon-septentrionalis:
The northern tooth fungus forms large, white, overlapping tiers with teeth underneath on living deciduous trees (especially maple), causing a white rot.
It is tough and not eaten.
clitocybe-agrestis:
A whitish funnel mushroom widespread in Europe, described by the Finnish mycologist Harmaja in 1969.
It is regarded as poisonous; some funnel mushrooms contain muscarine. Do not eat.
clitocybe-amoenolens:
The paralysis funnel is a funnel mushroom found around the Mediterranean. It has been reported to cause severe pain and redness (erythromelalgia) of the hands and feet lasting weeks after eating.
It must not be eaten.
clitocybe-dealbata:
The ivory funnel is a small, white, funnel-shaped mushroom of lawns and meadows. It contains muscarine.
It causes sweating, excess saliva, tears, slow pulse and blurred vision, and can occasionally be fatal. It forms rings in the same grass as the fairy ring mushroom (Marasmius oreades) and is confused with it, a frequent cause of poisoning.
clitocybe-fragrans:
The fragrant funnel is known for its sweet aniseed-like smell and grey-beige, funnel-shaped cap. It fruits in woods in autumn.
It is regarded as edible, but it has many poisonous (muscarine-containing) look-alikes, so it is not recommended.
clitocybe-maxima:
The large white clitocybe is a big, cream-beige, funnel-shaped Clitocybe with gills running down the stem.
It is regarded as edible; it is not recommended because it can be confused with poisonous funnel mushrooms.
clitocybe-nebularis:
The clouded agaric is a large mushroom with a grey, smoky cap that fruits in clusters and rings in late autumn. It has a strong, sweetish-sharp smell.
It is eaten cooked, but it clearly upsets some people's stomachs, and some sources therefore regard it as poisonous. Try only a small, well-cooked amount at first, and not with alcohol.
clitocybe-odora:
The aniseed toadstool is easily recognised by its blue-green colour and strong aniseed smell and fruits in woods in autumn.
Because of its smell it is also dried and used as a flavouring; it is regarded as edible.
clitocybe-phyllophila:
The frosty funnel grows in leaf litter and looks dusted with a white bloom. It contains muscarine.
It is poisonous and must not be eaten.
clitocybe-rivulosa:
The fool's funnel (false champignon) is a small, pale, funnel-shaped mushroom of lawns, often in the same places as the fairy ring mushroom. It contains high amounts of muscarine.
It causes sweating, salivation, blurred vision, slow heartbeat and breathing difficulty and can be fatal. It is confused with the fairy ring mushroom and the field mushroom.
clitocybe-vibecina:
The mealy funnel is a common, inedible funnel mushroom that often grows in rings on needle litter late in the year.
It should not be eaten.
clitopilus-prunulus:
The miller is known for its flour and fresh-dough smell: a white-grey, slightly funnel-shaped mushroom with gills running down the stem and a pinkish spore print. It fruits in woods and woodland edges in summer and autumn and is considered a good edible.
An important danger: it can be confused with the very similar, white-spored and poisonous (muscarine) Clitocybe dealbata; a pink spore print separates this species. The antibiotic class pleuromutilin was derived from this mushroom.
collybia-cirrhata:
The piggyback shanklet is a tiny white mushroom growing on decaying mushrooms.
It is inedible.
collybia-cookei:
The split-pea shanklet is a tiny mushroom with yellow sclerotia that grows on decaying mushrooms.
It is inedible.
collybia-tuberosa:
The lentil shanklet is a tiny mushroom growing on decaying mushrooms, with brown sclerotia that look like apple seeds.
It is inedible.
colus-hirudinosus:
The craypot stinkhorn is a red, cage-like mushroom found in Asia, Australia, North Africa and southern Europe.
It is inedible and smells foul.
colus-pusillus:
A small, cage-like stinkhorn found in Australia.
It is inedible.
conocybe-apala:
The dunce cap is a pale-white, conical-capped, very fragile and short-lived mushroom of lawns.
Do not eat it: some Conocybe species contain deadly amatoxins; do not collect small pale lawn mushrooms.
conocybe-cyanopus:
A small mushroom containing psychoactive indole alkaloids such as psilocybin and the rare aeruginascin.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
conocybe-rugosa:
The wrinkled conecap (Pholiotina rugosa) is a highly toxic mushroom found on lawns, in gardens and on wood chips across Eurasia and North America. It is small with a rusty-brown cap and a ring, and contains deadly amatoxins.
Symptoms are delayed and can lead to liver failure. It can be confused with other small brown, ringed mushrooms (such as the deadly Galerina marginata or edible look-alikes); never eat it.
conocybe-tenera:
The brown dunce cap is a slender, brown, conical-capped, fragile and short-lived mushroom of lawns and roadsides.
Do not eat it: some species of this genus contain deadly amatoxins.
conocybe-velutipes:
A small, bell-capped (8–22 mm) mushroom; some sources report that it contains psychoactive compounds.
It should not be eaten.
coprinellus-domesticus:
The domestic inky cap is a short-lived inky cap that grows on wood, even indoors, on an orange-brown, rug-like mat.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
coprinellus-impatiens:
The trooping inkcap is a short-lived inky cap that fruits in large groups.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
coprinellus-micaceus:
The mica cap is a honey-brown mushroom whose cap is covered, when young, in glistening mica-like granules, fruiting in clusters on buried hardwood from spring to autumn.
It can be eaten young, before it turns to ink; it melts quickly and should be cooked right after collecting.
coprinopsis-atramentaria:
The alcohol inky cap (tippler's bane) is a grey-brown, bell-capped mushroom that melts into black liquid with age. It fruits in clusters on lawns, around tree roots and on buried wood from spring to autumn.
Although edible on its own, a compound called coprine blocks alcohol breakdown: if alcohol is drunk within about 72 hours after eating it, a severe reaction with flushing of the face and neck, palpitations, nausea and sweating occurs; avoid alcohol before and after eating it.
coprinopsis-cinerea:
The gray shag is regarded as edible when young but must be eaten right after collecting. It is also an important laboratory model organism in fungal genetics.
It is found on buried wood and dung.
coprinopsis-lagopus:
The hare's foot inkcap is recognised by its white, woolly veil; it is a slender, very short-lived mushroom on wood chips and buried wood.
It is inedible.
coprinopsis-nivea:
The snowy inky cap is a small inky cap covered in white powder growing on dung.
It is regarded as edible but is worthless.
coprinopsis-picacea:
The magpie mushroom is a foul-smelling inky cap recognised by its black-and-white blotched cap. It occurs in beech woods on limy soils.
It is inedible.
coprinus-comatus:
The shaggy ink cap (shaggy mane) is a very distinctive mushroom with a tall, cylindrical, white cap covered in shaggy scales. It fruits from spring to autumn on lawns, roadsides and disturbed ground, and can even lift asphalt. The Turkish name comes from 'pösteki' (sheepskin).
With age it melts into black ink starting from the bottom. It is therefore collected only when young and fully white and cooked within a few hours; it has a light, delicate, soft taste.
A reaction with alcohol has been reported, so eating it without alcohol is safest.
coprinus-sterquilinus:
The midden ink cap is a short-lived inky cap that grows on animal dung.
It is inedible.
cordyceps-militaris:
The caterpillar fungus is an orange, club-shaped fungus that grows from buried insect pupae. It is used in traditional Asian medicine and cooking and is now cultivated commercially. The effects of its cordycepin are not yet well proven.
Cultivated fruit bodies are edible.
cortinarius-alboviolaceus:
The silvery-violet webcap is a Cortinarius with a pale violet-silver, bell-shaped cap. Although sometimes called edible, it is not definitely safe.
This genus includes kidney-damaging species; do not eat it.
cortinarius-anomalus:
The variable webcap is a medium-sized Cortinarius in purple-brown tones.
It is inedible; do not eat it because of the genus's risks.
cortinarius-armillatus:
The red-banded cort is a Cortinarius with brick-red bands on its stem, fruiting under birch.
It is inedible; do not eat it because of the genus's risks.
cortinarius-camphoratus:
The stinking (goatcheese) webcap is a pale violet-blue-toned Cortinarius of coniferous forests, known for its sharp smell of rotten goat's cheese or cabbage.
It is inedible; do not eat it because of the genus's risks.
cortinarius-caninus:
A Cortinarius with a cream-brown cap up to 9 cm and a sturdy stem.
It is inedible; do not eat it because of the genus's risks.
cortinarius-caperatus:
The gypsy mushroom (wrinkled cort) is a Cortinarius with a wrinkled, honey-brown cap dusted with a frosty bloom and a distinct ring on the stem. It fruits in autumn in acidic, mossy coniferous and birch forests and is a much-loved edible in northern and eastern Europe.
It must be cooked well. It can accumulate radioactive caesium and heavy metals, so it should not be picked in polluted areas. Because the genus Cortinarius includes deadly species, do not collect it unless with someone who knows it; the ring and rusty-brown spore print belong to this species but similar poisonous species exist.
cortinarius-cinnamomeus:
The cinnamon webcap is a small, slender Cortinarius with a bright orange-brown cap.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
cortinarius-collinitus:
The belted slimy cortinarius has a slimy, sticky cap and a stem banded with bluish-violet belts.
It is inedible.
cortinarius-delibutus:
The bluegill webcap is a Cortinarius with a yellow, slimy cap and bluish gills when young.
It is inedible; do not eat it because of the genus's risks.
cortinarius-flexipes:
The Pelargonium webcap is a small, brown Cortinarius of Europe and North America recognised by its geranium-like smell.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
cortinarius-glaucopus:
The blue-foot webcap is a Cortinarius with bluish tones on the stem and a bulbous base.
Although eaten in some districts, it is not recommended because of the genus's risks.
cortinarius-hemitrichus:
The frosty webcap is a Cortinarius whose young brown, conical cap is covered in white, frost-like fibres.
It is inedible.
cortinarius-mucosus:
The orange webcap (slimy cortinarius) is a Cortinarius with an orange-brown, very slimy cap growing in pine forests.
It is inedible; do not eat it because of the genus's risks.
cortinarius-orellanus:
The fool's webcap is a deadly poisonous Cortinarius with an orange-brown, scaly cap and rust-coloured gills. It fruits in autumn in deciduous woods on acidic soils and contains the kidney-damaging toxin orellanine.
Symptoms start very late: 2–3 days (sometimes up to 3 weeks) after eating, with thirst, nausea, vomiting and back pain, followed by kidney failure; dialysis or a kidney transplant may be needed. The toxin was discovered after a mass poisoning of hundreds of people in Poland in the 1950s.
Because edible Cortinarius species are very hard to tell apart, do not collect mushrooms from this genus.
cortinarius-praestans:
The goliath webcap is a very large Cortinarius with a reddish-chestnut cap that grows in beech woods on limy soils. It is rare and protected in some countries.
Although regarded as edible, it is not recommended because of the dangers of the genus Cortinarius.
cortinarius-purpurascens:
The bruising webcap is a Cortinarius that turns bluish purple when cut or touched.
Although listed as edible in some sources, it is not recommended because of the genus's risks.
cortinarius-rainierensis:
A member of the Orellani group (seven Cortinarius species containing orellanine) in North America.
It contains the deadly kidney-damaging orellanine; symptoms start days later.
cortinarius-rubellus:
The deadly webcap is an orange-reddish, pointed-capped, deadly poisonous Cortinarius that fruits in autumn in coniferous, mossy forests. It contains orellanine; symptoms appear days to weeks later as kidney failure.
Do not collect mushrooms from the genus Cortinarius.
cortinarius-salor:
The blue cobweb is a Cortinarius with a blue-violet, slimy cap, spread across Europe and Asia as far as Japan and New Guinea.
It is inedible.
cortinarius-sanguineus:
The blood red webcap is a small, entirely blood-red Cortinarius used to make red natural dye.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
cortinarius-semisanguineus:
The poison dye cort is a medium-sized Cortinarius with a pale brown to ochre cap and bright blood-red gills.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
cortinarius-splendens:
The splendid webcap is a large, bright yellow Cortinarius.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
cortinarius-traganus:
The gassy (lilac) webcap is a lilac-purple Cortinarius of coniferous forests, recognised by its sharp acetylene/gas-like smell and saffron-orange flesh.
It is regarded as mildly poisonous; do not eat it.
cortinarius-triumphans:
The birch webcap (yellow girdled webcap) grows under birch, with a yellow cap and yellow belts on the stem.
Although regarded as edible in some places, it is not recommended.
cortinarius-trivialis:
The early cortinarius is an inedible Cortinarius with a slimy grey-brown cap 3–12 cm wide and a stem with slimy belts.
Do not eat it.
cortinarius-uliginosus:
The orange willow (marsh) webcap is a Cortinarius with an orange, conical cap growing under willow in damp places.
It is inedible.
cortinarius-varius:
The contrary webcap is a Cortinarius with an orange-yellow cap and violet gills when young.
Although regarded as edible in some sources, it is not recommended because of the genus's risks.
cortinarius-violaceus:
The violet webcap is a dark violet-purple, scaly Cortinarius with a slight metallic sheen, one of the most distinctive of the genus. It occurs in coniferous and deciduous woods.
It is inedible; do not eat it.
craterellus-atrocinereus: The California black chanterelle is an ash-grey to black, funnel-shaped edible mushroom of western North America, especially under oak.
craterellus-calicornucopioides: An edible mushroom resembling the black trumpet, found in California and described by David Arora and Jonathan Frank in 2015.
craterellus-cornucopioides:
The horn of plenty (black trumpet) is a hollow, ash-grey to black, funnel- or trumpet-shaped mushroom. Its name comes from the cornucopia, the horn of plenty of Greek mythology. Because of its black colour it is hard to spot in leaf litter; its surface is smooth and without ridges. It fruits from June to November in deciduous woods such as oak and beech, on mossy limy ground and in hazelnut orchards; in Türkiye it is found especially in the Aegean.
It has an intense, smoky aroma and is used fresh or dried in sauces and soups, even ground as a seasoning. Drying intensifies its aroma.
Because it is hollow it must be washed well. No dangerous look-alike is known, but confirming the identification is still advised.
craterellus-fallax: A black trumpet of eastern North America, an edible relative of the horn of plenty. Because of look-alikes in the genus, confirm the identification.
craterellus-ignicolor: The flame-coloured chanterelle is a thin, yellow-orange, funnel-shaped, smooth-surfaced edible mushroom.
craterellus-lutescens:
The yellow foot is a chanterelle with an orange-brown cap and a hollow yellow-orange stem that fruits in autumn in mossy coniferous forests.
Edible and tasty.
craterellus-tubaeformis:
The winter chanterelle (yellowfoot) is a hollow, funnel-shaped chanterelle with a brown-yellowish cap and a yellow-orange stem. It fruits from late autumn into winter in mossy coniferous forests, often in dense groups.
Edible and popular; it can be dried.
crepidotus-applanatus:
The flat crep is a small, whitish, shell-shaped mushroom on dead wood.
It is inedible.
crepidotus-cesatii:
The roundspored oysterling is a small, shell-shaped saprotroph on dead wood.
It is inedible.
crepidotus-mollis:
The peeling oysterling (soft slipper) is a soft, jelly-skinned, brown-cream mushroom on dead wood.
It is inedible.
crepidotus-variabilis:
The variable oysterling is a small, white, shell-shaped mushroom on dead twigs and wood.
It is inedible.
cudonia-confusa:
The cinnamon jellybaby is a small, cinnamon-coloured mushroom with a little cap and stem growing in coniferous duff.
It is inedible.
cuphophyllus-pratensis:
The meadow waxy cap is an orange-buff mushroom with a waxy surface and gills running down the stem. It fruits in autumn in nutrient-poor, unfertilised meadows and pastures.
Edible and tasty. It has become rare in many countries because fertilisation has reduced its habitat.
cuphophyllus-virgineus:
The snowy waxcap is a pure white, waxy mushroom that fruits in autumn in unfertilised, old meadows and pastures, an indicator of such grassland.
It is regarded as edible but is small and bland.
cyanoboletus-pulverulentus:
The ink stain bolete has yellow pores that instantly turn dark blue-black when touched or cut. It fruits in summer and autumn in deciduous woods, especially under oak.
Edible; the dark colour partly remains when cooked. Young, sound specimens are preferred.
cyathus-olla:
The field bird's nest is a small cup-shaped fungus holding spore-filled 'eggs' that raindrops splash out to spread them.
It is inedible.
cyathus-stercoreus:
The dung bird's nest is a small, cup-shaped fungus with 'eggs' inside that grows on animal dung and rich soil.
It is inedible.
cyathus-striatus:
The fluted bird's nest resembles a miniature bird's nest with a grooved inner surface and is a common saprotroph on wood fragments.
It is inedible.
cyclocybe-aegerita:
The poplar mushroom (Agrocybe aegerita) is a brown-capped, ringed mushroom of poplar and willow stumps. It is well known and cultivated in southern Europe, with a distinct, mildly spicy aroma.
It is eaten well cooked; it is brown-spored, so check the spore print and ring to separate it from similar poisonous wood-growing mushrooms (such as Galerina).
cyclocybe-erebia:
The dark fieldcap is a ringed, dark-brown-capped mushroom with a wide distribution in Europe, found in woods, mulch and decaying woody debris.
It is regarded as edible; it can be confused with brown-spored poisonous mushrooms.
cyclocybe-parasitica:
Tawaka (in Māori) is a poplar-mushroom relative found in New Zealand, growing on dead wood and rotting trees.
It is regarded as edible.
cystoderma-amianthinum:
The common powdercap is a small, mustard-yellow mushroom with a granular surface growing in conifer litter and mossy places.
It is inedible.
cystoderma-carcharias:
The pearly powdercap is a small, pale, grey-white granular mushroom of coniferous forests.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
cystodermella-cinnabarina:
A small, red-cinnamon, granular-surfaced mushroom of coniferous forests.
ultimate-mushroom.com classes it as inedible; some sources regard it as edible.
cystolepiota-seminuda:
The bearded dapperling is a tiny, white to pale pink, granular mushroom found on humus along forest tracks.
It is inedible; its small Lepiota relatives can be deadly.
cyttaria-espinosae: Digüeñe (local name in Chile) is an orange-white, ball-shaped edible fungus that grows parasitically on Nothofagus (southern beech) trees. The Mapuche traditionally eat it raw in salads.
cyttaria-gunnii: The myrtle (beech) orange is an orange-white edible fungus native to Australia (Tasmania) that grows on Nothofagus trees.
cyttaria-hariotii: Llao llao ('Indian bread') is an edible fungus on southern beech trees in Patagonia and southern Chile. It is sweetish and eaten raw.
dacrymyces-chrysospermus:
