Orange jelly is a bright orange, jelly-textured fungus that appears on coniferous wood after rain. It shrinks and hardens when dry and swells again with moisture.
It is regarded as edible but tasteless.
dacryopinax-spathularia:
A spatula-shaped, gelatinous, orange-yellow fungus that grows on rotting wood.
It is regarded as edible but of little value.
daedalea-quercina:
The oak mazegill is a thick, tough bracket fungus with maze-like pores that grows on oak and chestnut wood, causing brown rot.
It is as hard as wood and not eaten.
daedaleopsis-confragosa:
The thin-walled maze polypore (blushing bracket) is a zoned bracket fungus on willow, alder and other deciduous wood whose pores redden when touched.
It is regarded as edible but is tough and tasteless.
daldinia-concentrica:
King Alfred's cake (coal fungus, cramp balls) is a hard, charcoal-black, ball-shaped fungus on ash, beech and other wood, with concentric rings when cut.
It is inedible. It was sometimes used to carry embers for starting fires.
deconica-coprophila:
The dung-loving deconica is a small, brown-capped mushroom growing on dung.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
dermoloma-cuneifolium:
The crazed cap is a small mushroom of grassland with a grey-brown cap covered in fine cracks and a flour-like smell.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
disciotis-venosa:
The bleach cup is a veined, brown, cup-shaped spring mushroom with a sharp bleach-like smell. It is related to the morels.
It can be eaten when well cooked; it is not eaten raw and the smell disappears with cooking.
dumontinia-tuberosa:
A small, brown, stalked cup fungus that grows in spring from an underground tuber under wood anemones.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
echinoderma-asperum:
The freckled dapperling (Lepiota aspera) is a large mushroom with a brownish, sharp-scaled cap and white gills found at woodland edges.
It is regarded as poisonous, and it has deadly Lepiota relatives; do not eat it.
elaphomyces-granulatus:
The deer truffle is a round, hard, granular-skinned underground fungus resembling a truffle but not a true truffle, found in North America, Europe and Asia and eaten by deer and other wildlife.
It is not eaten by people.
entocybe-nitida:
The shining pinkgill is a small, bluish-grey, slender member of the Entolomataceae.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
entoloma-abortivum:
The aborted entoloma (shrimp of the woods) is a grey-brown-capped mushroom found with misshapen, rounded bodies caused by honey fungus (Armillaria) parasitism. The misshapen parts have a shrimp-like texture when cooked.
It can be eaten well cooked; since the genus Entoloma includes many poisonous species, only with expert confirmation.
entoloma-bloxamii:
The big blue pinkgill is a grassland mushroom with a dark blue-violet cap and a pink spore print.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
entoloma-cetratum:
The honey pinkgill is a small honey-yellow Entoloma that appears from May in coniferous forests among moss.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
entoloma-conferendum:
The star pinkgill is a small Entoloma of grassland recognised by its star-shaped spores.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
entoloma-hochstetteri:
The blue pinkgill (sky-blue mushroom) is a striking small, entirely blue mushroom native to New Zealand.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
entoloma-mougeotii:
A small saprotrophic Entoloma.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
entoloma-prunuloides:
The mealy pinkgill is a grey-white, flour-scented Entoloma of grassland.
Although regarded as edible, it is not recommended because Entoloma species are easily confused with poisonous ones.
entoloma-rhodopolium:
The wood pinkgill is a poisonous grey-brown-capped mushroom of Eurasian deciduous woods associated with certain trees.
It causes gastrointestinal poisoning; do not eat it.
entoloma-sericellum:
The cream pinkgill is a slender, cream-coloured Entoloma with a cap up to 5 cm.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
entoloma-serrulatum:
The blue edge pinkgill is a North American Entoloma with blue gill edges and a dark blue-black cap.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
entoloma-sinuatum:
The livid entoloma (leaden entoloma) is a fleshy, cream-grey, flour-scented mushroom whose gills turn pink with age; it fruits in summer and autumn in oak and beech woods and parks in Europe. The pink spore print is the diagnostic feature.
It causes nausea, severe vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain, sometimes liver damage and hospital admission. It is often confused with the edible field mushroom and St George's mushroom (Calocybe gambosa) and is one of the leading causes of mushroom poisoning in Europe.
exidia-glandulosa:
Witch's butter is a black, glossy, jelly-textured fungus fruiting in clusters on dead deciduous wood. It swells after rain and hardens like a crust when dry.
It is inedible; it has no taste.
exidia-recisa:
The willow brain (amber jelly) is an amber-brown, jelly-textured, folded fungus on willow branches.
It is regarded as edible but tasteless.
exidia-thuretiana:
The white brain is a white, gelatinous, folded fungus growing on dead deciduous branches.
It is inedible.
exidiopsis-effusa:
White hair ice is a fungus associated with the strange hair-like ice formations that appear on frozen wood and form only where the fungus is present.
It is inedible.
favolaschia-calocera:
The orange pore fungus is a bright orange, small, jelly-like, honeycomb-pored fungus native to Madagascar that has spread worldwide and is considered invasive in some places.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
fistulina-hepatica:
The beefsteak fungus (ox tongue) is known for its raw-meat colour and look; it bleeds a red, blood-like juice when cut. It grows on trunks of oak, chestnut and plane trees, especially at their bases, from August to November, and is common around Mersin. It causes brown rot and turns the timber into dark 'brown oak'.
It has a sour, lemony taste and is a valued edible with a short season and scarce supply. Young, soft specimens can be cooked or sliced thinly raw into salads.
flammulaster-erinaceellus:
A small, granular-scaly mushroom described in 1876 that grows on dead wood.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
flammulina-filiformis:
The winter mushroom (enoki, enokitake) grows on stumps (elm, willow, poplar) in the cold season, with a sticky orange-brown cap and a velvety dark stem. The wild form is orange-brown, while the commercial form grown without light is long, thin and white; it is widely used in East Asian soups and hotpots.
It is eaten well cooked.
Important warning: it can be confused with the very similar deadly Galerina marginata that grows on wood. The winter mushroom's spore print is white, while Galerina's is rusty brown; its stem is velvety and dark.
flammulina-velutipes:
The velvet shank (wild enoki) grows on deciduous stumps in cold weather, with a sticky orange-brown cap and a velvety dark stem.
It is eaten well cooked. It can be confused with the deadly Galerina marginata; collect it only with someone who knows it, noting its white spore print.
floccularia-albolanaripes:
A mushroom with a yellow cap with brownish scales and a woolly white stem, found in coniferous forests.
It is regarded as edible.
fomes-fomentarius:
The tinder fungus (ice man fungus) is a hoof-shaped, grey-brown, hard bracket fungus that grows on beech, birch and similar trees. Its soft inner tissue (tinder) has been used to make fire throughout history; the 5,000-year-old Ötzi the Iceman carried pieces of it.
It is inedible; it is as hard as wood.
fomitopsis-betulina:
The birch polypore (razor strop) is a half-moon-shaped, white-brown, rubbery bracket fungus on living or dead birch trees. It was found with Ötzi the Iceman and has been used medicinally.
Very young it is regarded as edible, but it is bitter and tough; most sources advise against eating it.
fomitopsis-pinicola:
The red-belted conk is a hard, perennial bracket fungus with red-orange bands on conifers and some deciduous trees, causing brown rot.
It is inedible; it is very hard.
fuscoporia-torulosa:
The tufted bracket is a hard, brown, perennial wood-decay bracket fungus on rotting wood.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
galerina-hypnorum:
The moss bell is a tiny mushroom 4–15 mm across that grows among moss and whose cap turns translucent in damp.
Do not eat it: some Galerina species contain deadly amatoxins.
galerina-marginata:
The funeral bell (deadly skullcap) is a small, rusty-brown, deadly poisonous mushroom. The cap is 2–6 cm and yellowish brown; the stem is slender with a ring remnant near the top. It fruits in autumn on rotting wood, mossy stumps and coniferous debris. It contains the same deadly amatoxins as the death cap (A. phalloides).
Symptoms begin after about 6–24 hours and can lead to liver failure. It is a frequent cause of fatal poisonings because it is mistaken for edible wood-growing mushrooms, especially honey fungus (Armillaria) and the winter mushroom (Flammulina). To tell them apart check the spore print: Galerina's is rusty brown.
galerina-sulciceps:
A dangerously toxic Galerina distributed in the tropics, containing deadly amatoxins.
Do not eat it; symptoms start late.
galerina-vittiformis:
The hairy leg bell is the type species of the genus Galerina, a small mushroom of mossy places.
Do not eat it, since some Galerina species contain deadly amatoxins.
galiella-rufa:
The rubber cup is a hairy, rubbery, brown cup fungus on rotting wood.
It is inedible.
ganoderma-applanatum:
The artist's conk (bear bread) is a large, flat, bracket-shaped, brown wood fungus whose white underside leaves a brown mark when scratched; artists draw on this surface.
It is hard and woody, not eaten; it has some traditional uses.
ganoderma-australe:
The southern bracket is a plant pathogen on living and dead trees.
It is hard and woody; it is not eaten.
ganoderma-oregonense:
The western reishi (western varnished conk, American ling-chi) is a Ganoderma with a varnished reddish-brown look on conifers. It is traditionally used as tea and in supplements; its effects are not proven.
It is hard and bitter and not eaten as food.
geastrum-coronatum:
The crowned earthstar splits its outer wall into a star shape in leaf litter, with a round spore sac in the middle.
It is inedible.
geastrum-fimbriatum:
The fringed earthstar is recognised by its fringed-mouth sphere and star-shaped outer wall.
It is inedible.
geastrum-fornicatum:
The acrobatic (arched) earthstar lifts itself off the ground on arched outer rays.
It is inedible.
geastrum-minimum:
The tiny earthstar is a very small earthstar of dry, sandy places, rare but widely distributed.
It is inedible.
geastrum-pectinatum:
The beaked earthstar is an earthstar that stands on a long stalk, with a beaked mouth.
It is inedible.
geastrum-quadrifidum:
The rayed (four-footed) earthstar is a short-stalked, four-rayed earthstar found in coniferous forests.
It is inedible.
geastrum-rufescens:
The rosy earthstar is a pinkish-brown, star-shaped earthstar.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
geastrum-triplex:
The collared earthstar is among the best-known earthstars, its outer wall splitting into three layers and its middle looking like a collared bowl.
It is inedible.
geoglossum-cookeanum:
An earth tongue: a black, matchstick-shaped fungus of mossy, grassy places.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
geopora-cooperi:
The pine truffle (fuzzy truffle) is a fungus with a hairy brown outer surface that grows underground or at the soil surface and forms mycorrhizae with pine roots.
It is regarded as edible.
geopora-sumneriana:
The cedar cup is a European round, brown, hairy fungus emerging from the soil under cedars.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
gliophorus-graminicolor:
A sticky, greenish waxcap found in grass in Australia and New Zealand.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
gliophorus-irrigatus:
The slimy waxcap is a grey-brown, very sticky, waxy mushroom of grassland in autumn.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
gliophorus-laetus:
A waxy, sticky waxcap in orange-yellow-greenish tones found on heaths and damp grassland.
It is regarded as edible but worthless.
gliophorus-psittacinus:
The parrot waxcap is a colourful, slimy, waxy mushroom that can combine green, yellow, pink and orange. It is bright green when young and turns yellow-pink with age. It fruits in autumn in unfertilised grassland.
It is regarded as edible but attracts little interest because of its slimy texture and poor flavour.
gloeophyllum-sepiarium:
The conifer mazegill (rusty gilled polypore) is a rust-coloured, gilled, hard bracket fungus on coniferous stumps and timber, causing brown rot.
It is inedible.
gomphidius-glutinosus:
The glutinous gomphidius is covered in a thick slime layer, grey-purple, and grows under spruce. It depends on a Suillus species for its growth, and its stem base is yellowish.
Edible; the slimy skin is peeled and it darkens when cooked.
gomphidius-maculatus:
The larch slime spike is a slimy, reddish-brown mushroom growing under larch.
Edible.
gomphidius-oregonensis:
A slimy Gomphidius of North American coniferous forests that blackens when cooked or cut.
It is regarded as edible.
gomphidius-roseus:
The rosy spike-cap is a pink-red, slimy mushroom of European pine forests that grows together with the bolete Suillus bovinus.
Edible; the slimy skin is peeled.
gomphidius-smithii:
Smith's slime spike is a slimy Gomphidius growing under conifers in North America.
It is regarded as edible.
gomphidius-subroseus:
The rosy gomphidius is a mycorrhizal mushroom of North America with a pink-red, slimy cap.
It is regarded as edible.
gomphus-clavatus:
Pig's ears (violet chanterelle) is a violet-purple, funnel-shaped mushroom with wrinkled, vein-like ridges. It fruits in late summer and autumn, especially under spruce in coniferous forests. It has become rare in many parts of Europe and is protected there.
It is regarded as edible and tasty, but because it is rare it is better left uncollected.
gomphus-floccosus:
The scaly vase is a deep, funnel-shaped, orange-red scaly mushroom resembling a chanterelle, found in coniferous forests of North America and Asia.
Some people eat it, but many get gastrointestinal upset; it is not recommended.
grifola-frondosa:
Maitake (hen-of-the-woods) is a large mushroom made of overlapping grey-brown fronds in clusters at the base of old oaks and other deciduous trees; it looks like a bush and can exceed 10 kg. It fruits in autumn and often returns to the same spot for many years. In Japanese 'maitake' means 'dancing mushroom': finders are said to dance for joy.
It is eaten young and tender, with a strong aroma and a springy texture. It is important in East Asian cooking and grown commercially. It should be well cooked.
guepinia-helvelloides:
Apricot jelly is a salmon-pink, funnel-shaped, jelly-textured mushroom that grows on soil.
It is regarded as edible but its taste is bland.
guepiniopsis-alpina:
The jelly cup is a small, orange, jelly-textured, cone-like fungus on dead wood.
It is inedible.
gymnopilus-aeruginosus:
A blue-green, bitter-tasting Gymnopilus with a rusty orange spore print that contains psychoactive compounds (psilocybin).
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
gymnopilus-braendlei:
A Gymnopilus on dead wood containing psilocybin and psilocin.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
gymnopilus-dilepis:
The magenta rustgill is a Gymnopilus with a purple-magenta cap, found in India, Malaysia and North America.
It is inedible.
gymnopilus-liquiritiae:
A widely distributed, bitter-tasting Gymnopilus that fruits in dense clusters on decaying coniferous wood.
Most sources advise against eating it.
gymnopilus-luteofolius:
The purple gym (yellow-gilled gymnopilus) is a large, widely distributed mushroom with purple-red scales that grows on rotting wood.
It is bitter; eating it is not recommended.
gymnopilus-luteoviridis:
A Gymnopilus common in eastern North America that contains psilocybin and psilocin.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
gymnopilus-luteus:
The yellow gymnopilus is a common mushroom of eastern North America on rotting wood that contains psilocybin and psilocin.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
gymnopilus-purpuratus:
A Gymnopilus that grows in clusters on dead wood, stumps and wood chips and contains psilocybin.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
gymnopilus-sapineus:
The scaly rustgill is a small, plain-looking, bitter Gymnopilus on coniferous debris.
It is inedible.
gymnopilus-validipes:
A Gymnopilus widespread in North America and Europe on rotting wood. Some sources note that it may contain psychoactive compounds.
This is not consumption advice.
gymnopilus-viridans:
A Gymnopilus that turns green when touched and contains psilocybin and psilocin.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
gymnopus-dryophilus:
The oak-loving collybia (formerly Collybia dryophila) is a small, cream-brown mushroom common in deciduous and coniferous woods in summer and autumn.
It is regarded as edible but small and worthless, and can upset some people's stomachs.
gymnopus-fusipes:
The spindleshank grows parasitically on oak roots in clusters, with twisted, spindle-shaped stems. It fruits at the tree base in autumn.
It is regarded as edible but has tough, fibrous stems.
gymnosporangium-clavariiforme:
Tongues of fire is a rust fungus that alternates between juniper and hawthorn; in spring it forms orange, jelly-textured, tongue-shaped structures on juniper branches.
It is inedible.
gyrodon-lividus:
The alder bolete grows under alder trees and is a close relative of Paxillus.
It is regarded as edible but of low value.
gyromitra-esculenta:
The false morel (in Turkish 'kuzugöbeği ebesi', 'ekşi memet') is recognised by its reddish-brown, brain-like folded cap, which is cottony inside. It fruits in spring in coniferous forests on sandy soils. Unlike the true morel (Morchella), its cap is not honeycomb-pitted but brain-folded.
It contains gyromitrin, which is converted in the body to monomethylhydrazine, affecting the liver and nervous system. Symptoms start after 6–12 hours: vomiting, diarrhoea and headache; severe cases end in death. In some countries such as Finland it is eaten after repeated boiling and drying, but even its fumes can be toxic and it is not safe.
In Türkiye deaths have occurred because it was mistaken for the morel; do not eat it.
gyromitra-fastigiata:
The brown false morel is a Gyromitra with a brown, folded cap that fruits in spring in mountain forests.
Gyromitra species can be deadly raw or undercooked; do not eat it.
gyromitra-gigas:
The snow mushroom (giant false morel) is a large false morel with a folded, yellowish-brown cap that fruits in spring near melting snow in mountain forests.
It may contain gyromitrin; although eaten cooked in some regions it is not safe. Do not eat it.
gyromitra-infula:
The hooded false morel (elfin saddle) is a saddle-shaped mushroom with a reddish-brown cap that fruits in autumn.
It is inedible; it may contain gyromitrin.
gyroporus-castaneus:
The chestnut bolete is a small bolete with a chestnut-brown cap, white pores and a stem that quickly turns hollow. It grows under oak and chestnut on sandy soils.
It is regarded as edible; raw it can upset some people, so cook it well.
gyroporus-cyanescens:
The bluing (cornflower) bolete is a pale yellowish, spongy, hollow-stemmed bolete that turns an intense dark blue instantly when cut. It grows on sandy soils under birch and oak.
It is regarded as edible and tasty when cooked.
gyroporus-purpurinus:
A small purple-red-toned bolete found in eastern North America.
It is regarded as edible.
hapalopilus-nidulans:
The cinnamon polypore is a soft-fleshed bracket fungus on dead deciduous wood, cinnamon-orange in colour; a drop of KOH turns it purple because of polyporic acid.
'Bracket fungi are never poisonous' is a common false belief: if eaten, this species is poisonous because polyporic acid can damage the kidneys and nervous system. It must not be eaten.
harrya-chromipes:
The yellowfoot bolete is a pink-brown-capped bolete with a yellow stem found in eastern North America.
It is regarded as edible.
hebeloma-crustuliniforme:
The poison pie (fairy cakes) is a pale clay-coloured mushroom with a radish-like smell and a sticky cap. It fruits in autumn at woodland edges and along tracks.
It is a poisonous mushroom causing nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea and must not be eaten.
hebeloma-mesophaeum:
The veiled poisonpie is a Hebeloma with a dark centre and pale edge on the cap, found in coniferous and mixed woods.
It is poisonous; do not eat it.
hebeloma-radicosum:
The rooting poison pie is a ringed, almond-scented Hebeloma whose stem roots deep into the soil, fruiting from rodent burrows.
It is poisonous; do not eat it.
hebeloma-sinapizans:
The scaly-stalked hebeloma is a large, fleshy Hebeloma with a radish or mustard smell and a scaly stem, found at woodland edges.
It is regarded as poisonous, causing gastrointestinal poisoning. Do not eat it.
heliocybe-sulcata:
The sunray sawgill grows on coniferous wood and causes brown rot.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
helvella-acetabulum:
The ribbed-stalked cup is a large, brown, cup-shaped spring mushroom of woods with a ribbed stalk.
It is regarded as poisonous raw and is not eaten.
helvella-atra:
The dark elfin saddle is a black Helvella with a drooping, saddle-shaped cap.
It is inedible.
helvella-costifera:
A Helvella with a grey, cup-shaped body sitting on a distinctly ribbed stalk.
It is inedible.
helvella-crispa:
The fluted white elfin saddle is recognised by its cream-white, lobed cap and fluted white stem and fruits in autumn in woods.
Poisonous raw; in some countries it is eaten cooked but can cause stomach upset. Not recommended.
helvella-dryophila:
A black-brown, saddle-shaped Helvella of western North America associated with oak.
Poisonous raw; it must be cooked, and many authorities advise against eating it.
helvella-elastica:
The flexible helvella (elastic saddle) is a brown-grey, saddle-shaped mushroom with a thin, flexible stem.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
helvella-ephippium:
A Helvella with a white stem and a grey saddle-shaped cap that appears in summer and autumn.
It is inedible.
helvella-lacunosa:
The slate grey saddle (elfin saddle) is recognised by its grey-black, folded, saddle-shaped cap and grey, fluted and pitted stem. It fruits in autumn in woods and along roadsides.
In parts of Europe it is eaten after thorough cooking; it is poisonous raw and undercooking can cause poisoning. Many authorities advise against eating it.
helvella-latispora:
A Helvella with a grey, cup-shaped body and a pale stem that appears in late summer and autumn.
It is inedible.
helvella-leucomelaena:
The white-footed elf cup is a spring mushroom of burned ground and coniferous forests with a grey-brown cup and a white, fluted stalk.
It is inedible.
helvella-macropus:
The long-stalked gray cup is a grey, cup-shaped mushroom with a long, slender stalk that fruits in woods in summer and autumn.
It is inedible.
hemileccinum-hortonii:
The corrugated (Horton's) bolete has a dry, wrinkled-cracked cap and occurs in deciduous woods of eastern North America.
It is regarded as edible.
hemileccinum-impolitum:
The iodine bolete is a European bolete of oak woods with a dry, pale brown cap, yellow pores, a yellowish stem base and a faint iodine/phenol smell, fruiting in summer and autumn.
It is regarded as edible; the smell disappears when cooked. Make sure it is not bitter.
hemileccinum-subglabripes:
A bolete of eastern North America described by Charles Peck in 1887 as a Boletus, fruiting in deciduous woods.
It is regarded as edible.
hericium-abietis:
The conifer coral hericium (bear's head) is a coral-shaped mushroom on old conifer trunks in western North America, its branches hung with spines.
Edible while young and white; a good one.
hericium-americanum:
The bear's head tooth fungus is a white, clustered mushroom of long hanging spines on deciduous trunks.
Edible when young, with a taste close to the lion's mane.
hericium-cirrhatum:
The tiered tooth fungus forms overlapping white-cream shelves with short spines on deciduous trunks, especially beech.
Edible when young; it yellows and turns bitter with age.
hericium-clathroides:
An edible Hericium with branches covered in spines, growing on dead wood.
Edible while young and white.
hericium-coralloides:
The coral tooth fungus (comb tooth) is a coral-shaped mushroom on old beech and oak stumps and trunks, with branches hung with fine, long white spines. It fruits in autumn and is protected in some countries.
Edible and tasty while young and white; it yellows with age.
hericium-erinaceus:
The lion's mane (yamabushitake) is a ball-shaped mushroom of long, white, hanging spines that resembles a lion's mane or beard. It fruits in autumn on wounds of old deciduous trees such as beech and oak. It is rare and protected in some countries.
Edible while young and white; when cooked it has a crab- or lobster-like texture and taste. It is sliced and fried in butter. It yellows and turns bitter with age.
It is used in East Asian traditional medicine and research looks at its effect on nerve cell growth, but these are not yet proven treatments in people. It has also been grown under laboratory conditions in Türkiye.
hericium-novae-zealandiae:
A coral-shaped, spiny mushroom endemic to New Zealand, formerly classed as H. coralloides.
It is regarded as edible.
heterobasidion-annosum:
Annosum root rot is considered the cause of one of the most economically costly diseases in forestry, rotting the roots and trunks of conifers.
It is inedible; it is hard and woody.
hortiboletus-bubalinus: An edible bolete with a reddish-beige cap found in deciduous woods, described as a Boletus in 1991.
hortiboletus-rubellus:
The ruby bolete is a small, dainty bolete with a bright red cap and yellow pores that turns blue when cut. It fruits in deciduous woods and along tracks in summer and autumn.
Although sometimes called edible, its flavour is poor and it is hard to digest; some sources regard it as poisonous. Not recommended.
humaria-hemisphaerica:
The hairy fairy cup is a small cup fungus on soil with a whitish inside and a brown hairy outside.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
humidicutis-marginata:
A waxcap-family mushroom with a small, orange-yellow, slimy cap found in grassland and woods.
It is regarded as edible but worthless.
hydnellum-aurantiacum:
The orange spine is a hard, corky, orange-brown mushroom with spines underneath, found in pine forests in summer and autumn and used for dyeing.
It is bitter and tough and not eaten.
hydnellum-auratile:
A hard, spiny mushroom in golden-orange tones described by Max Britzelmayr in 1891.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
hydnellum-caeruleum:
The blue-gray hydnellum (blue tooth) is a hard, spiny mushroom in bluish-grey-green tones.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
hydnellum-concrescens:
The zoned tooth fungus is a hard-textured tooth fungus with concentric zones.
It is inedible.
hydnellum-cyanopodium:
The blue foot (bleeding blue tooth) is an inedible, hard tooth fungus with a blue stem.
It is inedible.
hydnellum-ferrugineum:
The mealy tooth is a rusty-brown, corky tooth fungus found in damp forests.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
hydnellum-peckii:
The bleeding hydnellum is a very odd-looking mushroom whose young fruit bodies ooze red, blood-like droplets that make it look like strawberries and cream; an anticoagulant compound, atromentin, can be obtained from the droplets.
It is bitter and tough and not eaten.
hydnellum-scrobiculatum:
The rough hydnellum (ridged tooth) is a hard, inedible tooth fungus with a rough surface.
It is inedible.
hydnellum-spongiosipes:
The velvet tooth is a tooth fungus of Europe and North America with a spongy, velvety stem.
It is inedible.
hydnellum-suaveolens:
The fragrant hydnellum is a funnel-shaped, bluish-toned mushroom with a pleasant aniseed-like smell found in pine forests.
It is inedible: tough and bitter.
hydnum-albidum: The white hedgehog is an edible white-to-cream mushroom with spines underneath, native to North America.
hydnum-oregonense: An edible hedgehog mushroom described in 2018, named after Oregon, forming mycorrhizae with tree roots.
hydnum-repandum:
The hedgehog mushroom (sweet tooth) is a cream-orange, fleshy mushroom with spine-like teeth under the cap instead of gills, which makes it easy to recognise safely. The cap surface is bumpy (hence 'ox tongue'). It fruits in mixed and coniferous forests from summer through autumn and even into winter; in Türkiye it is common in Marmara, the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
It is very tasty and is rarely infested by insects and larvae. It is not eaten raw; cooked it is delicious, and young specimens are preferred because older ones may turn bitter. It can be dried or pickled. It has no poisonous look-alike.
hydnum-rufescens:
The terracotta hedgehog is a smaller, orange-terracotta relative of the hedgehog mushroom with spines underneath.
Edible and tasty.
hydnum-umbilicatum:
The depressed hedgehog is a small, orange hedgehog mushroom with a dipped centre.
Edible.
hygrocybe-aurantiosplendens:
The orange waxcap is a bright orange, waxy mushroom of unfertilised grassland.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
hygrocybe-cantharellus:
The chanterelle waxy cap is a small, yellow-orange waxcap with a long thin stem and gills running down it.
It is regarded as edible but is tiny and worthless.
hygrocybe-chlorophana:
The golden waxcap is a lemon-yellow, sticky, waxy mushroom of meadows and pastures.
It is regarded as edible but worthless.
hygrocybe-coccinea:
The scarlet hood is a small mushroom with a bright red, bell-shaped, waxy cap. It fruits in unfertilised meadows and pastures in autumn.
It is regarded as edible but flavourless.
hygrocybe-conica:
The witch's hat is a waxcap with a pointed, conical cap in orange-red-yellow that blackens when touched and with age.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
hygrocybe-flavescens:
The golden waxy cap is a yellow-orange waxcap described from Michigan.
It is regarded as edible.
hygrocybe-intermedia:
The fibrous waxcap is a waxcap with a red-orange, fibrous cap found in grassland.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
hygrocybe-miniata:
The vermilion waxcap is a small, bright red-orange waxcap of mossy places.
It is regarded as edible but worthless.
hygrocybe-punicea:
The crimson waxcap is a large, deep-red, sticky waxy mushroom of old, unfertilised grassland in autumn.
It is regarded as edible with a poor flavour.
hygrocybe-quieta:
The oily waxcap is a red-orange mushroom with an oily smell found in damp grassland.
It is inedible.
hygrocybe-reidii:
The honey waxcap is a honey-coloured, sweet-honey-scented mushroom of grassland.
It is regarded as edible.
hygrocybe-spadicea:
The date waxcap is a waxcap with a dark date-brown cap and yellow gills.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
hygrocybe-splendidissima:
The splendid waxcap is a bright red, waxy mushroom of grassland.
It is regarded as edible.
hygrophoropsis-aurantiaca:
The false chanterelle is an orange, funnel-shaped mushroom with thin, forked, true gills, growing under pines on humus and sandy soils. It looks very much like the chanterelle, but the chanterelle has vein-like ridges instead of gills.
It is regarded as poisonous or inedible and can cause gastrointestinal upset.
hygrophoropsis-rufa:
A European orange-brown mushroom resembling the false chanterelle that grows on wood chips or near conifers.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
hygrophorus-agathosmus:
The gray almond waxy cap is a grey-capped, almond-scented mushroom of coniferous forests.
It is regarded as edible, with a strong smell.
hygrophorus-bakerensis:
The brown almond waxy cap is a brown-capped, almond-scented mushroom of North American mountain forests.
It is regarded as edible.
hygrophorus-camarophyllus:
The arched woodwax (smoky waxy cap) is a thick-fleshed mushroom with a smoky-brown cap that fruits in coniferous forests in autumn.
It is edible and considered a good table mushroom.
hygrophorus-chrysodon:
The flaky (gold-flecked) waxy cap is a white-capped waxy mushroom with golden-yellow flecks at the cap edge and on the stem, fruiting in deciduous woods in autumn.
It is regarded as edible.
hygrophorus-eburneus:
The ivory waxy cap (cowboy's handkerchief) is an entirely white mushroom with a slimy cap and stem, fruiting on forest ground in autumn.
Edible; the slimy skin is peeled.
hygrophorus-erubescens:
The blotched woodwax is a white-capped mushroom with pink-red blotches found in coniferous forests.
It is not eaten because of its bitterish taste.
hygrophorus-hypothejus:
The herald of the winter (olive-brown waxy cap) is an olive-brown, slimy-capped mushroom of pine forests that fruits until the first frosts.
Edible; the slimy skin is peeled.
hygrophorus-latitabundus:
The ebony woodwax is a dark-brown, slimy-capped waxy mushroom of Europe.
It is regarded as edible.
hygrophorus-marzuolus:
The March mushroom is a firm-fleshed, grey-brown-capped waxy mushroom that appears very early in spring in coniferous forests as the snow melts. It is valued because it fruits so briefly.
Edible and tasty.
hygrophorus-nemoreus: The oak woodwax is an orange-yellow, waxy, edible mushroom of oak woods.
hygrophorus-olivaceoalbus:
The olive wax cap has a dark olive-brown slimy cap and a stem with a sheath-like pattern, found in spruce forests.
It is regarded as edible.
hygrophorus-pudorinus:
The blushing (turpentine) waxy cap is a pinkish-orange, slimy-capped mushroom with a turpentine smell found in spruce and fir forests.
Edible; its smell and taste do not suit everyone.
hygrophorus-russula:
The pinkmottle woodwax (false russula) is a fleshy mushroom with pink-red mottling that resembles a Russula, fruiting in oak woods in autumn.
It is regarded as edible; it is thick-fleshed and not bitter.
hygrophorus-speciosus:
The larch waxy cap is an orange-red, slimy, waxy mushroom that grows under larch.
It is regarded as edible.
hygrophorus-subalpinus:
The subalpine (snowbank) waxy cap is a white, thick-fleshed, plump mushroom that appears as snow melts on high mountains.
It is regarded as edible.
hymenochaete-corrugata:
Glue crust is a plant pathogen that forms hard, glue-like crusts on branches.
It is inedible.
hymenopellis-radicata:
The rooting shank (beech rooter) has a slimy cap and a long stem that reaches deep into the soil to buried wood or roots. It fruits in deciduous woods in summer and autumn.
It is regarded as edible; because the stem is tough only the cap is preferred, and it is cooked well.
hypholoma-capnoides:
The conifer tuft is a honey-brown-capped mushroom that fruits in clusters on conifer stumps; its gills are grey-violet.
It is regarded as edible; the sulphur tuft (H. fasciculare, poisonous and bitter) has greenish gills while this species' are grey-purplish. The confusion risk is high.
hypholoma-fasciculare:
The sulphur tuft is a sulphur-yellow, very bitter mushroom that fruits all year in large clusters on stumps. The cap centre is rust-coloured, the edge varies from canary yellow to greenish; the stem is sulphur yellow; the gills are light yellow at first, then greenish grey and finally purple-brown.
It is poisonous and causes gastrointestinal poisoning, sometimes severe. That slugs and insects eat it does not mean it is safe for people.
hypholoma-lateritium:
The brick cap (kuritake) is a brick-red-capped mushroom that fruits in autumn in clusters on deciduous stumps. It is cultivated in Japan and sold as 'kuritake'.
It is regarded as edible; to avoid confusion with the sulphur tuft, check gill colour and bitterness.
hypomyces-lactifluorum:
The lobster mushroom is not a single species but a parasitic fungus that covers Russula or Lactarius mushrooms. It transforms the host, turning it bright orange-red and firm; its colour and taste recall lobster.
A highly valued edible. If the host is a poisonous mushroom the risk can increase, so choose specimens whose inner flesh is solid and white.
hypomyces-lateritius:
The ochre gillgobbler is a parasitic fungus that covers the gills of Lactarius mushrooms.
It is regarded as edible.
hypsizygus-tessulatus:
The beech mushroom (buna shimeji) is a brown mushroom with a cracked-pattern cap on deciduous trees, especially beech. It is cultivated in East Asia.
It is eaten cooked; raw it is bitter.
hypsizygus-ulmarius:
The elm oyster mushroom is a cream-white, thick-fleshed mushroom on trunks of elm and other deciduous trees.
It is eaten well cooked.
ileodictyon-cibarium:
The white basket fungus is a stinkhorn of New Zealand and Australia that emerges from an egg-shaped structure as a white, lattice-like cage.
The egg stage is regarded as edible but is rarely eaten because of the smell.
ileodictyon-gracile:
The smooth cage is a white, cage-like stinkhorn native to Australia.
It is inedible and smells foul.
imleria-badia:
The bay bolete has a chestnut-brown cap, glossy when wet, a stem paler than the cap and yellowish pores that stain blue-grey on touch. It fruits in summer and autumn under pine, spruce and sometimes beech.
A good edible; its taste is like the cep but milder. Young mushrooms are preferred, and since the pores absorb water they are wiped rather than washed. It is sold in markets in Mexico. Some people may have allergic reactions.
imperator-rhodopurpureus:
The oldrose bolete grows under deciduous trees with red-purple tones and flesh that turns blue when cut.
It is inedible; it has poisonous relatives.
imperator-torosus:
The brawny bolete is a thick-fleshed bolete with reddish tones and a red-netted stem, found in deciduous woods on limy soils.
It is regarded as poisonous, causing gastrointestinal poisoning.
infundibulicybe-geotropa:
The trooping funnel (monk's head) is a large, funnel-shaped, cream-coloured mushroom that fruits in rings in woods in autumn.
It is regarded as edible; it can upset some people's stomachs and has poisonous look-alikes.
infundibulicybe-gibba:
The common funnel is a clay-beige, funnel-shaped, faintly almond-scented mushroom common in woods in summer and autumn, with gills running down the stem.
It is regarded as edible, but it is not recommended because it can be confused with many poisonous (muscarine-containing) white funnel mushrooms.
infundibulicybe-mediterranea:
A pale, funnel-shaped mushroom from the Mediterranean region.
It is regarded as edible; because funnel mushrooms are easily confused with poisonous ones, identify it carefully.
inocybe-aeruginascens:
An Inocybe widespread in Europe that contains psilocybin and turns blue-green when cut.
It is psychoactive and may also contain muscarine and other toxins. It is illegal in many countries; this is not consumption advice.
inocybe-corydalina:
The greenflush fibrecap is an Inocybe whose stem flushes green-blue; it is reported to contain psychoactive compounds.
Do not eat it; many Inocybe species contain muscarine.
inocybe-fraudans:
The pear fibrecap is an Inocybe with a yellowish-brown cap and a pear-like smell. It contains muscarine.
It is poisonous and must not be eaten.
inocybe-geophylla:
The little white inocybe is a small, entirely white mushroom with a conical cap that fruits on woodland soil in summer and autumn. It contains high amounts of muscarine.
It is poisonous: sweating, salivation, tearing, blurred vision and slow heartbeat. It can be confused with other small white mushrooms.
inocybe-godeyi:
Godey's fibrecap is a European Inocybe with a cone-shaped cap that turns red when cut. It contains muscarine that can be poisonous and even deadly.
Do not eat it.
inocybe-hystrix:
The scaly fibrecap is an Inocybe with a scaly cap that forms mycorrhizae with deciduous trees.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
inocybe-lacera:
The torn fibrecap is a brown Inocybe with a torn-fibrous cap found on sandy soils. It contains muscarine.
It is poisonous; do not eat it.
inocybe-pallidicremea:
The lilac fiberhead is a fibrous-surfaced, lilac-toned Inocybe.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
inocybe-praetervisa:
A small yellow-brown Inocybe.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
inocybe-whitei:
The blushing inocybe (also called Inocybe pudica) has a white cap that turns pink-red with age or touch. It contains muscarine.
It is poisonous; do not eat it.
inonotus-hispidus:
The shaggy bracket is an orange-brown, hairy, cushion-shaped mushroom on deciduous trees (especially ash, oak and apple) in Europe, Asia and North America, and a plant pathogen.
When young and soft it is regarded as edible, but it is tough and bitterish.
inonotus-obliquus:
Chaga is a hard, black, charcoal-like cracked mass (sclerotium) on birch trees with an orange-brown inside. In Russia, Finland and other northern countries it is traditionally boiled and drunk as a tea.
It is not a food but is used as a tea or extract. Its health claims are not firmly proven, and because of its high oxalate content people at risk of kidney stones and those on blood thinners should be careful.
inosperma-bongardii:
Bongard's fibrecap is an Inosperma first described as an Agaricus that turns red when cut and has a fruity smell. It contains muscarine.
It is poisonous; do not eat it.
inosperma-cookei:
The straw fibrecap is a very small Inosperma with a pale straw-yellow cap. It contains muscarine.
It is poisonous; do not eat it.
inosperma-erubescens:
The deadly fibrecap (formerly Inocybe patouillardii) is a whitish-cream mushroom with a fibrous cap that turns red with age or touch. It fruits in early summer on limy soils and contains muscarine.
It causes sweating, excess saliva, visual disturbance and slow heartbeat, and death from heart and respiratory failure can occur. It is very often confused with St George's mushroom (Calocybe gambosa) because it fruits in the same places and season.
inosperma-maculatum:
The frosty fibrecap is a brown, fibrous-capped Inosperma containing muscarine.
It is poisonous; do not eat it.
irpex-lacteus:
A common crust fungus of temperate regions that spreads as a white crust on dead wood.
It is inedible.
ischnoderma-resinosum:
The late fall polypore is a brown, resin-surfaced bracket fungus on deciduous trunks in late autumn, with an aniseed smell and juicy flesh when young.
It is regarded as edible only when very young and soft.
kalapuya-brunnea:
The Oregon brown truffle is a truffle found only in the Pacific Northwest, the sole species of the genus Kalapuya.
It is regarded as edible.
kretzschmaria-deusta:
The brittle cinder forms charcoal-black crusts at the base of deciduous trees (especially beech), silently rotting their roots and trunks; affected trees can suddenly fall.
It is inedible.
kuehneromyces-mutabilis:
The sheathed woodtuft fruits in clusters on deciduous stumps, with a honey-brown cap that darkens in damp and a ringed stem. The cap looks two-toned as it dries.
Although a good edible, it is very easily confused with the deadly Galerina marginata that grows in the same places, and this confusion has caused deaths. Spore print (rusty brown) and scaly stems can tell them apart, but it is not safe for beginners.
laccaria-amethysteo-occidentalis:
A Laccaria with amethyst-purple gills found under conifers, usually pine, singly or in groups.
It is regarded as edible.
laccaria-amethystina:
The amethyst deceiver is a bright amethyst-purple, small mushroom that fades as it dries. It fruits in deciduous and coniferous woods in summer and autumn.
It is regarded as edible; the purple colour disappears when cooked. It can be confused with purple Cortinarius species.
laccaria-bicolor:
The bicoloured deceiver is a small mushroom with a tan cap and lilac gills found in pine woods. It forms mycorrhizae with tree roots and is an important model in scientific studies.
Edible but not choice.
laccaria-fraterna:
The gumtree deceiver is a mycorrhizal Laccaria growing under eucalyptus and acacia.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
laccaria-laccata:
The deceiver is a small orange-brown mushroom whose colour changes a lot with moisture. It is common on woodland soil and heaths in summer and autumn.
It is regarded as edible, but it is small, thin-fleshed and of modest flavour.
laccaria-proxima:
The scurfy deceiver is a Laccaria with a long, slender stem and a red-brown cap found in coniferous forests.
It is regarded as edible.
laccocephalum-mylittae:
Native bread is an Australian fungus that forms a large underground sclerotium eaten by Aboriginal people. The mass can reach 25 kg and is called 'blackfellow's bread'.
Edible after special preparation.
lacrymaria-lacrymabunda:
The weeping widow has a brown fibrous cap that beads with water droplets at the margin in damp and a fibrous ring on the stem. It fruits on lawns and roadsides in summer and autumn.
It is regarded as edible but spoils quickly; it is brown-spored and has poisonous look-alikes.
lactarius-argillaceifolius:
The clay-gilled milkcap is a brown Lactarius with an incurved cap.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
lactarius-aspideus:
The bright yellow milkcap is a pale yellow, slimy-capped Lactarius growing under willow.
It is regarded as edible but bitterish.
lactarius-blennius:
The slimy (beech) milkcap is a greenish-grey, slimy-capped, very acrid Lactarius that fruits in beech woods in autumn.
It is not eaten because it is acrid and burning.
lactarius-camphoratus:
The curry milkcap (candy cap) is a red-brown Lactarius that gives off a sweet maple-syrup/curry-like smell when dried. It occurs in coniferous and mixed forests.
Edible; dried, it is used as a flavouring in desserts (especially its North American 'candy cap' relatives).
lactarius-chrysorrheus:
The yellowdrop milkcap is a Lactarius of deciduous forests whose white milk turns yellow within minutes of cutting.
It is acrid and regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
lactarius-controversus:
The poplar milkcap is a large, funnel-capped Lactarius growing under poplar and willow, with a white cap marked with pink zones.
It is acrid and not eaten.
lactarius-corrugis: The corrugated-cap milky is an edible North American mushroom with a dark brown, wrinkled cap (Lactifluus corrugis).
lactarius-deliciosus:
The saffron milk cap (kanlıca, melki, çıntar) is among the best-known and most eaten wild mushrooms in Türkiye. It is an orange-carrot mushroom with a zoned cap that bleeds carrot-red milk when cut; the milk may turn green with time. It fruits in pine forests on acidic soils after autumn rain; the western Black Sea (Kastamonu, Bolu) is especially rich.
It is highly valued in the kitchen: sautéed in butter or grilled. Urine may turn reddish afterwards, which is harmless.
Together with L. salmonicolor (under fir) and L. deterrimus (under spruce) it is called 'kanlıca'. Do not take mushrooms that do not give milk or are not orange for kanlıca.
lactarius-deterrimus:
The false saffron milkcap grows under spruce, orange, bleeding milk and turning green when cut. It leaves a bitter taste in the mouth and is less tasty than other kanlıca.
Edible.
lactarius-fuliginosus:
The sooty milkcap is a Lactarius with a dark brown, sooty cap and flesh that turns pink when cut.
It is acrid, not eaten, and regarded as poisonous.
lactarius-fulvissimus:
The tawny milkcap is a Lactarius with an orange-brown cap.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
lactarius-glyciosmus:
The coconut milk cap is a grey-brown-capped Lactarius with a coconut smell that grows under birch.
It is usually regarded as inedible and may be bitter; in some places it is used dried as a seasoning.
lactarius-helvus:
The fenugreek milkcap is a pale-brown-capped Lactarius that smells of fenugreek/lovage when dried.
Although used as a seasoning in some places, it is poisonous raw and causes gastrointestinal upset; do not eat it.
lactarius-hygrophoroides: An edible orange-brown milk-cap of North America with a dry, velvety cap.
lactarius-indigo:
The indigo milk cap is a strikingly indigo-blue mushroom that bleeds dark blue milk when cut; with age the blue fades to grey-green. It occurs in deciduous and coniferous forests of North and Central America and East Asia.
Edible; it is sold in markets in Mexico and Guatemala. The taste is slightly bitterish, and the blue colour is lost when cooked.
lactarius-lignyotus:
The chocolate milky (velvet milkcap) is a Lactarius with a dark chocolate-brown, velvety cap found in coniferous forests.
It is regarded as edible.
lactarius-mairei:
The whiskery milkcap is a Lactarius with a hairy cap margin, first found in Morocco.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
lactarius-mammosus:
The pap milkcap is a Lactarius with a nipple-like bump in the middle of the cap and a coconut smell.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
lactarius-pallidus:
The pale milkcap is a pale Lactarius growing under beech.
It is regarded as edible but is often bitter and of low value.
lactarius-paradoxus: An edible North American milk-cap in grey-purple tones that stains reddish when cut.
lactarius-piperatus:
The peppery milk cap (blancaccio) is a white, funnel-shaped mushroom with very crowded gills and a burning peppery taste. It fruits in deciduous woods in summer and autumn.
Raw it is burning; in some places it is eaten after boiling removes the acridity, but most sources do not recommend eating it.
lactarius-porninsis:
The larch milkcap is an orange, milk-bleeding Lactarius growing under larch.
It is regarded as edible.
lactarius-psammicola:
A Lactarius growing on sandy soils.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
lactarius-pubescens:
The downy milk cap is a whitish-pink Lactarius with a hairy margin under birch. It is very acrid.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
lactarius-pyrogalus:
The fire-milk lactarius is a grey-brown, intensely acrid milk-cap growing under hazel. Although classed as inedible in most of the world, in Türkiye it is traditionally collected, especially in the hazelnut orchards of the Black Sea (Central Black Sea), and eaten fresh, pickled or brined.
Warning: it is not eaten raw because of its acridity; outside Türkiye sources regard it as inedible.
lactarius-quietus:
The oak milkcap is a reddish-brown, zoned-capped Lactarius under oak with an oily, bug-like smell.
It is regarded as edible but of low flavour.
lactarius-repraesentaneus:
The purple-staining bearded milkcap is a large northern Lactarius with a yellow, bearded cap that stains purple when cut.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
lactarius-resimus:
A white, funnel-shaped milk-cap known in Russia as 'gruzd', prepared by salting and brining and regarded as a delicacy in Russia and some other countries. It grows under birch.
Raw it is bitter and acrid; it is always prepared by long soaking and salting or boiling.
lactarius-rubrilacteus:
The bleeding milk cap is a mushroom of western North America that bleeds blood-red milk when cut.
It is regarded as edible.
lactarius-rufulus:
The rufous (southern) candy cap is a Lactarius that smells of maple syrup when dried. It is used to flavour desserts, ice cream and cake.
Edible.
lactarius-rufus:
The rufous milkcap is a red-brown-capped, very acrid Lactarius under pine. In northern Europe it is eaten after boiling and drying or brining.
Raw it is burning and causes upset; not recommended.
lactarius-salmoneus: An orange, edible mushroom close to the Lactarius deliciosus group.
lactarius-salmonicolor:
The salmon milk cap (köknar kanlıcası) is an orange-reddish, salmon-coloured Lactarius that grows near the roots of fir trees. It is one of the three species called 'kanlıca' in Türkiye.
Edible and tasty; it is eaten sautéed in butter.
lactarius-sanguifluus:
The bloody milk cap is an orange-pink-capped mushroom that bleeds dark wine-red milk when cut. It fruits in Mediterranean pine forests in autumn.
A very tasty edible, especially sought after in Spain and Catalonia.
lactarius-scoticus:
The hoary milkcap is a pale, very acrid Lactarius of Europe.
It is inedible.
lactarius-scrobiculatus:
The scrobiculate (potholed) milk cap has a yellow-mustard cap and a pitted stem, and its white milk quickly turns sulphur yellow.
It is acrid and not eaten.
lactarius-semisanguifluus:
Çıntar is a kanlıca with an orange cap that bleeds milk starting orange and quickly turning wine red when cut. It grows in pine forests.
Edible and tasty.
lactarius-subdulcis:
The mild milkcap is a red-brown Lactarius under beech with a mild, slightly sweet taste.
It is regarded as edible with a modest flavour.
lactarius-tabidus:
The birch milkcap is a small orange-brown Lactarius under birch whose white milk turns yellow.
It is inedible.
lactarius-torminosus:
The woolly milkcap is easily recognised by its pinkish zoned cap with a long, hairy margin. It fruits under birch in summer and autumn.
Poisonous raw, causing gastrointestinal poisoning; in countries such as Russia and Finland it is eaten after long boiling and salting, but many sources regard it as poisonous. Not recommended.
lactarius-turpis:
The ugly milk cap is an olive-brown, slimy, very acrid Lactarius under birch and spruce. It has been reported to contain a mutagenic compound (necatorin).
Although eaten salted in Russia and northern Europe, it is not recommended for that reason.
lactarius-uvidus:
The purple-staining milk cap is a Lactarius up to 10 cm across whose white milk turns purple when cut, growing in damp places under birch and willow.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
lactarius-vellereus:
The fleecy milk-cap is a large, white, felty-capped mushroom that is very hard and acrid, fruiting in deciduous woods in summer and autumn.
It is not eaten because it is acrid and burning.
lactarius-vietus:
The grey milkcap is a grey-capped, acrid Lactarius of peaty and damp birch woods.
ultimate-mushroom.com classes it as inedible; some sources regard it as edible.
lactarius-vinaceorufescens:
The yellow-staining milkcap is a Lactarius with wine-red blotches whose white milk turns yellow when cut.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
lactifluus-volemus:
The weeping milk cap (in Turkish 'tirmit') is an orange-brown mushroom 5–15 cm across with a dry cap that bleeds abundant white milk when cut. It develops a fishy smell with age. It fruits in mixed and deciduous woods, especially at the base of hazel trees, in late summer and autumn; it is much loved in the Black Sea region (especially Central Black Sea).
It is eaten cooked, and pickled or brined in the Black Sea. Its mild, slightly sweet, non-acrid milk separates it from many acrid milk-caps.
laetiporus-conifericola:
A bright yellow-orange chicken-of-the-woods that grows on conifers in western North America.
Edible when young, soft and well cooked; it causes digestive upset in some people.
laetiporus-gilbertsonii:
An orange-yellow chicken-of-the-woods on deciduous trees in western North America.
Eaten when young and soft, well cooked.
laetiporus-huroniensis:
A chicken-of-the-woods of the Great Lakes region growing on conifers.
Edible when young and soft, well cooked.
laetiporus-persicinus:
The white chicken mushroom is a pinkish-white chicken-of-the-woods at the base of deciduous trees.
Eaten when young and soft, well cooked; it can upset some people.
laetiporus-sulphureus:
Chicken of the woods (kükürt mantarı, kiraz mantarı) is a bright sulphur-yellow-to-orange mushroom that grows in shelves on trunks of cherry, wild pear, willow, beech, plum, apple, oak, walnut and mahaleb trees. It lives as a saprotroph-parasite and can dry out and rot the tree. It is common from summer to autumn on the coastal parts of Türkiye.
Its taste and texture resemble chicken; the young, soft edges are eaten well cooked. Older parts are tough and bitterish.
Warning: it upsets some people's digestion; toxic reactions have been reported in specimens growing on eucalyptus, linden, spruce and cypress-type trees. Its colour carries a risk of confusion with poisonous mushrooms.
lanmaoa-fragrans:
A rare European bolete with a brownish cap whose flesh turns blue when cut, noted for a pleasant smell.
It is regarded as edible.
lanmaoa-pseudosensibilis:
A North American bolete described in 1971 that turns blue when cut.
It is regarded as edible.
leccinellum-corsicum:
A bolete named after Corsica that forms mycorrhizae with Cistus (rock-rose) shrubs in the Mediterranean.
It is regarded as edible.
leccinellum-crocipodium:
The saffron bolete has a yellowish-brown, cracked cap and turns black when cooked or cut. It grows under oak.
Edible; the blackening when cooked is normal.
leccinellum-griseum: The hornbeam bolete is a common, edible bolete that grows in small groups under hornbeam trees.
leccinellum-rugosiceps: The wrinkled Leccinum is an edible bolete with a wrinkled-cracked cap.
leccinum-aurantiacum:
The red-capped scaber stalk has an orange-red cap and a stem covered in blackish scales, and its flesh turns grey-black when cut. It grows under poplar and oak in summer and autumn.
It is eaten well cooked; raw it upsets some people's stomachs.
leccinum-cyaneobasileucum: The greyshank bolete is an edible Leccinum in grey-white tones.
leccinum-duriusculum: An edible Leccinum under poplar, first described as a Boletus by the Hungarian-Croatian scientist Schulzer.
leccinum-holopus:
The ghost bolete (white birch bolete) is a Leccinum with a white-cream cap in peaty and damp birch woods.
It is regarded as edible.
leccinum-insigne:
The aspen bolete is a Leccinum with an orange-brown cap and a scaly stem under aspen.
It is regarded as edible; cook it well.
leccinum-lepidum: Leccinellum lepidum is an edible bolete-like mushroom.
leccinum-manzanitae: An edible Leccinum described in 1971 from western North America, usually associated with manzanita shrubs.
leccinum-pseudoscabrum: The hazel bolete is an edible bolete under hazel and hornbeam.
leccinum-rufum: An edible bolete with an orange-red cap.
leccinum-scabrum:
The birch bolete has a brown cap, a stem covered in blackish scales and whitish pores. It fruits under birch in summer and autumn. The flesh changes little when cut and darkens when cooked.
Edible and widely collected in Europe and Russia; it must always be well cooked (not eaten raw).
leccinum-variicolor: The mottled bolete is an edible Leccinum with a grey-brown mottled cap.
leccinum-versipelle:
The dark-stalked bolete has an orange-red cap, a stem with dark scales and flesh that turns grey-black when cut. It grows under birch.
It is eaten well cooked; not raw.
leccinum-vulpinum: The foxy bolete is an edible bolete with a red-brown cap in European pine forests.
lentinellus-cochleatus:
The aniseed cockleshell is an edible, aniseed-scented mushroom fruiting in clusters on wood.
The flesh is tough and fibrous, so its value is low.
lentinellus-ursinus:
The bear lentinus has a cap 2–10 cm across, grows on wood and is bitter and acrid.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
lentinula-boryana: An edible shiitake relative found in the subtropical Americas.
lentinula-edodes:
The shiitake is an East Asian mushroom with a brown, white-flecked, cracked cap. In the wild it grows on dead deciduous stumps (beech, oak, shii); today it is the second most cultivated mushroom in the world, grown on oak logs or sawdust blocks. It has a dense, meaty (umami) taste and aroma.
The stem is tough so mostly the cap is eaten, in soups, stir-fries and pan dishes, and drying intensifies its aroma. Eaten raw or undercooked it can cause 'shiitake dermatitis', an itchy, streaky skin rash in some people; cook it well.
lentinula-novae-zelandiae: The New Zealand shiitake is an edible saprotroph on dead wood in New Zealand.
lentinula-raphanica: An edible, radish-scented shiitake relative of tropical regions.
lentinus-arcularius:
The spring polypore is a small, tough mushroom with fine pores that appears on dead wood in spring.
It is inedible because it is so tough.
lentinus-strigosus:
The ruddy panus is a purple-red, hairy, fan-shaped mushroom on dead deciduous wood.
It is regarded as edible when young; it is tough and of low value.
lentinus-tigrinus:
The tiger sawgill is a scaly, tiger-patterned mushroom on dead wood, especially willow and poplar. It is not poisonous.
Edible when young; it becomes woody when older.
leotia-lubrica:
The jelly baby is an olive-yellow, gelatinous, club-shaped mushroom that fruits in groups in damp woods in autumn.
It is inedible.
lepiota-brunneoincarnata:
The deadly dapperling is a small to medium, brown-scaled, ringed Lepiota that fruits in autumn on lawns, in gardens, parks and along roadsides. It contains amatoxins like the death cap.
Symptoms start after 6–24 hours and can lead to liver failure; it has caused deaths. Do not eat small, brown-scaled parasol-like mushrooms.
lepiota-brunneolilacea:
The star dapperling is a small, brown-lilac-scaled, deadly poisonous Lepiota found on sandy ground. It contains amatoxins.
Symptoms start late and can lead to liver failure.
lepiota-castanea:
The chestnut dapperling (petite parasol) is a small, chestnut-brown-scaled, deadly poisonous Lepiota that is uncommon. It contains amatoxins.
Do not eat it.
lepiota-clypeolaria:
The shield dapperling is a common small-to-medium Lepiota with a shaggy stem found in coniferous and deciduous woods.
It is regarded as poisonous; small Lepiotas can be deadly. Do not eat it.
lepiota-cristata:
The stinking dapperling is a small, white-ground Lepiota with red-brown scales and a rubber/rotten-cabbage smell, found in parks and woods in autumn.
Its toxicity is debated; do not eat it.
lepiota-helveola:
A small, brown-pinkish-scaled, deadly poisonous Lepiota described by the Italian mycologist Bresadola. It contains amatoxins.
Do not eat it.
lepiota-ignivolvata:
The orange-girdled parasol is a rare, fairly large Lepiota of coniferous or deciduous woods.
It is inedible.
lepiota-magnispora:
The fluffstem parasol (yellowfoot dapperling) is a beautiful woodland Lepiota with a coarsely scaled yellowish-brown cap.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
lepiota-subincarnata:
The fatal dapperling (deadly parasol) is a small, pinkish-brown-scaled, deadly poisonous Lepiota found in parks, gardens and woodland edges. It contains amatoxins.
It has been a frequent cause of poisoning; do not eat it.
lepista-irina:
The flowery blewit is a pale pink-beige, flower-scented choice edible mushroom that fruits in grassland and at woodland edges in autumn.
It is eaten well cooked.
lepista-luscina:
A saprotrophic funnel mushroom with a cosmopolitan distribution.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
lepista-nuda:
The wood blewit (in Turkish 'mavi cincile', 'mor mantar') has a lilac-violet cap, a bluish-purple stem, a pleasant smell and a pinkish-cream spore print. It fruits in deciduous and coniferous woods and on compost heaps from late autumn into winter.
It is eaten well cooked; it is poisonous raw and causes allergies in some people. It has a distinct aroma.
Important warning: it can be confused with deadly lilac-toned Cortinarius species (rusty spore print, cobweb-like veil). The blewit's spore print is pinkish cream and its stem has no cobweb-like veil.
lepista-personata:
The field blewit has a pale cream-beige cap and a lilac-purple stem and fruits in grassland in autumn. It has a pleasant smell.
It is eaten well cooked; it is poisonous raw.
lepista-sordida:
The sordid blewit is a purple-grey-brown, small mushroom of rich soils such as compost, gardens and grassland, common in the northern hemisphere.
It is eaten well cooked.
leratiomyces-ceres:
The chip cherry is a bright red-orange-capped mushroom growing on wood chips and mulch, native to Australia and New Zealand and now widespread.
It is inedible.
leratiomyces-erythrocephalus:
The red pouch fungus is a red, closed-capped mushroom found in Australia and nearby.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
leratiomyces-squamosus:
The slender roundhead is a small, inedible mushroom on wood chips and mulch.
It is inedible.
leucangium-carthusianum:
The Oregon black truffle is an aromatic truffle of the Pacific Northwest valued in cooking.
Edible.
leucoagaricus-leucothites:
The smooth parasol ('woman on motorcycle') is an entirely white mushroom of lawns and gardens whose ring hangs down like a skirt. It occurs on manured grassland and roadsides.
Although called edible in some places, it can cause gastrointestinal poisoning and closely resembles deadly white mushrooms (Amanita, Lepiota); do not eat it.
leucocoprinus-birnbaumii:
The flower pot parasol is a bright lemon-yellow, delicate, short-lived mushroom that appears in potting soil and greenhouses.
It is inedible and may be poisonous.
leucocoprinus-brebissonii:
The gray-eyed dapperling is a small white mushroom with a grey-black centre on the cap.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
leucocoprinus-cepistipes:
The onion-stalk parasol is a delicate white mushroom with a bulbous stem base found in greenhouses, gardens and woods.
It is regarded as edible but is not recommended because it can be confused with poisonous white mushrooms.
leucopaxillus-gentianeus:
The bitter false funnelcap is a very bitter, inedible mushroom with a thick-fleshed, pale brown cap seen in woods.
It is inedible.
leucopaxillus-giganteus:
The giant funnel is a huge, cream-white, funnel-shaped mushroom that can exceed 30 cm and fruits in rings in grassland and woodland edges.
It is regarded as edible when young; it must not be confused with similar poisonous white funnel mushrooms.
leucopholiota-decorosa: The decorated pholiota is a densely scaly, cream-white edible mushroom on wood.
lichenomphalia-umbellifera:
The lichen agaric is a small yellow mushroom that lives in partnership with algae (lichenised), growing on peat and rotting wood.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
lycoperdon-echinatum:
The spiny puffball is a brown puffball covered in large spines. It fruits in deciduous woods, especially under beech, in spring to autumn.
It is edible while the inside is entirely white.
lycoperdon-excipuliforme:
The pestle puffball is a puffball with a long, thick stalk topped by a rounded spore-bearing head, found in grassland and woodland edges.
It is edible while the inside is white.
lycoperdon-mammiforme:
The flaky puffball is a rare puffball of deciduous woods.
It is inedible.
lycoperdon-molle:
The smooth (soft) puffball is a soft-textured, cream-brown puffball found in woods.
It is edible while the inside is white.
lycoperdon-nigrescens:
The dusky puffball is a foul-smelling puffball that darkens with age.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
lycoperdon-perlatum:
The common puffball (gem-studded puffball) is a white, pear-shaped puffball covered in needle-like spines that leave net-like marks when they fall. It is very common in woods, grassland and tracks in summer and autumn.
It is edible while the inside is pure white; yellowed or darkened ones are not eaten. Cut the mushroom lengthwise and check that there is no cap and stem outline inside: young deadly Amanita 'eggs' look similar.
lycoperdon-pratense:
The meadow puffball is a white, flat-topped puffball of meadows and pastures.
It is edible while the inside is white.
lycoperdon-pulcherrimum:
The long-spined puffball is a puffball with long, pointed spines found in woods.
It is edible while the inside is white.
lycoperdon-umbrinum:
The umber-brown puffball is a dark brown, fine-spined puffball of coniferous and deciduous woods.
It is edible while the inside is white.
lyophyllum-decastes:
The fried chicken mushroom is a thick-fleshed mushroom that fruits in large clusters of grey-brown caps along roadsides and in deciduous woods in summer and autumn, and blackens when touched.
It is eaten well cooked, with a firm texture and a pleasant flavour. Identify it carefully because it can be confused with poisonous Entoloma and funnel mushrooms.
lyophyllum-littoralis: A grey, edible saprotroph closely related to the fried chicken mushroom.
lyophyllum-shimeji:
Hon-shimeji is a mycorrhizal mushroom of pine forests highly valued in Japan and hard to cultivate commercially.
Edible and tasty.
macrocystidia-cucumis:
The cucumber cap is a common, inedible mushroom with a cucumber or fish smell and a dark red-brown cap, often found in large numbers on needle litter.
It is inedible.
macrolepiota-excoriata:
A parasol mushroom of meadows and pastures with a pale cream-brown, flat cap and white gills.
It is regarded as edible; identify it carefully since it can be confused with deadly Lepiota and Amanita species.
macrolepiota-mastoidea:
The slender parasol is like the parasol mushroom but smaller and more delicate, with a pointed-topped cap, fruiting in grassland and woodland edges in autumn.
It is regarded as edible.
macrolepiota-procera:
The parasol mushroom (in Turkish 'şemsiye mantarı', 'turnabacağı') is very distinctive with a height of over 40 cm, a thin snakeskin-patterned stem and a movable, double ring. The cap is closed like a drumstick when young, then opens like an umbrella to 10–40 cm and is covered in brown scales. It fruits in grassland, woodland edges and clearings from late summer to autumn.
A large and very tasty edible: the cap is breaded and fried ('mushroom schnitzel'). The stem is fibrous and tough and not eaten. Cook it well.
Important warning: it can be confused with the poisonous Chlorophyllum molybdites (green spore print) and with small deadly Lepiota species; small, young specimens are especially risky. The snakeskin-patterned stem and movable ring distinguish this species.
macrolepiota-zeyheri: An edible parasol mushroom of Africa known by local names.
marasmiellus-ramealis:
The twig parachute is a tiny mushroom growing on thin twigs.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
marasmius-bulliardii:
A tiny mushroom of leaf litter described by the French mycologist Bulliard.
It is inedible.
marasmius-haematocephalus:
The purple pinwheel is a very small, purple-red mushroom of tropical and subtropical forests.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
marasmius-oreades:
The fairy ring mushroom grows in rings (fairy rings) on lawns and pastures, with a beige-tan, bell-shaped cap, a tough stem and distant gills. It fruits after summer and autumn rain, and can revive with rain after drying out.
It is edible and tasty, with a sweet, almond-like aroma. Because the stems are tough only the caps are used; they add flavour to soups and sauces.
Important warning: it is confused with poisonous white funnel mushrooms (Clitocybe rivulosa, C. dealbata) that grow in the same grass; those contain muscarine and have caused poisonings. The fairy ring mushroom has distant gills and a tough, springy stem and a sweet smell.
marasmius-rotula:
The pinwheel mushroom is a tiny mushroom with a pleated, wheel-like cap and a thin black stem on dead wood in summer and autumn.
It is inedible.
marasmius-siccus:
The orange pinwheel is a tiny orange mushroom of leaf litter in Eurasia and eastern North America.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
melanogaster-ambiguus:
The stinking slime truffle is a sticky, foul-smelling, truffle-like fungus near the soil surface, described by Vittadini.
It is inedible.
melanoleuca-cognata:
The spring cavalier is a fairly large mushroom with a beige-brown cap that fruits in spring in coniferous forests.
It is regarded as edible.
melanoleuca-melaleuca:
The type species of the genus Melanoleuca, a mushroom with a dark brown cap and white gills found in grassland and woodland edges.
It is regarded as edible.
melastiza-chateri:
The false eyelash cup is a small, orange, cup-shaped fungus on bare soil in Europe.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
meripilus-giganteus:
The giant polypore (blackening polypore) is a huge cream-brown mushroom of overlapping fronds in large clusters at the base and over the roots of deciduous trees (especially beech); it turns black when touched. It causes white rot and can bring the tree down.
When young and soft it is regarded as edible, but it toughens quickly and upsets many people's stomachs.
meripilus-sumstinei:
The giant (black-staining) polypore forms large clusters at the base of deciduous trees in North America and blackens when touched.
It is regarded as edible when young.
metuloidea-murashkinskyi:
A small, spiny-surfaced fungus on dead wood in Europe and Asia.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
microglossum-olivaceum:
The olive earthtongue is an olive-green, matchstick-shaped fungus of damp meadows and woods.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
microglossum-viride:
The green earth tongue is a green, tongue-shaped fungus of damp mossy places.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
microstoma-floccosum:
The shaggy scarlet cup is a deep, funnel-shaped red cup fungus with white hairs growing on dead twigs.
It is inedible.
microstoma-protractum:
A small, red, long-stalked cup fungus on dead twigs, first described as a Peziza.
It is inedible.
mitrula-paludosa:
The swamp (bog) beacon is a small, bright yellow-headed, white-stalked fungus on decaying leaves in shallow, still water.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
morchella-americana:
The yellow morel is a widespread North American morel with a yellowish, honeycomb-patterned cap.
It must always be eaten well cooked; it is poisonous raw.
morchella-anatolica:
The Anatolian morel is a rare morel described from Anatolia.
It must always be eaten well cooked; it is poisonous raw.
morchella-angusticeps:
The black morel is a narrow, dark morel native to eastern North America.
It must always be eaten well cooked; it is poisonous raw.
morchella-australiana:
A morel native to Australia described as new to science in 2014.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-brunnea:
A brown morel described in 2012 from Oregon.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-conica:
The conical (black) morel is the group of morels with a pointed conical cap and dark brown-black ridges; it is an old binomial covering many close species.
It must always be eaten well cooked; it is poisonous raw.
morchella-cryptica:
A morel species described in 2012 that fruits near elm and old trees.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-deliciosa:
The yellow morel is an edible spring morel.
It must always be eaten well cooked; it is poisonous raw.
morchella-diminutiva:
A small morel native to North America.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-elata:
The black morel has a pointed cap covered in dark brown-black, elongated ridges. It fruits in spring in burned areas and coniferous forests.
It must always be eaten well cooked; it is poisonous raw.
morchella-eohespera:
A North American morel described in 2016.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-esculenta:
The common morel (kuzugöbeği, höbelen) is easily told from other mushrooms by its pitted, honeycomb-like, completely hollow cap and is one of the most collected and exported wild mushrooms of Türkiye. The cap is honey yellow to brown, and the stem is whitish and hollow. It fruits in spring, singly or in small groups, on limy, damp soils under hazel, beech, maple and elm and in pine forests. Dried it sells at a high price.
Morels must not be eaten raw: raw or undercooked they are poisonous. They must be cooked thoroughly; discomfort has also been reported when eaten with alcohol.
Important warning: mistaking the false morel (Gyromitra esculenta) for it has caused deaths in Türkiye. A true morel cut lengthwise shows cap and stem forming a single, completely hollow cavity; the false one is filled with cottony tissue and has a brain-like folded cap.
morchella-galilaea:
A morel described in 2012 from Galilee that fruits very early in spring.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-importuna:
The black landscape morel can fruit in gardens, mulch and disturbed ground and is now being grown in fields and tunnels.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-populiphila:
A morel found under cottonwood (poplar) trees in northwestern North America.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-prava:
A morel described as new to science in 2012 that fruits in disturbed areas and after burns.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-pulchella:
A morel with folded ridges described in 2012.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-punctipes:
A widely distributed North American morel with a half-free cap.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-purpurascens:
The purple morel is a morel whose ridges take on purple tones.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-rufobrunnea:
The blushing morel is a morel that turns reddish-brown and fruits in disturbed ground, gardens and mulch; it is cultivated commercially.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-semilibera:
The half-free morel fruits in spring with a cap that is attached to the stem only in its upper half; the stem is longer than the cap.
It must always be eaten well cooked; it is poisonous raw. Its aroma is milder than the true morel.
morchella-septentrionalis:
A North American morel described in 2012.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-septimelata:
A morel described in 2012 that fruits in burned forests.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-sextelata:
A morel described in 2012 that fruits in burned areas and is grown commercially.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-snyderi:
A morel described in 2012 that occurs in mountainous regions.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-spongiola:
The spongy morel, described by the French mycologist Jean Louis Boudier, is an important species in the morel trade.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-steppicola:
The morel of the steppes is a blistered-surfaced morel of the steppes of Central Asia.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-tomentosa:
The gray (fuzzy foot, black foot) morel fruits in burned areas, with a velvety-hairy stem and a grey-brown cap.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-tridentina:
A cosmopolitan, widespread morel.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
morchella-vulgaris:
A widespread morel that fruits in spring in woods and disturbed ground.
It must always be eaten well cooked.
mutinus-caninus:
The dog stinkhorn is a thin, finger-shaped woodland mushroom with a tip covered in dark olive foul-smelling spores. It emerges from an egg stage.
It is inedible; the smell is bad.
mutinus-ravenelii: Ravenel's red stinkhorn is a pink-red, slender, finger-shaped stinkhorn of North America. The egg stage is regarded as edible but is not eaten because of the smell.
mycena-acicula:
The orange bonnet is a bright orange, needle-thin, tiny Mycena on dead twigs.
It is inedible.
mycena-adonis:
The scarlet bonnet is a bright red-orange, tiny Mycena relative growing in damp moss.
It is inedible.
mycena-aetites:
The drab bonnet is a small grey-brown Mycena growing in grass.
It is inedible.
mycena-alcalina:
The alkaline mycena (stump fairy helmet) is a small mushroom on stumps with a faint bleach-like smell.
It is inedible.
mycena-arcangeliana:
The angel's bonnet is a small brown-grey Mycena that fruits in late autumn.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
mycena-cyanorrhiza:
A small, white mushroom with blue colours; unlike hallucinogenic mushrooms, its blue colour is not related to psychoactive compounds.
This is not consumption advice.
mycena-epipterygia:
