The yellowleg bonnet is a small Mycena with a sticky yellow stem and a grey cap found in European coniferous woods in autumn.
It is regarded as edible but is tiny and worthless.
mycena-flavescens:
A small, yellowish Mycena described by the Czech mycologist Velenovský.
It is regarded as edible but worthless.
mycena-flavoalba:
The ivory bonnet is a cream-white, tiny mushroom found in grass and moss.
It is inedible.
mycena-galericulata:
The common bonnet is a very common brown-grey, bell-shaped Mycena that fruits in clusters on stumps.
It is inedible; the taste is dull and the smell unpleasant.
mycena-galopus:
The milky mycena (milking bonnet) is a small grey-brown Mycena whose stem drips white milk when broken.
It is inedible.
mycena-haematopus:
The bleeding fairy helmet is a Mycena that bleeds dark burgundy fluid when its stem is broken, fruiting in clusters on stumps.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
mycena-inclinata:
The clustered bonnet is a small brown Mycena fruiting in clusters on oak stumps with a toothed cap edge and an unpleasant smell.
It is inedible.
mycena-maculata:
The reddish-spotted Mycena is a small mushroom on stumps that develops red spots with age.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
mycena-metata:
The frost bonnet is a small pinkish-grey Mycena found in Europe.
It is inedible.
mycena-polygramma:
The grooved bonnet is a slender grey Mycena with long grooves on the stem found on stumps and at tree bases.
It is inedible.
mycena-pura:
The lilac mycena (lilac bonnet) is a lilac-purple-toned Mycena with a radish smell, common on leaf and needle litter in woods. It contains muscarine.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
mycena-purpureofusca:
The purple edge bonnet is a Mycena with a purple-brown stem and purple-edged gills in coniferous woods.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
mycena-renati:
The beautiful bonnet is a small pinkish-cream Mycena with a yellow stem on dead wood.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
mycena-rosea:
The rosy bonnet is a pink, radish-scented, bioluminescent Mycena of woodland leaf litter. It contains muscarine.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
mycena-strobilinoides:
The flame mycena (scarlet fairy helmet) is a bright orange-red, tiny mushroom of mossy places in coniferous forests.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
mycena-tintinnabulum:
A small European Mycena that can fruit until late winter; its mycelium, but not its fruit body, is bioluminescent.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
mycena-vitilis:
The snapping bonnet is a small Mycena whose thin, brittle stem snaps with a click when bent.
It is inedible.
mycenastrum-corium:
A widely distributed puffball whose leathery outer skin hardens and splits with maturity.
It is regarded as edible while the inside is white.
mycetinis-alliaceus:
The garlic parachute is a small mushroom with a strong garlic smell and a thin, long black stem, growing on buried twigs and roots of beech in summer and autumn.
Dried, it is used as a seasoning in place of garlic.
mycetinis-scorodonius:
The garlic mushroom is a small, garlic-scented mushroom with a thin black stem growing on rotting leaves.
Dried, it is used as a seasoning in place of garlic.
myriostoma-coliforme:
The saltshaker earthstar (pepper pot) is a rare earthstar with several pores on top, like a pepper pot.
It is inedible.
nectria-cinnabarina:
Coral spot is a plant pathogen that forms red-orange pustules on dead branches of broadleaf trees.
It is inedible.
neoalbatrellus-caeruleoporus:
The blue-pored polypore is a rare, endangered fungus with blue pores.
It is inedible.
neoboletus-luridiformis:
The dotted stem bolete has a yellow-brown cap, orange-red pores and flesh that turns dark blue quickly when cut; the stem is dotted with red. It fruits in European oak, beech and coniferous woods in summer and autumn.
It is edible when well cooked; it is poisonous raw or undercooked, and should not be eaten with alcohol. It resembles the devil's bolete (Rubroboletus satanas), which is poisonous and has red pores.
neofavolus-alveolaris:
The hexagonal-pored polypore is a small, yellowish bracket fungus with hexagonal pores underneath that fruits in spring on deciduous branches.
It is regarded as edible when young but is tough.
neolentinus-lepideus:
The scaly lentinus grows on coniferous stumps and railway sleepers with a scaly cap and resists creosote.
It is regarded as edible when young but is tough and bitterish; ultimate-mushroom.com lists it as poisonous, so it is not recommended.
neolentinus-ponderosus:
The giant sawgill is a large, cream-coloured mushroom on dead coniferous wood.
Edible when young.
omphalotus-illudens:
The eastern jack-o'-lantern is an orange, poisonous mushroom that fruits in clusters at stump bases and can glow faintly in the dark.
It causes severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and cramps and is confused with the edible chanterelle.
omphalotus-japonicus:
The tsukiyotake ('moonlit night mushroom') is an orange-brown, poisonous mushroom of Japan and nearby that can glow in the dark. It is a frequent cause of poisoning when mistaken for shiitake and other edibles.
Do not eat it.
omphalotus-nidiformis:
The ghost fungus is a poisonous mushroom of southern Australia that glows a greenish light in the dark, growing on dead trees.
It must not be eaten; it causes gastrointestinal poisoning.
omphalotus-olearius:
The jack-o'-lantern mushroom (in Turkish 'ağulu mantar', 'yalancı kanlıca') is a poisonous mushroom that fruits in clusters on stumps and on roots of trees such as olive and oak, ranging from orange-yellow to orange-brown. The cap is 7–10 cm and funnel-shaped; the gills are thin, run down the stem and are true gills; the stem is 7–15 cm. The gills can glow faintly in the dark (bioluminescence). It fruits in autumn.
Its illudin compounds cause severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and cramps, starting within 30 minutes to 3 hours. It is usually not fatal but is a hard illness.
It causes poisonings in Türkiye too because it is mistaken for the edible golden chanterelle (Cantharellus cibarius): the chanterelle has false (vein-like) ridges, while the jack-o'-lantern has true, sharp-edged gills and grows in clusters on stumps.
omphalotus-olivascens:
The western jack-o'-lantern is an olive-greenish orange poisonous mushroom that fruits in clusters at the base of oak and other trees.
Although not fatal it causes very severe gastrointestinal poisoning; do not eat it.
onnia-tomentosa:
The woolly velvet polypore is a velvety, rusty-brown, tough fungus on roots of conifers.
It is inedible.
otidea-bufonia:
The toad's ear is a dark brown, ear-shaped cup fungus that appears from late summer.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
otidea-leporina:
Rabbit ears is a yellow-brown, ear-shaped cup fungus that fruits in clusters in woods.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
otidea-onotica:
The hare's ear (donkey ear) is a yellow-orange-pinkish, long, ear-shaped cup fungus that fruits in deciduous and coniferous woods in summer and autumn.
In some places it is eaten cooked; the taste is modest and species are easily confused.
oudemansiella-mucida:
The porcelain fungus is a white, shiny, very slimy-capped mushroom that fruits in autumn on beech, usually on dead branches.
It is regarded as edible but its texture is very slimy and its flavour poor.
oudemansiella-raphanipes:
A mushroom with a long, deeply rooting stem growing from buried wood of deciduous trees (Hymenopellis raphanipes).
It is regarded as edible; the cap is preferred because the stem is tough.
panaeolina-foenisecii:
The lawnmower's mushroom is a small, brown, two-toned-when-dry mushroom of lawns, very common after summer and autumn rain.
Although listed as edible it is tiny and worthless, and because small brown lawn mushrooms include deadly Conocybe and Galerina species the risk of confusion is high. Do not eat it.
panaeolus-antillarum:
A small brown mushroom growing on dung.
Although listed as edible it is worthless; do not eat it.
panaeolus-bisporus:
A widely distributed, rarely identified small brown mushroom that bruises blue (Copelandia bisporus). It contains psilocybin.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
panaeolus-cambodginiensis:
A tropical dung-growing mushroom described in 1979 that contains psilocybin and psilocin.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
panaeolus-cinctulus:
The banded mottlegill is a small, brown, banded mushroom growing on manured lawns and horse dung. It is reported to contain psilocybin.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
panaeolus-cyanescens:
The blue-staining panaeolus grows on dung, turns blue when touched and contains psilocybin.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
panaeolus-fimicola:
The turf mottlegill is a widespread but rarely identified small brown mushroom of lawns, reported to possibly contain psilocybin.
This is not consumption advice.
panaeolus-olivaceus:
A widely distributed, rarely identified small brown mushroom containing psilocybin.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
panaeolus-papilionaceus:
The bell-capped (petticoat) mottlegill is a bell-shaped, pale grey-brown-capped mushroom of dung and manured grassland. Some sources note that it may contain psychoactive compounds.
This is not consumption advice.
panaeolus-semiovatus:
The shiny mottlegill is a glossy, beige-grey, ringed mushroom of horse and cow dung. Some sources call it psychoactive, but this is disputed.
This is not consumption advice.
panaeolus-tropicalis:
A psilocybin-producing mushroom (Copelandia) on dung in tropical regions.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
panellus-stipticus:
The bitter oyster (luminescent panellus) is a small, fan-shaped, intensely bitter and astringent mushroom on dead deciduous trees. It glows faintly in the dark (bioluminescence). It is called 'styptic' because it was once used to stop bleeding.
It is not eaten because it is bitter.
panus-conchatus:
The lilac oysterling (conch panus) is a lilac-toned, fan-shaped, tough mushroom on dead deciduous trees.
It is regarded as edible when young; it toughens quickly.
panus-neostrigosus:
The hairy oyster mushroom is a hairy, purple-brown, fan-shaped mushroom on dead deciduous trees.
ultimate-mushroom.com classes it as inedible; some sources regard the young form as edible.
paralepista-flaccida:
The tawny funnel is an orange-brown, funnel-shaped mushroom of leaf litter in coniferous and mixed woods in autumn, with gills running down the stem.
It is regarded as edible; it may be slightly bitter and must be cooked well.
paralepistopsis-acromelalga:
A poisonous funnel mushroom of Asia that causes painful redness (acromelalgia) of the hands and feet lasting weeks after eating.
Do not eat it.
parasola-auricoma:
The goldenhaired inkcap is a small, very short-lived inkcap with a golden-haired cap.
It is inedible.
parasola-plicatilis:
The pleated inkcap has a cap like a folded umbrella, is very delicate and lives for only a few hours; it grows in lawns.
It is inedible.
paxillus-cuprinus:
The coppery pax is a close relative of Paxillus involutus growing under birch.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
paxillus-involutus:
The brown roll-rim has an inrolled cap margin and is brown and funnel-shaped; the gills darken to brown on touch. It fruits in summer and autumn under birch and conifers, sometimes on rotting wood.
It was formerly regarded as edible because it was eaten in Eastern Europe, but with repeated consumption it causes an immune reaction (Paxillus syndrome: the immune system destroys red blood cells, with kidney failure) and has caused deaths. The German mycologist Julius Schäffer was a victim of it in 1944. It is also poisonous raw.
Never eat it.
peziza-ammophila:
The dune cup is a brown, cup-shaped fungus on sand dunes and beaches.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
peziza-arvernensis:
The boring brown cup fungus (fairy tub) is a brown, cup-shaped fungus of woods and freshly disturbed ground.
It is inedible.
peziza-badia:
The bay cup is a chestnut-brown, cup-shaped fungus of forest tracks and sandy ground.
Some sources regard it as edible, but it can be poisonous raw and is tasteless.
peziza-cerea:
The cellar cup is a cream-coloured cup fungus growing in damp cellars and basements.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
peziza-domiciliana:
The domicile cup fungus is a cup fungus that can appear in houses on damp walls and under carpets.
It is inedible.
peziza-phyllogena:
The common brown cup (pig-ear cup) is a brown, cup-shaped fungus under deciduous trees.
It is regarded as edible when cooked but of low value; it may be poisonous raw.
peziza-varia:
The spreading brown cup (palomino cup) is a brown cup fungus on wood and woody debris.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
peziza-vesiculosa:
The common dung cup is a cream-brown, cup-shaped fungus on dung and rich soil.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
peziza-violacea:
The violet fairy cup is a violet-toned, cup-shaped fungus on burned ground.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
phaeolepiota-aurea:
The golden bootleg is a large, golden-yellow-orange, thick, powdery mushroom with a broad ring that fruits along roadsides and in damp woods in autumn. Some sources regard it as poisonous; its safety is not certain.
Do not eat it.
phaeolus-schweinitzii:
The velvet-top fungus (dyer's polypore) is a large, velvety, yellow-brown, flat bracket fungus at the roots and base of conifers. It is called the dyer's polypore because it gives yellow, orange and green shades in wool dyeing. It causes brown rot.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
phallus-hadriani:
The dune stinkhorn emerges from a pinkish-purplish egg on dune ground and smells foul.
The egg stage is regarded as edible but is rarely eaten because of the smell.
phallus-impudicus:
The common stinkhorn emerges from a white egg as a long, white-stemmed mushroom with an olive-green tip and a smell of rotting meat. The smell attracts flies, which spread the spores. It fruits in gardens, woods and woodland edges in summer and autumn.
The egg stage is eaten in some places (Eastern Europe, France) and tastes like radish; the mature mushroom is not eaten because of its smell.
phallus-indusiatus:
The bamboo mushroom (basket stinkhorn) is a very curious mushroom with a long white stem and a fine, lacy 'skirt' hanging like a bridal veil, found near bamboo, stumps and rotting wood in tropical and subtropical regions.
In Chinese cuisine it is dried as 'zhu sun' and used in soups as a valued edible; the skirt and smelly cap portion are removed.
phallus-multicolor:
The yellow bridal veil stinkhorn is a stinkhorn of Australia and nearby with a yellow-orange lacy skirt.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
phallus-ravenelii: Ravenel's stinkhorn is a foul-smelling stinkhorn of North America. The egg stage is regarded as edible but is not eaten because of the smell.
phallus-rubicundus:
A red, finger-shaped, foul-smelling stinkhorn widespread in tropical and subtropical regions (Satyrus rubicundus), described in 1811.
It is inedible.
phellinus-igniarius:
The willow bracket (false tinder polypore) is a perennial, hard, hoof-shaped, dark grey-black bracket on willow and other deciduous trunks, causing white rot.
It is inedible; it is very hard.
phellinus-lundellii:
The birch bristle bracket is a hard, perennial bracket fungus on birch in Eurasia.
It is inedible.
phellinus-viticola:
A brown, hard bracket fungus on dead wood.
It is inedible.
phellodon-melaleucus:
The grey tooth is a hard, corky, grey-toned tooth fungus of coniferous forests.
It is inedible.
phellodon-niger:
The black tooth is the type species of Phellodon, a blackish, hard tooth fungus of coniferous forests.
It is inedible.
phellodon-tomentosus:
The zoned phellodon is a hard tooth fungus with a zoned, woolly cap found in pine forests.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
phlebia-radiata:
The wrinkled crust is a common orange-pink, wrinkled crust fungus on dead deciduous wood.
It is inedible.
phlebia-tremellosa:
The trembling Merulius (jelly rot) is an orange-white, honeycomb-patterned fungus that wobbles like jelly on dead wood.
It is inedible.
pholiota-adiposa:
The chestnut mushroom (Pholiota adiposa) is a slimy, scaly, yellow-brown mushroom on trunks and stumps of deciduous trees in North America and Eurasia.
It is regarded as edible; the slimy surface is peeled and it is cooked well.
pholiota-aurivella:
The golden pholiota is a sticky, golden-yellow mushroom with reddish scales on tree trunks.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
pholiota-flammans:
The flame scalecap is a bright yellow mushroom covered in pointed scales, growing on conifer stumps.
It is inedible.
pholiota-gummosa:
The sticky scalycap is a common mushroom with a sticky cap on woody debris and rotting wood.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
pholiota-limonella:
The lemon-yellow pholiota is a lemon-yellow, slimy mushroom on fallen beech trunks and other hardwoods.
It is inedible.
pholiota-microspora:
Nameko is an amber-brown mushroom with a gelatinous, slimy cap, widely known and cultivated in Japan and used in miso soup and hotpots.
Edible; cook it well.
pholiota-squarrosa:
The shaggy scalycap is a mushroom whose yellowish cap and stem are covered in recurved brown scales, fruiting in clusters at the base of trees, with a garlic/radish smell.
It is regarded as poisonous and can cause gastrointestinal poisoning, especially with alcohol. Do not eat it.
pholiota-squarrosoides:
The scaly pholiota resembles the shaggy scalycap and grows on trunks of deciduous trees.
It is regarded as edible but has poisonous look-alikes.
phylloporus-pelletieri:
The golden-gilled bolete is a bolete relative with yellow gills instead of pores.
It is regarded as edible.
phylloporus-rhodoxanthus:
The gilled bolete is a bolete relative with gills and a red-brown cap.
It is regarded as edible.
phyllotopsis-nidulans:
The mock oyster (orange oyster) is an orange, hairy, foul-smelling mushroom on dead wood, smelling of rotten cabbage.
It is inedible.
pisolithus-arhizus:
Dead man's foot (dyeball) is a potato-like, irregular, brown-yellow mushroom on the ground; as it matures its inside fills with pea-sized spore packets used in dyemaking. It forms mycorrhizae with pine and other tree roots.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
pleurocybella-porrigens:
The angel wing is a white, thin, fan-shaped mushroom on coniferous trunks.
In Japan in 2004, cases of fatal acute brain disease (encephalopathy) occurred in people with kidney disease after eating it, so it should not be eaten.
pleurotus-australis: The brown oyster mushroom is an edible oyster mushroom native to Australia and New Zealand, growing on dead wood.
pleurotus-citrinopileatus:
The golden oyster (tamogitake) is a commercially grown oyster mushroom with a bright lemon-yellow cap that grows in clusters; in East Asia it occurs on deciduous trees and has a nutty aroma.
It is eaten well cooked.
pleurotus-cornucopiae:
The white (horn of plenty) oyster is a funnel-shaped, cream-coloured, edible oyster mushroom on wood.
It is eaten well cooked.
pleurotus-djamor:
The pink oyster is a vivid pink oyster mushroom of the tropics that is also cultivated; it likes warmth. The pink colour fades when cooked.
It is eaten well cooked.
pleurotus-dryinus:
The veiled oyster is a white-cream oyster mushroom with a veil on living or dead trunks of deciduous trees such as oak.
Eaten when young and well cooked.
pleurotus-eryngii:
The king trumpet (king oyster; in Turkish 'kulacık' or 'diken mantarı') is a Mediterranean-origin oyster mushroom known for its thick, fleshy white stem and small brown cap. In nature it lives on roots and remains of umbellifers such as Eryngium and Ferula. Today it is grown commercially on a large scale worldwide.
With its meaty stem and mildly sweet, umami taste it is highly valued; it is sliced and fried or grilled. The stem is the tastiest part.
pleurotus-euosmus: The tarragon oyster is an edible oyster mushroom with a tarragon-like smell.
pleurotus-nebrodensis:
The white ferula mushroom ('basilisk mushroom') is a very rare and valuable close relative of the king trumpet that grows on the roots of Ferula plants in the Nebrodi mountains of Sicily. Its natural range is under threat.
It is a very tasty edible.
pleurotus-opuntiae: An edible oyster mushroom of semi-arid central Mexico and New Zealand growing on cactus and wood.
pleurotus-ostreatus:
The oyster mushroom (in Turkish 'kavak mantarı', 'kayın mantarı') grows in shelves on trees, with shell-shaped caps in grey-blue, brown or cream and gills that run down the stem. When winter comes it appears on trunks and root bases of deciduous trees, especially poplar, willow and beech; it lives as a saprotroph on dead or weak trees and sometimes as a weak parasite. It was first cultivated in Germany during World War I to make up for food shortages, and it is now among the most widely grown mushrooms in the world.
It has a mildly sweet aroma likened to oyster or lobster; it is sliced and fried, used in soups and sautéed. It must always be cooked and is not eaten raw. Young specimens are softer and it toughens with age.
A poisonous look-alike is rare, but still confirm identification with someone who knows this gill-decurrent, tree-growing species (for example, it can be confused with toxic tree mushrooms such as Pleurocybella and Omphalotus).
pleurotus-parsonsiae: The velvet oyster is an edible oyster mushroom with a velvety cap on dead wood in New Zealand.
pleurotus-populinus: The aspen oyster is an edible oyster mushroom on dead aspen wood in North America.
pleurotus-pulmonarius:
The summer (Indian, Italian) oyster is a thinner, paler oyster mushroom that fruits in warm weather and is grown commercially.
It is eaten well cooked.
pleurotus-purpureo-olivaceus: An edible oyster mushroom in purple-olive tones on dead wood, native to Australia and New Zealand.
pleurotus-tuber-regium: The king tuber mushroom is an edible oyster mushroom of the tropics of Africa and Asia that forms a large underground sclerotium (tuber), used in medicine and cooking.
pluteus-americanus:
A Pluteus of North America and Russia growing on hardwoods that is regarded as psychoactive.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
pluteus-cervinus:
The deer shield is a brown, plump-capped saprotrophic mushroom whose gills turn from white to pink, common on dead trees and stumps. The spore print is pink and the stem has no ring. It is widespread in Europe and North America in summer and autumn.
It is regarded as edible, with a faint radish-like smell. Some authorities do not recommend eating it and poisoning cases have been recorded.
pluteus-cyanopus:
A Pluteus of Africa, Europe and North America with a bluish stem that is reported to contain psilocybin.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
pluteus-leoninus:
The lion shield is a Pluteus with a golden-lion-coloured cap growing on deciduous wood debris.
It is regarded as edible with a modest flavour.
pluteus-pellitus:
The ghost shield is a white, wood-dwelling Pluteus.
It is regarded as poisonous and is not eaten.
pluteus-salicinus:
The willow shield ('Knackers Crumpet') is a European Pluteus with a grey-greenish cap on willow and other deciduous trees that is reported to contain psilocybin. Although described as edible after parboiling, it is not recommended.
It may be psychoactive; this is not consumption advice.
podaxis-pistillaris:
The false shaggy mane is a desert mushroom with a cylindrical cap on a long, thin white stem, related to puffballs and inkcaps; it turns powdery when mature.
It is regarded as edible when young.
podostroma-cornu-damae:
Kaentake ('fire mushroom'; Trichoderma cornu-damae) is a bright red-orange, coral- or finger-shaped, extremely poisonous mushroom that grows at the base of dead deciduous trees in Japan and South Korea. It contains trichothecene mycotoxins, and merely touching it can cause skin inflammation.
If eaten it causes very severe multi-organ failure, brain damage and death. Never touch or eat it.
polyozellus-multiplex:
The blue chanterelle is a dark blue-purple, folded, fan-like mushroom with fused narrow stems growing in coniferous forests. It is collected in years of abundance and is also known as the black chanterelle.
Edible; it may be slightly bitter and is also used as a dye.
polyporus-brumalis:
The winter polypore is a small, brown, tough mushroom on dead wood that can also be seen in winter.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
polyporus-ciliatus:
The fringed polypore is a small, thin, fringed-edge mushroom on dead deciduous wood in spring.
It is inedible.
polyporus-melanopus:
A tough, black-stemmed mushroom on dead wood or buried branches (Picipes melanopus).
It is inedible.
polyporus-tuberaster:
The tuberous polypore (stone fungus) grows on deciduous wood debris, with a cream-brown, scaly cap and a stem arising from a hard underground tuber (sclerotium). In Italy it is grown as the 'stone fungus' from its tuber embedded in soil blocks.
Edible when young and soft; it is tough and must be cooked well.
polyporus-umbellatus: The umbrella polypore (zhuling) is an edible mushroom with many small caps joined on a single stem at the base of deciduous trees; it is used in traditional Chinese medicine.
poronidulus-conchifer:
The little nest polypore is a small, thin, zoned bracket fungus on dead deciduous trees.
It is inedible.
porphyrellus-porphyrosporus:
The dusky bolete is a rare bolete with a dark brown-smoky cap and flesh that turns blue-black when cut; the spore print is purple-brown. It fruits in woods in summer and autumn.
It is regarded as edible but of modest flavour; ultimate-mushroom.com classes it as inedible.
porpolomopsis-calyptriformis:
The pink wax cap (ballerina waxcap) is a beautiful, rare mushroom with a pink, pointed, conical cap that fruits in unfertilised old meadows in autumn; it has become rare and protected in many countries.
It is regarded as edible, but being rare it is better left uncollected.
postia-tephroleuca:
The greyling bracket is a white-grey, soft, watery bracket fungus on deciduous trees.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
psathyrella-ammophila:
The dune brittlestem is a delicate cream-brown mushroom of European sand dunes near dune plants.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
psathyrella-corrugis:
The red edge brittlestem is the type species of Psathyrella, a delicate mushroom of woods.
It is inedible.
psathyrella-longipes:
The fringecap brittlestem (tall Psathyrella) is a long, thin-stemmed, brown, fragile mushroom.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
psathyrella-piluliformis:
The clustered brittlestem is a brown mushroom that fruits in clusters on deciduous stumps, with a cap that darkens in damp.
It is regarded as edible but of low value, and it can be confused with brown-spored poisonous mushrooms.
psathyrella-spadicea:
The chestnut brittlestem is a fragile mushroom with a chestnut-brown cap at the base of deciduous trees.
It is regarded as edible but of low value.
pseudoboletus-parasiticus:
The parasitic bolete grows on earthballs (Scleroderma) and is a pale yellow-brown bolete.
It is regarded as edible but of low value.
pseudoclitocybe-cyathiformis:
The goblet funnel cap is a dark brown-grey, goblet-shaped mushroom that fruits in leaf litter in late autumn.
It is regarded as edible but of low value and can be confused with poisonous funnel mushrooms.
pseudocolus-fusiformis:
The stinky squid is a carrion-smelling stinkhorn with three or four orange-red arms emerging from an egg stage.
It is inedible.
pseudohydnum-gelatinosum:
The toothed jelly fungus (cat's tongue) is a grey-translucent, tongue-shaped jelly fungus with spines underneath on coniferous stumps.
It is regarded as edible and used raw in salads or desserts, with a bland taste.
pseudoplectania-nigrella:
The ebony cup is a black, cup-shaped, hairy fungus that fruits in spring among moss in coniferous forests.
It is inedible.
pseudosperma-rimosum:
The straw-coloured fiber head ('Inocybe fastigiata') starts as an oval knob, then becomes bluntly conical with a straw-brown, fibrous cap and a dirty yellow, bulbous-based stem. It fruits in deciduous woods in spring to summer. It contains muscarine.
It is poisonous, causing sweating, excess salivation, tearing and slow pulse; do not eat it.
pseudosperma-sororium:
The corn-silk fiberhead is a small Pseudosperma with a corn-silk-coloured, fibrous cap. It contains muscarine.
It is poisonous; do not eat it.
psilocybe-allenii:
A Psilocybe described in 2012 that grows on wood chips and mulch on the Pacific coast.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-alutacea:
A psychoactive Psilocybe described in 2006.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-angulospora:
A psychoactive Psilocybe described from Taiwan.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-atlantis:
A rare Psilocybe containing psilocybin and psilocin.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-aucklandiae:
A psychoactive Psilocybe known from the Auckland Islands of New Zealand.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-aztecorum:
A psychoactive Psilocybe named after the Aztecs, known only from the mountains of central Mexico.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-azurescens:
The flying saucer (blue angel) mushroom grows on dune grass and wood chips on the coast of the Pacific Northwest, is regarded as one of the most potent Psilocybe species and turns deep blue when touched.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-baeocystis:
A Psilocybe of the Pacific Northwest containing psilocybin, psilocin and baeocystin, turning blue-green when touched.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-banderillensis:
A psychoactive Psilocybe known from Veracruz, Mexico.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-caeruleoannulata:
A psychoactive Psilocybe found in Uruguay and Brazil.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-caerulescens:
The landslide mushroom ('derrumbe' in Spanish) is a Psilocybe that fruits after landslides and on sugarcane debris and turns blue when touched.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-caerulipes:
Blue-foot is a rare Psilocybe on beech and birch wood in eastern North America whose stem turns blue.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-cubensis:
The magic mushroom (golden cap) grows on cattle and elephant dung in the tropics and subtropics, with a golden-brown cap that turns blue when touched, and is the world's best-known psychoactive mushroom. It takes its name from Cuba, where it was first found. It contains psilocybin and psilocin.
The effect of psilocybin in conditions such as depression is being studied in controlled clinical trials; this does not mean the mushroom can be tried on its own. It is illegal in many countries and carries risks of panic, psychosis and other serious health harms. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-cyanescens:
The wavy cap ('potent psilocybe') is a Psilocybe with a wavy edge, dark brown colour, fruiting in winter on wood chips and mulch and turning blue when touched. It occurs on the Pacific coast and in Europe.
It is potent, psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-cyanofibrillosa:
The rhododendron psilocybe is a Psilocybe with blue fibres found on wood chips and around rhododendrons on the Pacific coast.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-fagicola:
A psychoactive Psilocybe native to Mexico that grows on beech (Fagus) wood.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-fimetaria:
A dung-loving Psilocybe usually found on horse dung.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-galindoi:
A Psilocybe in the section Mexicana that contains psilocybin and psilocin.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-guilartensis:
A psychoactive Psilocybe containing psilocybin and psilocin.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-heimii:
A psychoactive Psilocybe described in 1978.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-hispanica:
A small, brown, conical-capped Psilocybe found at altitude in Spain.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-hoogshagenii:
A psychoactive Psilocybe with a brownish cap known from Mexico.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-laurae:
A psychoactive Psilocybe containing psilocybin.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-magnispora:
A psychoactive Psilocybe found in Thailand.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-makarorae:
A psychoactive Psilocybe native to New Zealand.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-medullosa:
A widespread but rather rare psychoactive Psilocybe in Europe.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-meridionalis:
A psychoactive Psilocybe containing psilocybin and psilocin.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-mescaleroensis:
A psychoactive Psilocybe containing psilocybin and psilocin.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-mexicana:
A Psilocybe known to have been used in rituals by the native peoples of Mexico for centuries ('teonanácatl'). In 1958 Albert Hofmann first isolated psilocybin from this mushroom.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-moseri:
A psychoactive Psilocybe containing psilocybin.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-muliercula:
A Psilocybe native to Mexico known for ritual use.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-neoxalapensis:
A psychoactive Psilocybe found in Veracruz, Mexico.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-ovoideocystidiata:
The 'river teacher' is a Psilocybe of riverbanks in eastern North America, growing on flood-deposited woody debris.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-papuana:
A psychoactive Psilocybe described in 1978 from Papua New Guinea.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-pelliculosa:
The conifer psilocybe is a small, brown Psilocybe of conifer forest beds in the Pacific Northwest.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-pseudoaztecorum:
A psychoactive Psilocybe described from Mexico.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-quebecensis:
A moderately active psychoactive Psilocybe treated as a synonym of P. aztecorum.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-samuiensis:
A psychoactive Psilocybe described from Koh Samui island in Thailand.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-semilanceata:
The liberty cap is recognised by its small, pointed, bell-shaped, yellowish-brown cap and is one of the most widespread psychoactive mushrooms, fruiting in autumn in unfertilised meadows and pastures in Europe. It contains psilocybin. Its English name comes from its resemblance to the Phrygian cap of the French Revolution.
It is psychoactive, illegal in many countries and carries serious health risks. Collecting it is also dangerous because small brown grass mushrooms can be confused with deadly Conocybe and Galerina species. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-serbica:
A Psilocybe named after Serbia containing psychoactive compounds.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-silvatica:
A Psilocybe in the section Semilanceatae that contains psilocybin.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-strictipes:
A psychoactive Psilocybe of lawns and meadows in cool temperate regions.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-stuntzii:
Stuntz's blue legs ('blue ringers') is a ringed, bluing Psilocybe of wood chips and urban areas in the Pacific Northwest.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-subaeruginosa:
A psychoactive Psilocybe described in 1927 and known from Australia.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-subcubensis:
A psychoactive Psilocybe resembling the Cuban magic mushroom (P. cubensis).
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-subtropicalis:
A subtropical Psilocybe containing psychoactive compounds.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-tampanensis:
A very rare Psilocybe first found in Tampa, Florida, that forms underground tuber-like sclerotia ('truffles').
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-weraroa:
A secotioid (closed-cap) Psilocybe endemic to New Zealand (formerly Weraroa novae-zelandiae).
It is regarded as psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-yungensis:
A psychoactive Psilocybe found in Mexico.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
psilocybe-zapotecorum:
A Psilocybe named after the Zapotec people that contains psilocybin and psilocin.
It is psychoactive and illegal in many countries. This is not consumption advice.
pulveroboletus-curtisii: Curtis's bolete is an edible bolete of eastern North America with powdery sulphur-yellow pores that turns blue when cut (formerly in Pulveroboletus).
pulveroboletus-ravenelii: Ravenel's bolete (powdery sulphur bolete) is an edible bolete in sulphur yellow that turns blue when cut, found in deciduous and coniferous forests.
pycnoporellus-fulgens:
A soft, orange, saprotrophic bracket fungus on conifers in Eurasia and North America.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
pycnoporus-cinnabarinus:
The cinnabar polypore is a bright red-orange bracket fungus on dead deciduous wood that causes white rot.
It is inedible.
ramaria-abietina:
The green-staining coral is a yellowish coral fungus of coniferous forests that stains green when touched.
It is inedible; bitter.
ramaria-araiospora:
The red coral is a red-orange branched coral fungus of North America.
It is regarded as edible; identify it carefully.
ramaria-aurea:
The golden coral is a golden-yellow branched coral fungus of North America and Europe that forms mycorrhizae with tree roots.
It is regarded as edible; it has look-alikes that can cause gastrointestinal upset.
ramaria-botrytis:
The clustered coral (pink-tipped coral) is a coral fungus branching from a thick white-cream stem with pink-purple-red tips, fruiting in deciduous woods in summer and autumn.
It is eaten young and well cooked; large amounts can cause gastrointestinal upset. Identification is essential to avoid confusion with poisonous pink-tipped coral look-alikes (such as R. formosa).
ramaria-botrytoides:
A pinkish-tipped coral fungus described by Charles Horton Peck.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
ramaria-flaccida:
A drooping, pale coral fungus first described by Fries as a Clavaria.
It is inedible.
ramaria-flava:
The yellow coral is a coral fungus of European forest floors recognised by a thick stem and yellow branches that reach upward, with a white base.
It is eaten in some districts, but it can cause gastrointestinal upset and similar corals are poisonous. Not recommended.
ramaria-formosa:
The pinkish coral (beautiful clavaria) is a coral fungus with salmon-pink branches and yellowish tips that fruits in beech and other deciduous woods in summer and autumn.
It is poisonous, causing severe diarrhoea and gastrointestinal poisoning. Because it can be confused with edible corals, do not eat it.
ramaria-magnipes:
A thick-stemmed coral fungus of western North American forests.
It is regarded as edible; identify it carefully.
ramaria-rasilispora:
The yellow coral is a yellow, branched coral fungus.
It is regarded as edible; it has look-alikes that can cause gastrointestinal upset.
ramaria-rubrievanescens:
The fading pink coral is a coral fungus whose pink tones fade with age.
It is regarded as edible; identify it carefully.
ramaria-rubripermanens:
A coral fungus described in 1973 whose red tones are permanent.
It is regarded as edible; identify it carefully.
ramaria-stricta:
The strict-branch coral is a bitter, upright-branched coral fungus on rotting wood.
It is inedible.
ramaria-subbotrytis:
A coral fungus resembling the clustered coral, with whitish branches and pink tips.
It is regarded as edible; identify it carefully so as not to confuse it with poisonous corals.
ramaria-vinosimaculans:
The wine-staining coral is a coral fungus that stains wine-red when touched.
It is regarded as edible; identify it carefully.
ramariopsis-kunzei: A white, fine-branched edible coral fungus, the type species of Ramariopsis.
resupinatus-applicatus:
The smoked oysterling is a tiny, grey-black, jelly-like mushroom on dead wood.
It is inedible.
retiboletus-griseus:
The gray bolete has a grey-brown cap and a net-patterned stem and grows in oak and pine woods of eastern North America.
It is regarded as edible.
rheubarbariboletus-armeniacus:
A small, apricot-yellow bolete native to Europe.
It is regarded as edible.
rhizopogon-luteolus:
The yellow false truffle is an underground fungus that forms mycorrhizae with pine roots and is used as a soil inoculant in agriculture and horticulture.
It is inedible.
rhizopogon-roseolus:
The false truffle (Japanese 'shōro') is a round, pinkish-white, potato-shaped fungus that grows underground or at the soil surface near pine roots and turns pink when cut.
When young and white inside it is collected in Japan as 'shōro' and eaten in soups.
rhizopogon-vulgaris:
An underground fungus forming mycorrhizae with pine roots and used as a soil inoculant in agriculture and horticulture.
It is regarded as edible but worthless.
rhodocollybia-butyracea:
The buttery collybia has a greasy, slippery, red-brown cap and grows in woods on leaf and needle litter in autumn.
It is regarded as edible; the flavour is not pleasant.
rhodocollybia-maculata:
The spotted toughshank is a bitter, cream-coloured mushroom that develops red-brown spots with age in woods.
It is inedible.
rhodonia-placenta:
The pink pancake crust is a pinkish, crust-like fungus that causes brown rot and is used in laboratories to test wood durability.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
rhodotus-palmatus:
The wrinkled peach is a rare mushroom with a pink-peach, net-wrinkled cap on old elm trunks.
It is inedible; bitter.
rickenella-fibula:
The orange moss navel is a bright orange mushroom only millimetres across found among moss.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
roridomyces-roridus:
The dripping bonnet is a tiny, translucent mushroom with a thin stem coated in a slimy layer, growing on deciduous woody debris.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
royoporus-badius:
The black-footed polypore (Picipes badius) is a glossy brown, black-stemmed, tough mushroom on deciduous branches.
It is inedible.
rubroboletus-dupainii:
Dupain's bolete is a bolete of warm, limy deciduous woods in Europe with red pores and flesh that turns blue when cut.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
rubroboletus-legaliae:
Le Gal's bolete (Boletus splendidus, B. satanoides) is a bolete of warm deciduous woods with a pink-red cap, red pores and flesh that turns blue when cut, resembling Satan's bolete.
It is poisonous and causes gastrointestinal poisoning. Do not eat it.
rubroboletus-lupinus:
The wolf bolete is a red-pored bolete of warm, limy woods in Europe.
Although sometimes called edible, it is not recommended because it resembles poisonous red-pored boletes.
rubroboletus-pulcherrimus:
The red-pored bolete (known as Boletus pulcherrimus until 2015) is a bolete of the Pacific Northwest of North America with red pores and flesh that turns blue when cut.
It is regarded as deadly poisonous; severe gastrointestinal and nervous-system symptoms and a death have been recorded. Do not eat it.
rubroboletus-rhodoxanthus:
The ruddy bolete is native to Europe, with red pores and a red-yellow net-patterned stem that turns blue when cut, found in warm, limy deciduous woods.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
rubroboletus-rubrosanguineus:
A bolete of European coniferous forests with red pores that turns blue when cut.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
rubroboletus-satanas:
Satan's bolete (devil's bolete) is a large, thick bolete with a pale grey-white cap, red pores and a red net-patterned stem that turns blue when cut. It fruits in summer and autumn in warm, limy deciduous woods (oak, beech). In Türkiye it occurs in many districts, especially in the Black Sea forests.
It is poisonous: raw or undercooked it causes severe nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. The flesh can smell foul and rotten. Although it resembles the edible cep (Boletus edulis), it differs by its red pores and by turning blue when cut.
In some sources the name 'ayı mantarı' is used for this species too; do not rely on that name.
russula-adusta:
The blackening brittlegill is a grey-brown Russula under pine whose flesh first reddens and then blackens when cut.
It is regarded as edible with a modest flavour.
russula-aeruginea:
The green brittlegill is a grass-green-capped Russula found in deciduous and coniferous woods, especially under birch.
It is regarded as edible with a modest flavour.
russula-albonigra:
The blackening russula is a whitish Russula whose flesh blackens directly when cut without reddening first.
It is regarded as edible.
russula-atropurpurea:
The purple brittlegill is a Russula with a dark wine-purple cap, almost black in the centre, found in woods.
It is regarded as edible but can be a little bitter.
russula-aurea:
The gilded brittlegill is a rare Russula with a golden-yellow-orange cap and a yellow stem and gills, fruiting in deciduous woods in summer and autumn.
It is regarded as edible and tasty.
russula-betularum:
The birch brittlegill is a small, very pale Russula under birch.
It is acrid and not eaten.
russula-brevipes:
The short-stemmed russula is a cream-white, thick-fleshed Russula with a short stout stem and a funnel-shaped cap in coniferous woods of North America and Eurasia.
It is regarded as edible although it can be quite acrid.
russula-caerulea:
The humpback brittlegill is a Russula with a pointed hump and a dark purple-brown cap growing under pine.
It is regarded as edible but can be acrid.
russula-claroflava:
The yellow russula is a Russula with a bright lemon-yellow cap and flesh that turns grey when cut, growing in damp places under birch and aspen.
It is regarded as edible and tasty.
russula-crustosa:
The crusty russula is a greenish-brown Russula with a cracked, crusty surface.
It is regarded as edible.
russula-cyanoxantha:
The charcoal burner is a Russula with a variable cap that can combine purple, green and grey. Its gills are flexible and slightly greasy and do not break easily, which separates it from other Russulas. It fruits in deciduous and coniferous woods in summer and autumn.
It is one of the tastiest and safest species of the genus; eat it well cooked.
russula-decolorans:
The graying russula is an orange-red-capped Russula of coniferous woods whose flesh turns grey when cut.
It is regarded as edible.
russula-delica:
The milk-white brittlegill is a large, white, funnel-shaped, firm-fleshed Russula in deciduous and coniferous woods in summer and autumn, also widely collected in Türkiye.
It is regarded as edible; it is sometimes slightly bitter, so cook it well.
russula-densifolia:
The crowded russula is a large Russula with very crowded gills that reddens and then blackens when cut.
Sources disagree: some regard it as edible, others list it as poisonous because it can cause stomach upset. It is not eaten raw.
russula-emetica:
The sickener is a Russula with a bright red cap, white gills and a very acrid, burning taste that fruits in damp coniferous woods and peat bogs in autumn.
Eaten raw it causes severe vomiting and diarrhoea; cooking may lessen the acridity but it is not recommended. That is why it is called the sickener.
russula-fellea:
The geranium-scented russula (bitter russula) is a straw-yellow, very bitter Russula under beech.
It is bitter and not eaten.
russula-foetens:
The stinking russula is a foul-smelling, sticky, dirty-yellow-brown-capped Russula with an acrid taste in deciduous and coniferous woods.
It is inedible.
russula-fragilis:
The fragile russula is a very brittle, small Russula with an acrid taste.
It is inedible.
russula-gracillima:
The slender brittlegill is a slim, pinkish-purple-capped, acrid Russula.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
russula-grata:
The bitter almond brittlegill is a Russula with a dirty yellow cap and a bitter-almond smell.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
russula-graveolens: An edible Russula of European woods.
russula-heterophylla:
The greasy green brittlegill is a tasty Russula with a green-grey cap and white, crowded gills.
It is regarded as edible.
russula-illota:
The freckled brittlegill is an inedible Russula found in deciduous and coniferous woods.
It is inedible.
russula-integra:
The entire russula is a Russula with a chestnut-brown cap and a nutty-sweet taste found in coniferous woods.
Edible and well liked.
russula-laeta:
A rare and endangered Russula described by Julius Schäffer in 1952.
It is regarded as edible; being rare, it is better left uncollected.
russula-nobilis:
The beechwood sickener is a red-pink-capped, very acrid and poisonous Russula of beech woods.
Do not eat it; it causes gastrointestinal poisoning.
russula-ochroleuca:
The ochre brittlegill is a common, pale-yellow-capped Russula in deciduous and coniferous woods.
It is regarded as edible but is acrid and of low value.
russula-olivacea: The olive russula is an edible, non-poisonous Russula that fruits in groups from June in deciduous and coniferous woods.
russula-paludosa:
The tall bog russula is a red-orange-capped, thick-fleshed edible Russula growing under pine with a nutty taste.
Edible and well liked.
russula-queletii:
The gooseberry (fruity) russula is a purple-brown-capped, fruity-smelling but acrid and inedible Russula growing under spruce.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
russula-risigallina:
A colour-changing Russula formerly known as R. chamaeleontina.
It is regarded as edible.
russula-rosea:
The rosy russula is a pink-red, firm-fleshed Russula of the north temperate zone.
It is regarded as edible although it can be slightly bitter.
russula-sanguinaria:
The bloody brittlegill is a blood-red-capped, acrid Russula under pine.
It is inedible.
russula-sardonia:
The primrose brittlegill is an acrid Russula with a purple-greenish cap and yellow gills, growing under pine.
It is inedible.
russula-turci:
The purple-plush brittlegill is a purple-brown edible Russula of coniferous woods with an iodine smell.
It is regarded as edible.
russula-vesca:
The bare-toothed russula (the flirt) has a pink-brown cap with the gill tips showing at the edge and grows in deciduous woods.
It is regarded as edible and tasty; cook it well.
russula-vinosa:
The graying olive brittlegill is a wine-red-capped Russula whose flesh darkens when cut.
It is regarded as edible.
russula-violeipes:
The velvet brittlegill is a yellow-green, violet-flushed Russula with a velvety stem surface.
It is regarded as edible.
russula-virescens:
The green cracking russula is a light-green, leathery-cracked-capped, white-gilled, thick-fleshed Russula that fruits in deciduous woods (oak, beech) in summer and autumn and is much sought after in Europe and Asia.
It is regarded as one of the tastiest of the genus, with a nutty, sweetish taste. It is easy to recognise and not bitter, so it is a reliable Russula; still, check the gills and stem base so as not to confuse it with the deadly Amanita phalloides (greenish cap, but with a ring and volva).
russula-xerampelina:
The shrimp russula has a wine-red to greenish cap, smells like shrimp or crab with age and browns when cut. It grows under pine.
It is regarded as edible and tasty; because of the smell it should be collected fresh and cooked quickly.
saproamanita-thiersii:
Thiers' lepidella is a white, scaly, saprotrophic mushroom of North American lawns.
It is regarded as poisonous; because it resembles white Amanitas, do not eat it.
sarcodon-imbricatus:
The shingled (scaly) hedgehog has a dark brown cap covered in large, overlapping, tile-like scales and spines underneath. It fruits in coniferous forests in autumn. It turns bitter with age.
Eaten when young and well cooked; dried, it can be bitter for some people and is parboiled before cooking.
sarcodon-leucopus:
A hard, bitter tooth fungus of Asia and Europe associated with pine and other trees.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
sarcodon-squamosus:
The scaly tooth is a brown-scaled mushroom with spines underneath that grows in woods.
It is regarded as edible when young; it can be bitter.
sarcomyxa-edulis: An edible ochre-brown mushroom with a gelatinous, slimy cap that grows in winter on deciduous trees (Sarcomyxa edulis).
sarcoscypha-austriaca:
The scarlet elfcup is a bright red, cup-shaped fungus on damp, mossy branches in late winter and spring.
It is regarded as edible but tasteless.
sarcoscypha-coccinea:
The scarlet elf cup is a vivid red, cup-shaped fungus on mossy branches and fallen sticks in damp woods in late winter and spring.
It is regarded as edible but tasteless; it is better known for its looks.
sarcoscypha-occidentalis:
The stalked scarlet cup forms small, red, stalked cups in damp woods of North America.
It is inedible.
sarcosoma-globosum:
The witches' cauldron is a rare black, gelatinous, cauldron-shaped fungus that fruits in coniferous forests in spring.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
sarcosphaera-coronaria:
The violet crown cup is at first a hollow ball, then splits open into a star or bowl shape, with a violet-pink inside and a dirty cream outside. It fruits in spring in coniferous forests on limy soils.
It is known to be deadly especially when eaten raw, yet it is eaten unknowingly in some regions. Never eat it.
schizophyllum-commune:
The split gill is one of the most widespread mushrooms in the world, a fan-shaped, hairy, whitish-grey, dry and tough fungus on dead wood whose gills split lengthwise.
It is eaten in tropical regions (Mexico, Thailand, India) but is tough and rubbery. In people with suppressed immunity it can cause respiratory and sinus infection. Most sources advise against eating it.
scleroderma-areolatum:
The leopard earthball is a poisonous fungus with a leopard-spotted, hard skin and a dark purple-black inside.
Do not eat it.
scleroderma-cepa:
The smooth (onion) earthball is a round, yellowish-brown, thick-skinned fungus with a purple-black inside.
It is poisonous and must not be confused with truffles or puffballs.
scleroderma-citrinum:
The common earthball ('pigskin poison puffball') is a round yellow-brown fungus with a thick, rough-scaled skin and a firm, purple-black, white-veined inside. It grows in woods on sandy soils, forming mycorrhizae with tree roots.
It is poisonous and causes gastrointestinal poisoning. It is dangerous because it is mistaken for truffles and puffballs; do not eat any 'puffball' whose inside is not pure white and homogeneous. The parasitic bolete (Pseudoboletus parasiticus) can also grow on it.
scleroderma-polyrhizum:
The star earthball (dead man's hand) is an earthball with a thick skin that opens into a star shape when dry, found in sandy places.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
scleroderma-verrucosum:
The scaly earthball is a small, coarsely scaled, brown earthball with a stalk.
It is inedible.
scutellinia-scutellata:
The eyelash pixie cup is a fungus of bright red, millimetre-sized cups fringed with black eyelashes that fruit in groups on rotting wood.
It is inedible; it is tiny.
serpula-lacrymans:
Dry rot is a fungus that rots timber in buildings, spreading in damp wood and potentially very destructive; it leaves 'weeping' droplets, hence its name.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
sparassis-crispa:
The cauliflower mushroom is a large, white-cream fungus of curly fronds that resembles lettuce or a bath sponge. It is usually 10–25 cm tall and 3–5 kg, with specimens of over 50 cm and 14–20 kg known. It lives as a parasite on roots of conifers, especially pine, and as a saprotroph on stumps; it occurs in the Mediterranean region.
A very tasty edible; its frills hold dust, so it must be washed well. It is fried fresh. It turns bitter when dried, so it is not suitable for drying but can be frozen.
sparassis-spathulata: The eastern cauliflower mushroom is a curly, beige-cream edible fungus at the base of deciduous trees in eastern North America.
spathularia-flavida:
The yellow earth tongue (fairy fan) is a small, yellow, fan-shaped fungus on mossy ground in coniferous forests.
It is regarded as edible but worthless.
spinellus-fusiger:
Bonnet mould is a parasitic mould with a strange appearance, covered in fine hairs, growing on mushrooms such as Mycena.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
spongipellis-pachyodon:
The spongy toothed polypore is a whitish, spongy-textured, toothed-surface fungus on deciduous wood.
It is inedible.
steccherinum-ochraceum:
The ochre spreading tooth is a pinkish-ochre, toothed-surface fungus spreading on dead deciduous wood.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
stereum-hirsutum:
The false turkey tail (hairy curtain crust) is a very common fungus forming orange-yellow, hairy, thin, zoned fans on dead deciduous wood.
It is inedible; thin and tough.
stereum-ostrea:
The golden curtain crust (false turkey-tail) is a thin, orange-golden, zoned fungus on dead wood.
It is inedible.
stereum-sanguinolentum:
The bleeding conk is a thin fungus on conifers that oozes red fluid when touched, causing red rot in wood.
It is inedible.
strobilomyces-strobilaceus:
The old man of the woods is a grey-black, cone-scaled bolete whose flesh turns first red and then black when cut, with a shaggy, net-patterned stem. It fruits in deciduous and coniferous woods in summer and autumn.
Edible; the taste is modest and it is cooked well. It turns black when cooked.
strobilurus-esculentus:
The spruce cone cap is a very common small mushroom on buried spruce cones in spring.
It is regarded as edible but of low value because it is so small.
strobilurus-tenacellus:
The pinecone cap is a small mushroom on buried pine cones in spring. The antifungal compound strobilurin was first discovered in this genus and inspired the strobilurin fungicides widely used in agriculture.
It is regarded as edible but is small.
strobilurus-trullisatus:
The Douglas-fir cone mushroom is a small mushroom native to North America on buried cones.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
stropharia-aeruginosa:
The blue-green stropharia (verdigris agaric) is a medium-sized mushroom with a bright blue-green, slimy cap found in woods and grassland; the colour fades with age.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
stropharia-caerulea:
The blue roundhead is a bluish-green, slimy-capped Stropharia found in woods.
It is inedible.
stropharia-coronilla:
The garland roundhead is a yellow-cream, short-stemmed mushroom with a distinct ring that grows on lawns and meadows.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
stropharia-hornemannii:
The luxuriant ringstalk is a large Stropharia with a hanging ring found in coniferous forests.
It is inedible.
stropharia-pseudocyanea:
The peppery roundhead is a Stropharia with a peppery taste in mossy woods.
It is inedible.
stropharia-rugosoannulata:
The wine cap (garden giant) is a large mushroom with a wine-red-brown cap and a wrinkled, star-shaped ring on the stem. It fruits on wood chips, mulch and in gardens in summer and autumn and is among the mushrooms easily grown in the garden.
It is eaten young, with a very pleasant, potato- or radish-like taste, and must be cooked well. Its smell and texture decline with age.
stropharia-semiglobata:
The hemispherical stropharia (dung roundhead) is a mushroom of dung with a hemispherical, yellow, sticky cap and a thin stem.
It is regarded as edible but worthless.
suillellus-luridus:
The lurid bolete has a brown-olive cap, orange-red pores and flesh that turns dark blue quickly when cut, with a net-patterned stem. It fruits in deciduous woods on limy soils in summer and autumn.
Edible when well cooked; it is poisonous raw or undercooked. Important: with alcohol it causes a severe reaction with palpitations, flushing and nausea. It can be confused with the poisonous devil's bolete and similar red-pored boletes.
suillellus-mendax:
A red-pored bolete of Europe associated with beech, oak and sweet chestnut.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
suillellus-queletii:
The deceiving bolete is an uncommon bolete resembling the lurid bolete and turning blue when cut.
It is regarded as edible when well cooked; it should not be eaten with alcohol and is poisonous raw.
suillus-acidus: An edible Suillus with a slimy cap that grows in pine forests, described by Charles Peck.
suillus-albidipes:
An edible Suillus native to North America that forms mycorrhizae with pines.
Eaten with the slimy skin peeled and well cooked.
suillus-americanus:
The American slippery cap is a bright yellow, red-brown-fibrilled, sticky Suillus growing under white pine in eastern North America.
Edible; the skin is peeled and it is cooked.
suillus-bellinii:
The champagne bolete is a pale cream-beige, slimy-capped Suillus growing under Mediterranean pines (especially maritime pine) and collected in Italy.
Edible; the slimy skin is peeled.
suillus-bovinus:
The Jersey cow mushroom (bovine bolete) is a bolete of pine forests with a pinkish-orange, slimy cap and wide, angular pores. It is widespread in Eurasia and grows together with fungi such as Gomphidius roseus.
Edible with a modest flavour; the skin is peeled and it is cooked well. It can upset people with sensitive stomachs.
suillus-bresadolae:
A rare European Suillus named after Bresadola.
It is regarded as edible.
suillus-brevipes:
The short-stemmed bolete is a short-thick-stemmed, slimy-capped Suillus growing under two-needle pines.
Edible; the skin is peeled and it is cooked.
suillus-caerulescens:
The Douglas-fir suillus (fat jack) is a Suillus growing under Douglas-fir in western North America.
It is regarded as edible.
suillus-cavipes:
The hollow foot is a Suillus under larch with a hollow stem and a hairy-scaly cap.
Edible; mild-flavoured.
suillus-collinitus:
The ringless yellow boletus is a ringless Suillus with a slimy, red-brown cap growing under Mediterranean pines.
Edible; the skin is peeled and it is cooked.
suillus-cothurnatus:
A Suillus species recorded in Malaysia, Brazil and North America.
It is regarded as edible.
suillus-decipiens:
A Suillus of eastern North American pine woods described by Charles Peck.
It is regarded as edible.
suillus-fuscotomentosus:
The poor man's slippery jack is a Suillus with a brown, hairy-scaly cap growing under pine.
Edible but not choice.
suillus-glandulosipes: An edible Suillus with glandular dots on the stem growing in pine forests.
suillus-granulatus:
The granulated bolete ('slippery jack') is a slimy, reddish-yellow-capped bolete of pine woods, especially pine plantations, whose pores weep milky droplets in wet weather. It fruits in late summer and autumn.
Edible; if the slimy skin is not peeled it can have a laxative effect. It is mild-flavoured.
suillus-grevillei:
The larch bolete (tamarack jack, Greville's bolete) is a bright yellow-orange, slimy-capped, ringed bolete growing under larch.
Edible; the skin is peeled and it is cooked.
suillus-intermedius:
The sour cap suillus is an edible Suillus under pine in North America.
The slimy skin is peeled and it is cooked.
suillus-lakei:
The matte Jack (Lake's bolete, western painted suillus) is a Suillus with a red-brown, scaly, dry-fibrous cap growing under Douglas-fir. It occurs in western North America and has also been recorded in Türkiye.
It is regarded as edible.
suillus-luteus:
The slippery jack is a bolete with a slimy, chocolate-brown cap, yellow pores and a ring on the stem whose underside is purple-tinged. It fruits in pine forests and pine plantations in late summer and autumn and has spread worldwide with pine plantings.
Edible; the slimy skin must be peeled and it must be cooked well (unpeeled, it can cause stomach upset). Its flavour is mild; it can be dried.
suillus-mediterraneensis: An edible, pale-coloured Suillus growing under Mediterranean pines.
suillus-neoalbidipes: An edible Suillus associated with pines, described as a new species.
suillus-ochraceoroseus:
The rosey larch bolete is a pink-ochre-toned Suillus growing under larch.
It is regarded as edible.
suillus-placidus: The white suillus is a cream-white edible bolete growing under five-needle pines.
suillus-plorans: An edible Suillus described as Boletus plorans that grows under five-needle pines such as the Swiss stone pine.
suillus-pseudobrevipes: The veiled short-stemmed slippery jack is an edible Suillus under pine in North America.
suillus-punctipes:
The spicy suillus is a dry, spicy-smelling Suillus under conifers.
It is regarded as edible.
suillus-pungens:
The pungent slippery jack is a slimy, sharp-smelling Suillus under California pines.
Edible; the skin is peeled and it is cooked.
suillus-salmonicolor:
The slippery Jill is a salmon-coloured Suillus under pine.
It is regarded as edible; the skin is peeled.
suillus-serotinus: A late-season edible Suillus of eastern North America.
suillus-sibiricus:
The chicken fat suillus is a Suillus with a greasy yellow-orange look growing under Siberian pine.
It is regarded as edible.
suillus-spraguei:
The painted slipperycap is a striking, multicoloured Suillus with red scales growing under white pine; it is common in eastern North America.
Edible with a mild taste; the skin is peeled and it is cooked.
suillus-subaureus:
A rare golden-yellow-toned Suillus of North America.
It is regarded as edible.
suillus-subluteus: An edible Suillus under pine, described by Charles Peck as Boletus subluteus.
suillus-tomentosus:
The blue-staining slippery jack is an orange-yellow, hairy-capped Suillus whose pores turn blue-green when touched, growing under pine.
Edible; the skin is peeled and it is cooked well.
suillus-tridentinus: The orange larch bolete is an uncommon, orange-red, edible bolete under larch in the Alps.
suillus-variegatus:
The velvet bolete is a velvety, yellowish-brown, mottled-capped bolete growing under pine that turns blue when cut. It is common in Eurasian pine forests.
Edible with a modest flavour; it is not slimy and is cooked well.
suillus-viscidus: The sticky bolete is an uncommon, sticky, grey-cream-capped edible bolete under larch.
sutorius-eximius:
The lilac-brown bolete is a dark purple-brown, dusty-capped bolete of eastern North America.
It is regarded as edible.
tapinella-atrotomentosa:
The velvet roll-rim is a mushroom on coniferous stumps with a dark brown-black velvety stem and an inrolled cap margin. It is bitter.
It is inedible.
tapinella-panuoides:
The oyster rollrim (fan pax) is a yellow-brown, fan-shaped mushroom on worked coniferous wood and timber. It was formerly regarded as edible; since it is known to cause an immune reaction similar to Paxillus involutus it is now regarded as poisonous.
Do not eat it.
tarzetta-cupularis:
The elf cup is a small, light brown, cup-shaped fungus on soil.
It is inedible.
terana-caerulea:
The cobalt crust fungus forms a vivid cobalt-blue, velvety crust on deciduous wood.
It is inedible.
termitomyces-heimii:
A valued edible mushroom that lives in partnership with termites and fruits from termite mounds in Africa and Asia.
It is eaten cooked.
termitomyces-titanicus:
The giant termite mushroom (chi-ngulu-ngulu) fruits from termite mounds in Zambia and is among the largest cap mushrooms in the world, with a cap that can reach 1 m.
It is eaten by local people.
termitomyces-tylerianus: An edible termite mushroom that fruits from termite mounds in Africa and China.
termitomyces-umkowaan: An edible termite mushroom that fruits from termite mounds in South Africa.
thelephora-anthocephala:
A coral-like, leafy mushroom on the forest floor.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
thelephora-ganbajun:
Ganba fungus (干巴菌) is a very valued, grey-brown, coral-shaped mushroom of pine forests in Yunnan, China, stir-fried with onion and chilli in local cooking.
Edible.
thelephora-palmata:
The fetid false coral (stinking earthfan) is a purple-brown, branched mushroom of the forest floor with a foul, garlic-like smell.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
thelephora-penicillata:
The urchin earthfan is a brush-shaped, mycorrhizal mushroom of woods.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
thelephora-terrestris:
The common fiber vase (earthfan) is a brown, fibrous, fan-shaped fungus on soil near young conifers.
It is inedible.
trametes-betulina:
The gilled polypore is a zoned, half-moon-shaped bracket with gill-like structures on dead deciduous wood.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
trametes-gibbosa:
The lumpy bracket is a cream-white, humped bracket fungus on deciduous trees that causes white rot.
When very young it is regarded as edible but it is tough.
trametes-hirsuta:
The hairy turkey tail is a hairy, grey-cream-zoned, tough mushroom on dead wood.
It is inedible.
trametes-ochracea:
The ochre bracket is a turkey-tail-like mushroom on dead wood in North America and Europe, though less common.
It is inedible.
trametes-pubescens:
A small, thin, cream-coloured, finely velvety bracket fungus.
It is inedible.
trametes-suaveolens:
The fragrant bracket is a white bracket fungus with an aniseed smell on willow, poplar and similar trees.
It is inedible.
trametes-trogii:
A hairy, tough bracket fungus on dead deciduous wood, almost worldwide.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
trametes-versicolor:
The turkey tail is a very common bracket fungus worldwide that grows on dead wood in multi-coloured, thin, concentrically zoned fan-shaped shelves and can be seen all year.
It is too tough to eat; it is used as a tea and extract. Its polysaccharides (especially PSK and PSP) are being researched and are used in Japan as an adjunct in some cancer treatments, but it is not a treatment on its own.
tremella-aurantia:
The golden ear is a bright yellow-orange, leafy, gelatinous fungus that lives as a parasite on Stereum hirsutum.
It is regarded as edible but bland.
tremella-encephala:
A pink, brain-shaped, gelatinous fungus that lives on Stereum sanguinolentum.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
tremella-foliacea:
The leafy brain is a brown-red, leafy, gelatinous fungus on deciduous trees.
It is regarded as edible but has no taste.
tremella-fuciformis:
The snow fungus (silver ear) is a white, translucent, leafy, gelatinous fungus widely used in China in sweet soups, desserts and cosmetics and grown on a large scale. It grows on dead deciduous wood.
It is dried and soaked to swell before eating, with a bland taste. Health benefits are traditionally claimed but are not sufficiently proven.
tremella-mesenterica:
Witch's butter (yellow brain) is a bright yellow, jelly-like fungus on dead deciduous wood that lives as a parasite on crust fungi such as Peniophora. It shrinks when dry and swells again in rain.
It is regarded as edible; it is bland and jelly-like.
trichaptum-abietinum:
A thin, purple-edged bracket fungus with toothed pores on dead conifer wood.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
trichaptum-biforme:
The violet-pored bracket is a hairy-surfaced bracket fungus with purple pores on dead deciduous wood.
It is inedible.
trichoglossum-hirsutum:
The hairy earth-tongue is a black, velvety, tongue-shaped fungus of meadows and damp woods.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
trichoglossum-walteri:
Walter's earth tongue is a black, tongue-shaped fungus of meadows.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
tricholoma-acerbum:
The bitter knight is a large, yellow-cream, thick-fleshed, flour-scented, bitter Tricholoma with an inrolled margin, found in deciduous woods in autumn.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
tricholoma-album:
The white knight is an all-white, bitter Tricholoma under birch.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
tricholoma-argyraceum:
A grey-capped Tricholoma often confused with T. scalpturatum.
It is regarded as edible, but this genus has many poisonous species; not recommended.
tricholoma-arvernense:
A Tricholoma described as a variety of T. sulphureum, found in coniferous woods.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
tricholoma-atrosquamosum:
The dark-scaled knight is a Tricholoma with a grey, dark-scaled cap that fruits in deciduous and coniferous woods in autumn.
It is regarded as edible; however, since this genus has many poisonous and bitter species it must be identified carefully.
tricholoma-bakamatsutake: Bakamatsutake ('fool's matsutake') is an edible Tricholoma resembling the matsutake in Japan but less valued.
tricholoma-caligatum:
The false matsutake is a large, brown-scaled Tricholoma with a ring on the stem and a strong, fruity-spicy smell, forming mycorrhizae with various trees around the Mediterranean and fruiting in autumn.
It is regarded as edible; its taste and smell are too strong for some people.
tricholoma-cingulatum:
The girdled knight is a Tricholoma with a grey, scaly cap and a ring on the stem growing under willow, first described in 1830.
It is regarded as edible; identify it carefully.
tricholoma-columbetta:
The dove-coloured tricholoma is a white-grey, silky-capped edible Tricholoma that fruits in deciduous woods in autumn.
It is regarded as edible; it can be confused with similar poisonous Tricholoma species.
tricholoma-equestre:
The man on horseback is a lemon-to-greenish-yellow, slimy-capped Tricholoma with yellow gills that fruits in pine woods on sandy soils in autumn. It was formerly collected in Europe as a good edible.
Warning: in the 1990s in France it was found to cause serious muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) and deaths after being eaten, so it is regarded as poisonous. It can occur even in people who have eaten it many times. Do not eat it.
tricholoma-fulvum:
The birch knight is a rust-brown, sticky-capped Tricholoma under birch.
One guide reports it as inedible and possibly bitter.
tricholoma-imbricatum:
The matt knight is a brown, scaly-capped Tricholoma under pine.
It is regarded as edible but can be bitter.
tricholoma-inamoenum:
The irksome cavalier is a pale Tricholoma with a bad, gas-like smell found in coniferous forests.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
tricholoma-magnivelare:
The white matsutake (pine mushroom) is a close relative of the matsutake that grows in pine forests of North America. It is white, thick and sturdy, with a distinctive spicy-cinnamon smell, and is exported to Japan.
Edible and highly valued. Mistaking the poisonous Amanita smithiana for it has caused serious poisonings.
tricholoma-matsutake:
The matsutake (松茸) is one of the most valued mushrooms in Japan; it grows on roots of pine trees in Asia, Europe and North America and cannot be cultivated. It is known for its thick, sturdy, white-brown body and spicy-cinnamon smell. It is used in rice, soup and grilled dishes in Japanese cooking and sells at very high prices.
Edible.
tricholoma-murrillianum: A matsutake-like edible Tricholoma found in North America.
tricholoma-orirubens: The blushing tricholoma is an edible mushroom of deciduous and coniferous woods whose gills redden with age.
tricholoma-pardinum:
The tiger tricholoma (spotted tricholoma) is a large, thick-fleshed, grey-brown-scaled, flour-scented Tricholoma that fruits in mountain forests on limy soils in autumn.
It is poisonous, causing severe gastrointestinal poisoning (vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain) that may require hospital admission. It is confused with the edible grey knight (T. terreum).
tricholoma-pessundatum:
A brown, slimy-capped Tricholoma under pine.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
tricholoma-portentosum:
The charbonnier (streaked tricholoma) is a Tricholoma with a grey-blackish, radially streaked cap and yellowish gills that fruits in pine forests in late autumn.
Edible and well liked; cook it well.
tricholoma-resplendens:
A white, silky-capped Tricholoma of Europe and North America.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
tricholoma-robustum: A thick-fleshed, edible mycorrhizal Tricholoma resembling the matsutake in Japan.
tricholoma-saponaceum:
The soap-scented toadstool is a fleshy Tricholoma with a soapy smell and a greenish-grey cap whose flesh turns pink when cut. It fruits in coniferous and deciduous woods in autumn.
It is regarded as poisonous and causes gastrointestinal upset. Do not eat it.
tricholoma-scalpturatum:
The yellowing knight is a common grey-capped Tricholoma that yellows with age.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
tricholoma-sejunctum:
The deceiving knight is a greenish-yellow-capped Tricholoma found in woods.
It is inedible; bitter.
tricholoma-sulphureum:
The stinker (sulphur knight, gas agaric) is a sulphur-yellow, thick-fleshed Tricholoma that is easily recognised by its smell of coal gas or tar. It fruits in oak and beech woods in late summer and autumn.
It is regarded as poisonous and causes gastrointestinal poisoning. Do not eat it.
tricholoma-terraria:
