The grey knight (dirty tricholoma) is a grey, fibrous-capped Tricholoma that fruits in pine forests in autumn and is collected and eaten in France and Spain.
Although regarded as edible, confusing it with the very similar, poisonous tiger tricholoma (T. pardinum) is dangerous; they differ in smell and size.
tricholoma-ustale:
The burnt knight is a red-brown, sticky-capped Tricholoma of beech woods and is very bitter.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
tricholoma-vaccinum:
The russet scaly tricholoma (scaly knight) is a red-brown, woolly-scaled Tricholoma growing under spruce.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
tricholoma-venenatum:
A poisonous Tricholoma described by an American mycologist.
Do not eat it.
tricholoma-virgatum:
The ashen knight is a grey, pointed-capped Tricholoma under pine and spruce with an acrid, bitter taste.
It is inedible.
tricholomopsis-decora:
Prunes and custard is a yellow mushroom with a brown-black scaly cap on rotting conifer stumps.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
tricholomopsis-rutilans:
Plums and custard (red-haired agaric) is a mushroom with a purple-red, hairy cap and yellow gills on coniferous stumps.
It is regarded as edible but bitter and worthless.
tubaria-conspersa:
The felted twiglet is a small brown mushroom on dead twigs and woody debris.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
tubaria-furfuracea:
The scurfy twiglet is a small, brown, scurfy mushroom on dead twigs and woody debris.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
tuber-aestivum:
The summer truffle (Burgundy truffle) is a black-skinned truffle with a cream-brown inside that grows underground on beech, oak and hazel roots and is harvested in summer and autumn.
Edible and valued; it is sliced thinly over dishes.
tuber-borchii:
The whitish truffle (bianchetto) is a small, common edible truffle harvested in late winter and spring.
Edible.
tuber-brumale:
The muscat (winter) truffle is a black-skinned, musk-scented truffle native to southern Europe, harvested in winter.
It is regarded as edible; its smell is pungent.
tuber-gibbosum:
The Oregon white truffle is a valued truffle that grows under Douglas-fir in the Pacific Northwest.
Edible.
tuber-indicum: The Chinese (Asian) black truffle is an edible truffle of China and India resembling the European black truffle but with a weaker aroma.
tuber-lyonii: The American brown (pecan) truffle is an edible brown truffle that grows under oak, hickory and pecan in eastern North America.
tuber-macrosporum:
The smooth black truffle is a valued, dark-skinned, garlic-scented truffle of Europe.
Edible.
tuber-magnatum:
The Italian white truffle (Alba white truffle) is one of the most expensive mushrooms in the world. It grows in northern Italy, especially in Piedmont, on riverside roots of poplar, oak and willow. It is found in autumn with trained dogs and cannot be cultivated. It has a strong garlic-and-cheese aroma.
Edible; it is sliced raw over hot dishes.
tuber-melanosporum:
The black truffle (Périgord truffle, in Turkish 'trüf' or 'domalan') is one of the world's most valuable mushrooms and gave its name to France's Périgord region. It grows underground, about 50 cm deep, near roots of oak, hazel and chestnut on limy soils, and is found in winter with dogs or pigs. It has a dark, warty outside and a black, white-veined inside. It lives by taking sugars and organic acids from tree roots.
With its very intense earthy, chocolate-like aroma it is added raw or lightly warmed to dishes. It also occurs in Türkiye and is known as trüf or domalan. It is cultivated in nurseries with inoculated trees.
tuber-microspermum: An edible truffle species described as new to science in 2012.
tuber-microspiculatum: An edible truffle species found in China.
tuber-oregonense: The Oregon white truffle is a valued edible truffle that grows on conifer roots in the Pacific Northwest.
turbinellus-kauffmanii:
The scaly vase false chanterelle is a scaly, funnel-shaped, orange-brown mushroom of coniferous forests.
It is regarded as poisonous and causes gastrointestinal poisoning.
tylopilus-alboater:
The black velvet bolete has a dark grey-black, velvety cap and white pores that turn reddish-black when touched. It grows in deciduous woods in eastern North America.
It is regarded as edible and mild-flavoured.
tylopilus-badiceps:
A bolete native to North America with a red-brown cap.
It is regarded as edible; most Tylopilus are bitter.
tylopilus-felleus:
The bitter bolete looks very much like the cep but has pink pores, a dark net pattern and an intensely bitter taste. It fruits in coniferous forests in summer and autumn.
It is not poisonous but even one piece ruins an entire dish; it is not eaten. If mistaken for the cep it spoils the meal; its pink pores separate it.
tylopilus-ferrugineus:
The rusty bolete is a North American bolete with a rusty-brown cap.
It is regarded as edible.
tylopilus-indecisus:
The indecisive bolete is a brown-capped bolete native to North America.
It is regarded as edible.
tylopilus-rhoadsiae:
The pale bitter bolete is a pale, slightly bitter bolete of North America.
It is regarded as edible.
tylopilus-rubrobrunneus:
The reddish brown bitter bolete is a red-brown-capped, bitter bolete of North America.
Although called edible, it is bitter and not recommended.
tylopilus-variobrunneus:
A brown-toned bolete native to the United States.
It is regarded as edible.
tyromyces-chioneus:
The white cheese polypore is a white, soft, scented bracket fungus on dead deciduous trees.
It is inedible.
urnula-craterium:
The devil's urn is a dark brown-black, hairy, urn-shaped fungus that appears in early spring on dead deciduous wood.
It is inedible.
ustilago-maydis:
Corn smut (huitlacoche, the 'Mexican truffle') is a parasitic fungus that swells corn ears into grey-blue, bulging galls. It is a disease of corn, but in Mexico it is collected young and used as a prized ingredient; its taste is earthy, mushroomy and slightly sweet.
Edible.
verpa-bohemica:
The early morel is a spring mushroom with a wrinkled, brown cap attached only at the top of the stem, resembling a morel; the stem is cottony-hollow.
In some people, especially when eaten in large amounts or repeatedly, it can cause nervous system effects (dizziness, impaired coordination); it is poisonous raw. It may be eaten only well cooked and in small amounts; not recommended.
verpa-conica:
The bell morel is a spring mushroom of riverbanks under poplar and ash, with a bell-shaped, brown cap attached to the stem only at the top.
Edible when well cooked; like the early morel (Verpa bohemica) it can cause complaints in some people.
volvariella-bombycina:
The silky volvariella is a rare white-cream, silky, hairy-capped mushroom with a sac-like volva at the base that grows on trunks and wounds of old deciduous trees.
It is regarded as edible; because of the volva it must be identified carefully so as not to confuse it with deadly Amanitas. Its spore print is pink.
volvariella-surrecta:
The piggyback rosegill is a white, volva-bearing mushroom growing on decaying Clitocybe nebularis.
It is inedible.
volvopluteus-gloiocephalus:
The big sheath mushroom is a white, slimy-capped mushroom with a distinct sac-like volva at the base and a pink spore print, growing on wood chips, mulch and in gardens.
Although regarded as edible, because of the volva it can be confused with deadly white Amanitas; the spore print must be pink. Do not eat it.
wynnea-americana:
Moose antlers (rabbit ears) is a dark brown, ear- or antler-shaped cup fungus that emerges from the soil.
It is inedible.
xanthoconium-affine: An edible, brown-capped bolete of eastern North American deciduous woods, first described as a Boletus.
xanthoconium-separans: An edible bolete of eastern North America resembling the cep.
xerocomellus-chrysenteron:
The cracked cap bolete is a brown, velvety bolete whose cap surface cracks to reveal red tissue underneath. It is very common in deciduous and coniferous woods in summer and autumn. The pores are yellow and turn blue-green when touched.
It is regarded as edible; its flavour is modest and its texture soft, so young, sound specimens are preferred.
xerocomellus-dryophilus: The oak-loving bolete is an edible, brown, cracked-cap bolete under oak in North America.
xerocomellus-porosporus:
The sepia bolete is a small, brown, cracking-capped bolete with yellow pores.
It is regarded as edible.
xerocomellus-pruinatus:
The matte bolete is a dark reddish-brown, matt-capped bolete of deciduous woods.
It is regarded as edible.
xerocomellus-zelleri:
Zeller's bolete is a bolete of western North America with a dark brown-black cap and red edges.
It is regarded as edible.
xerocomus-illudens:
A yellow-pored bolete of eastern North America described in 1898.
It is regarded as edible.
xerocomus-silwoodensis:
A bolete described in 2007 that forms mycorrhizae with tree roots.
It is regarded as poisonous; do not eat it.
xerocomus-subtomentosus:
The suede bolete has an olive-brown, velvety cap and yellow pores that do not blue or only slightly. It is common in deciduous and coniferous woods in summer and autumn.
Edible; its flavour is mild and its texture soft. A parasitic mould (Hypomyces chrysospermus) can grow on it; do not eat such specimens.
xeromphalina-campanella:
The pinewood gingertail (golden trumpets) is a very common, small mushroom whose hundreds of small orange-yellow caps fruit in groups on rotting conifer stumps.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
xeromphalina-cauticinalis:
A small orange-brown mushroom of forest litter.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
xeromphalina-kauffmanii:
A small brown-yellow mushroom on rotting wood in North America.
It is inedible and regarded as poisonous.
xylaria-hypoxylon:
The candlestick fungus is a black, velvety-based, white-powdered-tipped, antler-shaped, bioluminescent fungus on dead wood that can be seen all year.
It is inedible; hard and woody.
xylaria-longipes:
Dead moll's fingers is a hard, black, finger-like fungus on dead deciduous wood.
It is inedible.
xylaria-polymorpha:
Dead man's fingers is a hard, black, thick, finger- or club-shaped fungus at the base of stumps and dead wood. It is common worldwide and causes slow rot.
It is inedible; very hard.
